articles.title: What Russia Is Really Up To in Europe
articles.body:
What Russia Is Really Up To in Europe
Moscow doesn’t want a conventional war, but it is busy fighting a hybrid one.
On Russian state television, the Kremlin’s propagandists have for years threatened to bomb European capitals, even while the country’s diplomats insist that no such war is imminent. Lately, the denials have gotten hard to sustain, as European intelligence agencies have ascribed hundreds of clandestine sabotage operations—cyberattacks in Italy, arson in the United Kingdom, undersea-cable ruptures in the Baltic, severed pig heads left outside French mosques—to Russia.
U.S. intelligence assessments conclude that a conventional Russian attack on a NATO country is likely to happen sometime from this fall to 2029. But another possibility is that Moscow will remain content with sabotage and intimidation. This hybrid campaign is all the war Russia wants or needs—and stoking fear that Moscow just might directly strike Ukraine’s European allies is part of it.
If this is what Russian President Vladimir Putin is really up to in Europe, then he was telling the truth when he assured Trump this week that Russia has “no aggressive intentions against European statehood.” Moscow has not massed troops on any NATO member’s border. Rather, it has been sending a carefully calibrated message meant to persuade Europe to stop supporting Ukraine.
For Moscow, this has been a summer of setbacks in Ukraine. Russia stalled on the battlefield and sustained damage from thousands of Ukrainian long-range drones that plunged the country into fuel shortages. And so it escalated elsewhere in Europe: Fires broke out at ammunition plants in Italy, Bulgaria, and Estonia last month, and explosive-laden drones were discovered near a German power plant and at an airport in Leipzig, apparently intended to destroy Ukrainian cargo planes.
From the Kremlin’s point of view, Europe has been deepening its involvement in Ukraine. At the beginning of the full-scale war, Europe donated weapons to Ukraine from its own stocks. Within two years, European governments were paying Ukrainian factories to manufacture arms. Last year, Fire Point, a Ukrainian missile-and-drone manufacturer, announced that it would establish a solid-fuel production plant in Denmark, making it the first such arms company to expand production abroad. Today, Europe provides the bulk of financial assistance to Kyiv. It has also become Ukraine’s secure production base—Ukrainian weapons are manufactured in Germany, Britain, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, France, Romania, and Spain.
Because Kyiv is attacking Russia’s rear, it’s logical to worry that Moscow will attack Ukraine’s. Russian security services are almost certainly capable of carrying out a lethal attack on European soil. And Western war games have entertained many possibilities along those lines. Among them are a limited Russian incursion into a small Baltic town that has a Russian-speaking population; a full-scale invasion of the Baltic states, launched simultaneously from Belarus and Kaliningrad, Russia’s European exclave, to cut them off from the rest of Europe; the rapid creation of an impenetrable drone “kill zone” on European soil; and a strategic blockade of the Baltic Sea. Some of these scenarios are plausible; others would require hundreds of thousands of Russian troops to crisscross Europe.
Russia has not visibly prepared for any such scenario, however. Instead, it continues to wage its hybrid war—which European security services continue to thwart. Such are the headlines: Drones carrying explosives are discovered in Leipzig, improvised explosive devices are found near a German power plant, and flying objects are spotted near airports.
Moscow may not much care that these operations get foiled. In a way, the effect is similar to that of Russia’s harassment of journalists and embassy workers stationed in Moscow: Things in their apartment get rearranged, signs of eavesdropping are deliberately made obvious, or a window is left open in the middle of winter. Such interference conveys a sinister message: We’re watching you. We have access to you. You are not in control. But it’s still different from blowing up the apartment.
Putin has generally chosen to fully engage the Russian military only in conflicts that he feels (rightly or, in the case of Ukraine, wrongly) assured of winning. This does not describe any hypothetical attack on the Baltic states, which have heavily fortified borders, conduct regular military exercises, and spend 5 percent of their GDP on defense.
That’s not to mention the thousands of British, German, and Canadian troops stationed near the Baltics as part of NATO’s Enhanced Forward Presence. Moscow may be willing to wager that the United States won’t intervene should Russia attack Estonia. But Russia would then find itself at war with numerous European states armed with submarines, aircraft carriers, fifth-generation fighter jets, long-range cruise missiles, and even nuclear weapons—all while it was still fighting in Ukraine.
Russia’s hybrid war has not succeeded in its likely purpose: stopping weapons, money, and intelligence from flowing into Ukraine from Europe. Kyiv has more arms, funds, and—judging by its strikes on Russian soil—intelligence than ever before. Neither has the Russian campaign taken out a European satellite that supplies Ukraine with intelligence, say, or destroyed a shipment of Patriot missiles.
But Putin persists in this campaign for a reason. Through inexpensive means, expendable operatives, and a steady stream of chilling leaks, the Kremlin has millions of Westerners braced for it to wage a full-scale war against Europe. Regardless of whether that war is likely, Putin will be demanding concessions in exchange for bringing it to an end.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Russia's recruitment of foreign nationals 'amounts to human trafficking'
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Russia's recruitment of foreign nationals 'amounts to human trafficking'
Key developments on Sept. 10:
- Russia's recruitment of foreign nationals amounts to human trafficking, Amnesty International says
- US destroys 5 Iranian oil tankers, 3 linked to Russia's shadow fleet, Ukrainian official says
- NATO allies disrupt Russian exercise involving secret weapon targeting subsea cables, Reuters reports
- 4 dead after Russian attack on Pavlohrad shopping center
- Russian drone attacks hit Kyiv morning and evening, injuring 4
Russia exploits and deceives foreign nationals to enlist them in its armed forces and send them to fight in Ukraine, and in many cases these practices amount to human trafficking, the human rights organization Amnesty International said in a report published Sept. 10.
Russia primarily targets people from low-income countries in the Global South, the report said. Russian recruiters lure people from abroad under false pretenses and exploit the precarious situation of migrants in Russia by weaponizing overstayed work visas or supposed criminal offenses and offering military service as an alternative to detention or deportation, it added.
"Once victims sign the paperwork, often in a language they do not understand, military commanders restrict their movements, deploy them to the front lines with minimal preparation, and threaten those who seek a way out," the report stated.
The Russian army misrepresents the nature of the work and the risks involved to these foreign nationals as a key tactic to recruit them, according to Amnesty International. Russian recruiters also offer lucrative payments and pathways to Russian citizenship as incentives that rarely are fulfilled, the report said.
Many foreign recruits lack any kind of military training and get deployed to active combat zones after just two weeks of training, in what Amnesty International called "an apparent disregard for human life."
Two Sri Lankan nationals interviewed in the report said they were led to believe they would be working as cooks but were sent to fight on the front lines and captured within weeks by Ukrainian forces. "The scale of fighting is unimaginable. You do not see Ukrainian soldiers, only drones. Drones everywhere," one said.
"I would never go back there."
read also
US destroys 5 Iranian oil tankers, 3 linked to Russia's shadow fleet, Ukrainian official says
The U.S. military destroyed five Iranian crude oil tankers on Sept. 8, three of which have ties to Russia's shadow fleet, Ukraine's sanctions commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk said in a comment shared with the Kyiv Independent.
U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) on Sept. 9 said its forces struck the five vessels in response to attempts by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) to target a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles.
The five vessels were the Kaviz, Charminar, Horizon 1 and Riesco in the Gulf of Oman, as well as the Derya near Iran's Kharg Island. U.S. forces instructed the crews to abandon the vessels before striking them, CENTCOM said.
Three of the tankers, the Kaviz, Charminar, and Riesco, have direct links to Russia's shadow fleet and have been involved in transporting Russian oil, Vlasiuk said.
The Kaviz had called at the Russian ports of Ust-Luga and Novorossiysk and transported Russian oil, according to Vlasiuk. He added that the vessel had repeatedly switched off its Automatic Identification System (AIS), which ships use to broadcast information including their location and identity.
According to Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR), the Kaviz was previously affiliated with Fractal Marine DMCC, a company sanctioned by the U.K. for servicing Russia's energy sector and identified by HUR as a key operator of Russia's shadow fleet. HUR also lists the tanker as sanctioned by the U.S., Ukraine, the EU, Switzerland, the U.K. and Canada.
The Charminar had previously called at the Russian ports of Ust-Luga, Primorsk, Vysotsk and St. Petersburg, Vlasiuk said.
read also
NATO allies disrupt Russian exercise involving secret weapon targeting subsea cables, Reuters reports
NATO allies disrupted a covert Russian naval exercise near Norway's Svalbard archipelago involving technology designed to disable critical subsea cables without leaving a trace, Reuters reported on Sept. 10, citing Western officials.
The operation was carried out by Russia's Main Directorate for Deep Sea Research (GUGI), which used deep-sea submersibles to simulate deploying the technology, according to two Western officials who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity.
Britain, Norway, and the United States tracked and confronted the Russian vessels at sea, preventing them from completing the exercise before they eventually left the area, the officials said.
No subsea cables were damaged during the operation. The exercise focused on simulating how the technology could be used in the event of a conflict with NATO, while officials declined to explain how the system works.
"Through our joint operation, we sent a clear message to Russia that they cannot operate covertly," Norwegian Defense Minister Tore Sandvik said in a statement to Reuters.
"We have made it unequivocally clear to Russian authorities that any attempt to target our critical infrastructure will be detected and met with consequences," he added.
The operation took place near Svalbard, where two roughly 1,400-kilometer-long (870 miles) fiber-optic cables connect the Arctic archipelago with mainland Norway. The cables carry satellite data from the SvalSat ground station, which is part of NASA's Near Space Network.
Undersea sabotage has climbed up the political agenda across Europe with instances of damage to subsea cables and Russian vessels lurking near critical underwater infrastructure on an increasingly frequent basis since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
In April 2026, the U.K. said it had intercepted a Russian operation near critical underwater infrastructure in British waters. A Russian attack submarine entered U.K. waters while other vessels linked to GUGI were detected conducting what the British government described as "nefarious activity" over critical undersea infrastructure.
Between 2024 and 2026, more than 20 subsea cables in the Baltic and Arctic regions were damaged, though many of the incidents have not been formally attributed to Russia.
NATO has since stepped up patrols and monitoring around critical underwater infrastructure, including through missions in the Baltic and High North.
Russia's Defense Ministry did not respond to Reuters' request for comment on the Svalbard operation.
read also
4 dead after Russian attack on Pavlohrad shopping center
Four people have been killed and more than 60 injured after a Russian strike on a shopping center in Pavlohrad, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, authorities said on Sept. 10.
Among those injured are three teenage boys aged 13, 14, and 15.
"About an hour ago, the Russians struck a shopping centre in central Pavlohrad. In the middle of the day, when there were many people on the streets," Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said in a post on social media.
"The world sees what Russia is doing. There will be support for Ukraine. One hundred percent of our attention is focused on this," President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Telegram, stressing that decisions with partners on additional support, including strengthening Ukraine’s air defenses, were expected later in the day "to protect Ukrainians from such Russian terror."
It has not been confirmed which type of weapon Russia used in the attack, but videos posted on social media suggest at least one drone struck after the initial explosion.
The National Police said two emergency workers were among those injured.
Pavlohrad, roughly 75 kilometers (45 miles) from the front line, became a relatively safe haven for those fleeing the war further east, but the situation has changed dramatically in recent months.
On July 20, the first glide bomb (KAB) attacked the city. KABs, while having a shorter range than missiles, are cheaper to produce, launched from aircraft within Russian territory or Russian-occupied territories, and carry warheads up to 1,500 kilograms — enough to level an entire apartment block.
read also
Russian drone attacks hit Kyiv morning and evening, injuring 4
Russian jet-powered drones struck Kyiv early on Sept. 10, injuring four people and damaging a gas station in the Holosiivskyi district, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said, as Moscow continues its near-daily attacks on the Ukrainian capital.
The impact of the Russian drone sparked a fire and set one vehicle ablaze before emergency crews extinguished the flames, while three of the four injured were hospitalized, Klitschko said.
A non-residential building was also damaged in the district, according to the mayor.
Local Telegram channels published footage appearing to show a fire at a gas station near the Respublika Park shopping mall. Monitoring channels had earlier reported a drone falling in the area.
Separate morning attacks also hit the surrounding Kyiv Oblast, where one person was killed in the Obukhiv district and two others injured there and in Fastiv district, according to local authorities.
In Bucha district, private houses were damaged and a fire broke out in an open area. In Fastiv district, drone debris damaged a veterinary clinic and a private house.
In Obukhiv district a warehouse also caught fire following the attack, according to preliminary information.
Later in the evening, Russian drones again targeted Kyiv.
Klitschko said a drone fell on a two-story office building in the Obolonskyi district, while another struck the roof of a four-story business center in the Solomianskyi district.
Russia's attacks on Kyiv resumed almost immediately after a brief pause linked to the visit of U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to the capital.
A day earlier, on Sept. 9, Russian jet-powered drones struck residential buildings and other sites across Kyiv, killing one person and injuring at least 17 others, including two children.
On Sept. 8, a mass Russian missile and drone attack on the capital killed five people and injured 35, while large fires broke out across the city.
Russia has previously used drone attacks on gas stations to disrupt fuel supplies and road logistics, particularly in Kharkiv, Sumy, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts. By August, the tactic had spread into central regions, with dozens of gas stations struck over the summer.

articles.title: Report: Iran resumes ballistic missile production at underground sites despite heavy wartime damage
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Thursday evening that Iran is again attempting to rebuild its nuclear capabilities, vowing that Tehran would not obtain a nuclear weapon as long as he remains in office.
“President Trump announced this evening that Iran is trying to arm itself again with nuclear weapons. That is true,” Netanyahu said during remarks at the Western Wall ahead of Rosh Hashanah. “After we destroyed its immediate ability to produce nuclear bombs, both in Operation Rising Lion and Operation Roaring Lion, they are trying again.”
“I promise you here, at the Western Wall, ahead of Rosh Hashanah: As long as I am prime minister, Iran will not have nuclear weapons,” he said.
Netanyahu added that Israel was continuing to strike what he described as the Iranian axis. “At the same time, we are striking the Iranian axis, not only very hard in the Gaza Strip, but also in Lebanon. We destroyed the Beaufort Ridge and are now dealing with the Ali Taher Ridge. More will follow.”
His comments came as The Wall Street Journal reported that Iran has resumed producing ballistic missiles at underground facilities, assembling new weapons from components stockpiled before the war despite extensive damage inflicted by U.S. and Israeli strikes.
According to the report, Tehran is assembling both liquid-propellant missiles, which must be fueled shortly before launch, and solid-propellant missiles that can be stored ready to fire. Intelligence has detected activity at several underground facilities, including the Khojir military complex in southeastern Iran, while Iran is also trying to establish new underground assembly sites to make future production harder to target.
Production is still believed to be considerably lower than before the war. U.S. and Israeli strikes damaged factories and other industrial facilities required to manufacture missiles and their components, while the U.S. naval blockade has complicated Iran’s ability to import parts and materials used to produce solid rocket fuel.
Still, the renewed activity illustrates the difficulty of permanently dismantling Tehran’s missile program and chips away at what Washington and Jerusalem had presented as one of the war’s major military achievements. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in April that Iran’s missile program had been “functionally destroyed” and that Tehran had “no ability to replenish” the weapons it was firing.
The Pentagon told the Journal that U.S. forces had destroyed as much as 90% of Iran’s drone, ballistic missile and naval industrial base and had significantly degraded its ability to launch missiles and drones. A White House official did not directly address whether missile production had restarted, but said Iran’s military had been severely weakened.
A U.S. official said Iran likely resumed low-rate production after reaching a preliminary agreement with Trump in mid-June to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and begin negotiations aimed at winding down the war.
Before the fighting, Iran had accumulated stocks of finished warheads, airframes, guidance systems and other components, allowing it to assemble missiles without immediately restoring its entire manufacturing network.
Jim Lamson, a former CIA analyst specializing in Iran’s military, told the Journal that the number of missiles Tehran could assemble depends on the size of those stockpiles and how many underground facilities remain operational.
“We could be talking about hundreds of missiles or possibly thousands of missiles,” he said.
Iran depleted much of its stockpile of completed missiles during the war, forcing it to reduce the size of its barrages, but analysts believe it still possesses thousands of ballistic missiles. Tehran has continued firing missiles at U.S. military positions across the Middle East and has also launched several attacks on U.S. warships in recent days, though none was hit.
Satellite imagery reviewed by the Journal indicates Iran has been rapidly repairing military infrastructure, including roads, production sites and entrances to underground missile bases damaged in earlier strikes. Israeli military assessments cited in the report suggest weapons stored deep inside the tunnels may have survived largely intact.
Iran nevertheless faces substantial obstacles to restoring production to prewar levels, including damage to chemical facilities used to make liquid propellants and industrial mixers needed to manufacture solid fuel.
Experts said Iran deliberately dispersed and buried much of its missile infrastructure because it expected the program to face repeated attacks. The renewed production could help Tehran sustain a prolonged war of attrition, particularly as Iran’s missile stocks are pitted against increasingly strained U.S. and Gulf inventories of air-defense interceptors.
First published: 19:54, 09.10.26

articles.title: Why North Korea's Kim Jong Un doesn't need a US deal
articles.body:
Why North Korea's Kim Jong Un doesn't need a US deal
September 11, 2026
Last month, US President Donald Trump revived a charm offensive aimed at Pyongyang by drastically scaling back joint US military exercises with South Korea and pouring praise on North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.The US president said the North Korean dictator "has always treated me with great respect."
North Korea's response to Trump's overtures has been markedly less enthusiastic, ranging from firing a barrage of missiles to publicly denying Trump's claims that Kim has responded "very positively" to a request for talks.
This week, as the US and South Korea, along with Japan, kicked off a five-day military drill, there was no mention of any pullback from Washington, nor any sign of diplomatic progress with Pyongyang.
Instead, Kim on Monday commissioned a naval destroyer, while again emphasizing North Korea must establish a "powerful and reliable nuclear war deterrent" and strengthen "maritime defense." Kim also said North Korea would soon unveil a "significant" naval advancement.
No urgency for deal with US
Unlike the summit diplomacy of Trump's first term, Kim's dismissive stance comes at a time when North Korea has alternatives to a grand bargain with the United States.
"For Kim, the stakes are simply lower than they were in 2019. There is no longer the same sense of urgency in Pyongyang to get back to the negotiating table with Washington," Joon Ha Park, a correspondent at Korea Risk Group in Seoul, told DW.
"North Korea now has a treaty-based alliance with Moscow and is drawing closer to Beijing, while its military capabilities have expanded significantly. That's why a single reduction in ROK-US military exercises is not enough for Pyongyang to be swayed," he added, referring to military ties between South Korea and the US.
Kim rides high
Park agrees that Kim is arguably in his strongest position since taking power in 2011.
Just six years ago, amid crippling sanctions and the coronavirus pandemic, an emotional Kim stood at the lectern marking the 75th anniversary of the Korean Workers' Party and expressed regret for having failed the North Korean people.
Fast forward to today, and North Korea's economy appears to be on a stronger footing. Estimates released last year by South Korea's central bank showed the economy expanded by 3.7% in 2024, its fastest rate of growth in eight years.
Kim has brought North Korea closer to Russia and China than the traditionally isolated country has been in decades. This week, both Moscow and Beijing sent messages marking North Korea's 78th founding anniversary and praising the strategic importance of their deepening partnerships with Pyongyang.
Kim's recent spate of good fortune began in 2023 after a summit with Vladimir Putin in Russia's far east. The meeting opened the door for North Korea delivering arms to help Russia fight the Ukraine war, with Moscow sending back aid.
Since then, Pyongyang has heavily ramped up industrial military production, buoyed by fresh financing that skirts international sanctions.
Beijing responds to the Russia-North Korea alliance
China, North Korea's traditional benefactor, quickly took notice of the growing alignment between Moscow and Pyongyang, but initially kept its distance.
"The war in Ukraine has opened up a crucial lifeline for the (North Korean) regime, delivering weapons, ammunitions and soldiers to Russia in return for cash, foodstuff and ostensibly advanced military technology," Alexander Lipke, policy fellow with the Asia Program at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), told DW.
"These warming ties with Russia have also alarmed China, which is also actively attempting to cement its position as Pyongyang's preeminent partner," he added.
By 2025, Russia and North Korea's ever closer ties forced Beijing to pivot and showcase its leading role among the three countries. In September that year, Kim was invited to the "Victory Day" celebrations in Beijing, and for the first time, stood publicly on stage alongside Xi and Putin.
For a regime known for its international isolation, Kim standing shoulder to shoulder with the leaders of Russia and China was a major milestone. This was again the case when in June 2026, Xi's first foreign trip of the year took him to Pyongyang.
Denuclearization off the table?
Notably, any mention of "denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula" was omitted from communiques following these high-level meetings, despite the phrase previously being part of boilerplate diplomatic language from Beijing and Moscow.
This diplomatic softening comes as North Korea aggressively takes steps to ramp up its nuclear program. In February 2026, Kim said North Korea's status as a nuclear weapons state was "irreversible," while calling for the country's nuclear force to be expanded. Recent analysis of satellite imagery suggests increased activity at known North Korean nuclear sites.
Pyongyang has also insisted on US recognition as a nuclear weapons state as a precondition for any talks with Washington, while emphasizing that any future summits must omit language on "denuclearization."
North Korea is estimated to have nearly 60 nuclear warheads, which is double the 20-30 warheads Pyongyang is thought to have possessed during Trump's last diplomatic episode with Kim in 2018 and 2019.
"North Korea is no longer looking for talks centered on denuclearization or even traditional arms control. It increasingly wants recognition, implicitly or otherwise, as a nuclear weapons state," said Park from the Korea Risk Group.
He added that any Trump summit without denuclearization included as part of the official agenda "could be portrayed by Pyongyang both domestically and internationally as implicit US acceptance of North Korea's nuclear status."
Sanctions don't matter anymore?
Since its first nuclear test in 2006, North Korea has been subject to a strict sanctions regime, with the UN Security Council having passed nine sanctions resolutions aimed at restricting exports, along with asset freezes.
The last package was passed in 2017. At that point, it was combined with pressure and fiery rhetoric from the first Trump administration, raising tensions on the Korean Peninsula. Kim was under heavy economic pressure and seeking sanctions relief in return for concessions on his nuclear program. But that moment has now long passed.
"North Korea's diplomatic situation has vastly improved, reducing the pressure to come to the table to cut a deal with the US," said Lipke, adding that "independent sanctions enforcement has widely collapsed," with Russia and China no longer actively pursuing their non-proliferation stance of previous decades.
Lipke said North Korea no longer needs a bargain with the US regarding sanctions relief in return for partial denuclearization.
"But the bargain now on the table could potentially be much larger for North Korea, a freeze in nuclear development in exchange for the recognition by the US as a de-facto nuclear state in front of the whole world."
Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

articles.title: 9/11 – spies, strategy, missed opportunities and lessons learned
articles.body:
For decades, countless leaders have stated that a government’s primary duty is to protect its citizens, yet the 11th of September, 2001, demonstrated that this can fail: intelligence was available, but no one pieced the connections together, reports the BBC.
The attack on the Twin Towers shaped security, intelligence, and foreign policy for decades to come. On the 11th of September, 2001, as Al-Qaeda suicide pilots crashed into the World Trade Center skyscrapers, BBC journalist Frank Gardner had just finished a stint at the broadcaster’s Middle East bureau. While driving the journalist to Tel Aviv airport, a Palestinian taxi driver suddenly turned up the radio volume and said that something massive had happened in the US. The driver was not exaggerating—2,977 people lost their lives that day.
The attacks did not come out of the blue. The US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) had known for years about Al-Qaeda and the activities of its leader, Osama bin Laden. The CIA had even established a task force to capture bin Laden. Nine days after the attacks, then-US President George Bush declared a war on terror. The subsequent 25 years brought both significant successes and major failures in the field of intelligence on both sides of the Atlantic. Successes included the thwarting of terrorist plots and the arrest of criminals. What was the broader picture? How have intelligence, counter-terrorism operations, and strategic planning evolved over these 25 years?
No one disputes that the 9/11 attacks represented a serious intelligence failure.
At the time, both the CIA and the Federal Bureau of Investigation possessed information that—had it been properly shared between the agencies—could have prevented the terrorist attack. The subsequent report attributed the failure to shortcomings in imagination, policy, capabilities, and management within the US government. It concluded that the CIA and FBI failed to adequately assess and share intelligence, and to take the necessary steps to thwart the attack.
The major lessons have been learned—albeit not entirely—and information sharing among Western intelligence agencies has become far more comprehensive than it was in 2001. Since the 9/11 attacks, a comprehensive reorganization of US intelligence agencies has taken place, and the National Counterterrorism Center and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence have been established near Washington to facilitate the flow of necessary information among the 18 American intelligence agencies. The relationship between the CIA and Britain’s MI6 is arguably the closest of its kind in the world. This is complemented by the Five Eyes alliance, which coordinates the exchange of intelligence information among the US, Canada, the UK, Australia, and New Zealand.
However, catastrophic failures have occurred even after the Twin Towers terrorist attack. Prior to the US-led invasion of Iraq, MI6 allowed the intelligence in its possession to become politicized; this dealt the greatest blow to the British service’s reputation since the exposure of Soviet double agents in the 1950s and 1960s.
Facing immense political pressure to find evidence that Iraq—under Saddam Hussein—still possessed weapons of mass destruction,
MI6 passed flawed intelligence to the government of then-Prime Minister Tony Blair.
Iraq had previously possessed weapons of mass destruction, but these had been eliminated following the 1991 Persian Gulf War. After the 2003 invasion of Iraq, MI6 completely overhauled its procedures for evaluating intelligence obtained from field agents. There is now a clear separation between the work of active field agents (who gather information in places like North Korea or Iran, or from within terrorist groups) and the intelligence assessment team. The assessment team verifies the data and often requests additional information before drawing conclusions. General Richard Shirreff, who commanded a division in Iraq, stated that the 2003 invasion was based on flawed intelligence. He asked whether lessons had been learned from this, answered “no” himself, and remarked that “learning is not our strong suit.”
The invasion of Iraq prompted further inquiries, which eventually resulted in the Butler Report. It concluded that British intelligence regarding Iraq’s alleged weapons of mass destruction was deeply flawed and relied on unverified sources.
MI5, too, has made mistakes amidst its numerous successes.
Lord Jonathan Evans, who led the service from 2007 to 2013, noted that following the 9/11 terrorist attacks, the assessment was that Al-Qaeda—along with associated individuals and groups—posed the greatest security threat to Britain. However, with a database of 20,000 subjects of interest and numerous simultaneous investigations, MI5 did not always set its priorities correctly. In 2005, the service failed to prevent the terrorist attack carried out by suicide bombers in London, which claimed 52 lives. MI5 was aware of Mohammad Sidique Khan, the group’s leader, but did not know what he was planning to do. A similar error led to the Manchester Arena bombings in 2017.
Lord Evans noted that while the terrorist threat has not disappeared, the landscape has changed. Threats to national security—in various forms—emanate from Russia, Iran and its allied groups, and China.
One could argue that US President Donald Trump’s decision to launch attacks on Iran alongside Israel was also an intelligence failure. All US allies in the Persian Gulf region were aware of the possibility that Iran might close the Strait of Hormuz. The warning signs were clearly visible, yet Trump lacked a contingency plan when Tehran did exactly what had been predicted.
The immediate aftermath of the 9/11 terrorist attacks was marked by the fear that a similar event might occur again.
Al-Qaeda had even threatened a swarm of planes carrying out attacks on buildings. In their haste to prevent a recurrence of such attacks, the US and its allies committed numerous human rights violations. Suspects were captured in Afghanistan and Pakistan, often based on flimsy evidence. Hundreds of individuals were transported to the Guantanamo base, where they were imprisoned without trial and subjected to torture. Human rights groups have described this as a moral stain on the US conscience. Scandals also emerged regarding the cruel treatment of detainees in Iraq and Afghanistan. Although some of the individuals involved were held accountable, critics have pointed out that high-ranking figures escaped punishment. The US continues to practice detention without trial at the Guantanamo base. Human rights violations also occurred in Great Britain following the 9/11 terrorist attacks. MI6 was involved in the 2004 abduction of Libyan Islamist Abdelhakim Belhaj and his wife in Thailand, and their subsequent rendition to Libya. There, they spent years in prison, where they were subjected to torture. The case later came to light, and in 2018, Great Britain issued a public apology.
Sir Alex Younger, who headed MI6 from 2014 to 2020, stated shortly after leaving office that by focusing on counter-terrorism operations, the British had overlooked China’s emergence as a military power and a strategic challenge.
In 2016, General Shirreff published the political thriller War With Russia, in which he predicted a full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine. In the wake of the 9/11 attacks,
Western nations were preoccupied with the War on Terror
—fighting the Taliban and ISIS, and attempting to stabilize the situation in Iraq—while failing to notice Russia and China developing massive armament programs featuring innovations in hypersonic missile technology. The military successes of both superpowers have significantly eroded the military superiority NATO once enjoyed. Like Iran, Russia, and North Korea, China is considered a challenging target for intelligence gathering. While the use of biometric data was still in its infancy in 2001, technological advancements have since made it much harder for agents to infiltrate China.
Alongside Russia, China is one of MI6’s primary targets. Sam Olsen, a senior analyst at the security intelligence firm Sibylline, noted that while Western intelligence agencies possess a great deal of information about China, the threat lies in the fact that they often see only isolated fragments without fully grasping how they fit together. China’s strength no longer resides solely in missiles, ships, and troops; it increasingly lies in semiconductors, critical minerals, batteries, ports, communication systems, and industrial capacity. Olsen emphasized that the challenge often lies not in gathering intelligence, but in interpreting it strategically.
Twenty-five years ago, US intelligence personnel held the pieces of the puzzle but failed to assemble them and clearly see what lay ahead. Ultimately, intelligence gathering is pointless if the information cannot be utilized for strategic purposes.

articles.title: India and Russia are building something big in space
articles.body:
India and Russia are building something big in space
Space exploration and satellite navigation are fragile, failure-prone and enormously expensive. Yet they offer something few other fields can match: technological superiority and strategic prestige.
The main players in space remain Russia, the United States, and China, followed by India, the European Union, and Japan. Newer entrants include the United Arab Emirates, Iran, and a range of states in South America and West Asia. Because the sector is so costly and high-risk, cooperation is highly valued – it brings redundancy, speeds up technological progress, and cuts the price of getting there.
Russian First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov earlier this week, in the runup to Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to New Delhi, noted that Russia and India are considering the possibility of cross-flights involving mixed crews to their future national orbital stations. He said that this cooperation could eventually extend to joint scientific experiments and research.
In May this year, Indian National Security Adviser Ajit Doval visited the Roscosmos Joint Industry Information Center, while in August, Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar traveled to Moscow to co-chair the 27th session of the India-Russia Inter-Governmental Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific, Technological and Cultural Cooperation (IRIGC-TEC).
Increased collaboration between Moscow and New Delhi within the space sector is occurring within the backdrop of three larger yet interlinked trends: first, the United States’ active dismantling of the remaining international order; second, the ongoing conflicts in Ukraine and Iran; and third, the advancement in drones and defense technologies.
The current US administration has upended the established decades-long US foreign policy by targeting longstanding allies with tariffs and sanctions in the attainment of its goals. India has become a target more than once of American tariffs and economic pressure. Attempts to reach a deal with the Trump administration have failed to produce long-term tangible gains.
This, however, has had a deep impact on the Indian populace. Since the normalization of Indo-US ties, the Indian public had forgotten that historically, American interests had been antagonistic to India during the entire Cold War period. These buried emotions have been surfacing lately with public skepticism regarding American intentions. Deepening cooperation with Russia and attempts to normalize ties with China are New Delhi’s way of signaling its displeasure toward American actions.
Recent developments in Indo-Russian cooperation have involved mutual deployment of ground stations, co-production of engines, and development of national orbital stations. These will allow Russia to offset vulnerabilities by outsourcing joint-production capabilities of critical components to India out of Ukraine’s reach.
Third, the astronomical advancements in drone and smart defense technologies have underscored the significance of satellite-based constellations in warfare.
A variety of Russian munitions and weapon systems employ GPS/GLONASS and the upcoming Rassvet system in precision guidance and control. UMPK-equipped glide-bombs, cruise missiles such as the Kh-101, drones like the Shahed-136, Geran-3 & -4, and Orlan-10, along with ballistic missiles such as the Iskander-K, witness a significant increase in accuracy and precision with minimal falloff over large distances.
Furthermore, despite the destruction of existing Viasat infrastructure in Ukraine during the conflict’s opening days, the rapid deployment of Starlink prevented the complete collapse of Ukrainian command and control structures. These attributes make the systems vital to any future operational requirements against adversaries with both limited and significant electronic warfare capabilities.
India’s worst-case military scenarios stipulate for a two-front war. The ability to deploy these munitions and weapon systems may provide its forces with definite tactical and strategic advantages in critical sectors along and beyond the lines of engagement. However, all these require the backbone of GPS/GLONASS capabilities and/or the Rassvet/Starlink low-orbit constellations on which these systems rely. Russia is currently in the process of operationalizing its Rassvet constellation to full functionality.
India’s own NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation) is in dire straits. The indigenous satellite navigation system has dropped below the critical threshold of satellites required for accurate geolocation. Simultaneously, the quest for a reliable low-orbit satellite navigation system over the Indian subcontinent has led to multiple contenders, including the French-TATA venture Eutelsat, the American Starlink and Viasat systems, Reliance’s own planned constellation, and possibly the Russian Rassvet system in the near future.
Space-based cooperation need not be limited to the bilateral level. In August 2021, BRICS space agencies signed an agreement for cooperation in remote sensing satellite data sharing. In May of the following year, the BRICS Joint Committee on Space Cooperation was officially launched. This year, BRICS+ engaged in advanced discussions of cooperation with calls for a BRICS Space Economy being made. Whether civilian cooperation in satellite data constellation ultimately advances to include sensitive military collaboration remains to be seen. What is already clear, however, is that low-orbit constellations are set to become a major disruptor in both civilian and military technology, and this is one area in which the Russia-India partnership could deepen further.

articles.title: Canada will allocate $253 million for American air defense interceptors for Ukraine
articles.body:
Canada will allocate $253 million for American air defense interceptors for Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Canada will finance the purchase of American interceptor missiles for Ukraine through the JUMPSTART mechanism. The type and delivery timeline have not yet been disclosed.
Canada will allocate approximately 350 million Canadian dollars (approximately 253 million US dollars) to purchase critically needed air defense equipment for Ukraine through the US JUMPSTART mechanism. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said this on September 10 after a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, reports UNN.
According to the Canadian government, the funds will be used to purchase interceptor missiles to strengthen Ukraine’s air defenses. The decision was made amid an intensification of Russian air attacks and Ukraine’s growing need for means of protecting civilians and critical infrastructure.
At the same time, the Canadian side has not yet disclosed which specific missiles or what quantities will be purchased, nor has it announced specific timelines for their transfer to Ukraine.
What the JUMPSTART mechanism provides for
JUMPSTART is a US mechanism that enables allies and partners to finance the purchase of US weapons for Ukraine through the Foreign Military Sales (FMS) system. The scheme provides that the partner country allocates the funds, after which the United States organizes the purchase and delivery of the relevant weapons to Ukraine. Therefore, it is important to understand that the 350 million Canadian dollars announced by Canada do not mean the transfer of missiles to Ukraine from Canadian military stocks. It is specifically funding for the purchase of US air defense systems.
What official Kyiv previously asked Ottawa for
Canada’s decision is directly linked to previous negotiations between Kyiv and Ottawa. In June 2026, Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov discussed with his Canadian counterpart David McGuinty the possibility of purchasing PAC-3 interceptor missiles for Ukraine through the JUMPSTART mechanism.
PAC-3 is one of the key types of interceptors used by Patriot systems to counter ballistic missiles. The need for such munitions remains one of Ukraine’s priorities, as partners’ stocks of highly effective interceptors are limited and their production takes time.
However, as of September 10, the Canadian government is officially speaking only of critically needed air defense interceptors. Therefore, it is premature to claim that all 350 million Canadian dollars will be spent specifically on PAC-3 missiles.
It should be noted that Canada has already financed US weapons for Ukraine. The current agreement is part of Canada’s broader support for Ukraine’s air defenses.
Earlier, official Ottawa allocated funds to purchase US weapons for Ukraine through other mechanisms, including PURL. In August 2025, Ottawa announced the allocation of approximately 680 million Canadian dollars for a corresponding military aid package that included air defense systems. Through mechanisms of this type, Ukraine’s allies can pay for weapons manufactured in the United States without transferring their own stocks to Ukraine.
Other partners of Ukraine also joined JUMPSTART. In particular, Germany announced funding for the purchase of additional PAC-3 interceptors, while Norway and other European countries used the mechanism to finance US weapons for Ukraine.
Canada expands its defense partnership with Ukraine
The decision to finance air defense became part of a broader package of agreements announced during Zelenskyy’s visit to Canada. The two countries agreed to develop a long-term defense-industrial partnership, particularly in the areas of drone production, counter-drone systems, electronic warfare equipment, and munitions.
The Canadian authorities also announced their intention to provide Ukraine with one-third of the drones produced by Canadian companies. Separately, a partnership was announced between Canada’s General Dynamics Mission Systems-Canada and Ukraine’s Green Tech Harvest in the development and production of unmanned systems.
In addition, Ottawa plans to provide nearly 435 million Canadian dollars in guarantees to the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development to support Ukraine’s energy security, including the purchase of gas ahead of the heating season.
Context
During the meeting, Carney and Zelenskyy signed a declaration on a 100-year partnership between Canada and Ukraine. The document provides for deepening cooperation in the areas of defense, security, the Ukrainian recovery, technology, and people-to-people ties.
The Canadian side separately reaffirmed its continued support for Ukraine in the area of air defense and the supply of interceptors.
Ottawa also announced its support for Ukraine’s FREYJA program, aimed at developing a more affordable and mass-produced interceptor to counter Russian ballistic missiles.

articles.title: Ukraine Is Losing Its Tech Edge to Russia, Former Google CEO Says
articles.body:
Ukraine risks losing its technological advantage over Russia as Moscow adapts its weapons and expands military production, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt warned Wednesday, Sept. 9.
In an opinion column for The Washington Post, Schmidt said Russia was moving toward a strategy of “total war” by mobilizing its factories and manpower while developing technologies to counter Ukrainian innovations.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Schmidt, who now chairs the Special Competitive Studies Project, said he has repeatedly traveled to Ukraine and helped its military develop battlefield technologies.
He wrote that Ukraine’s main advantage during much of the full-scale war was its ability to develop, test and modify new weapons within weeks. Decentralized networks connecting Ukrainian soldiers, engineers and defense technology companies allowed Kyiv to innovate faster than Russia’s larger military bureaucracy.
That advantage is now “rapidly diminishing,” Schmidt warned.
After Ukraine developed interceptor drones capable of destroying Russian Shahed-type drones, Moscow began deploying faster jet-powered variants that are significantly more difficult to intercept, he said.
Russia is also developing a satellite constellation intended to rival Starlink, which Ukrainian drone units use to target Russian forces in occupied territory.
While Russia previously relied primarily on its larger industrial base to counter Ukrainian innovation, it is now combining mass production with its own technological advances, Schmidt wrote.
Russia Sends Bones of Medieval Warrior to Ukraine Front to Boost Morale
Drones can become obsolete within months
Schmidt described a battlefield where thousands of unmanned systems conduct reconnaissance, transport supplies and hunt soldiers and vehicles.
He wrote that around 80% of Ukrainian military casualties occur while troops are moving between positions. Some soldiers remain underground for months after reaching the front because movement above ground has become extremely dangerous.
Weapons are also becoming obsolete at unprecedented speed. A drone that proves effective when introduced can become virtually useless within months if the opposing side changes its radio frequencies, deploys electronic warfare systems or develops faster interceptors.
Ukraine remains highly effective at adapting its technology, Schmidt said, but innovation alone cannot meet the scale of demand created by a high-intensity war.
One Ukrainian commander told Schmidt that his unit had stopped looking for additional targets because it lacked enough drones to strike those it had already identified.
Schmidt argued that producing hundreds of highly advanced drones is less valuable than manufacturing effective systems in the hundreds of thousands.
Schmidt urges West to expand Ukrainian production
Russia is building the capacity to manufacture weapons in enormous quantities and is considering another large-scale military call-up that Ukrainian officials expect could occur this fall, Schmidt wrote.
He warned that the coming winter would be critical as Russia exploits Ukraine’s shortage of air defenses capable of intercepting ballistic missiles to strike power plants and electrical substations.
Ukraine cannot match Russia’s manufacturing capacity without substantial Western involvement, Schmidt said. Kyiv urgently needs air defense interceptors, ammunition and long-range weapons, alongside investment to expand domestic production.
He urged Western governments to treat Ukraine’s defense industry as an extension of their own by jointly manufacturing weapons, resolving supply-chain bottlenecks and ensuring Ukrainian commanders do not have to ration attacks because of equipment shortages.
Closer integration with Ukraine’s battle-tested military would also allow Western armed forces to learn lessons about modern warfare and prepare for future security threats, he added.
“Lauding Ukrainian resilience is not a strategy, and courage alone cannot defend its cities or win its war,” Schmidt wrote.

articles.title: ‘It was all hands on deck’: how the CIA responded to 9/11
articles.body:
A generation of spies had lost an enemy but not yet found a role. Then came 9/11.
A decade after the dissolution of the Soviet Union, al-Qaida’s devastating attacks on New York and Washington on 11 September 2001 announced to the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) that the long era of battling communism, for which it had been founded, was officially at an end.
It was to be replaced by a no-holds-barred “war on terror” that would leave the CIA with a soiled reputation over falsified intelligence that led to the invasion and occupation of Iraq, and an extraordinary rendition program in which suspects were subjected to “enhanced interrogations” at secret sites that official US inquiries subsequently defined as torture.
The US intelligence community was dramatically transformed after two planes flew into the World Trade Center, a third smashed into the Pentagon, and a fourth crashed in the Pennsylvania countryside after passengers overcame the hijackers.
Accounts of what unfolded inside the CIA’s headquarters in Langley, Virginia, suggests an organization unprepared for the drastically changed world the attacks ushered in, despite an awareness among some in the intelligence community that al-Qaida and its leader, Osama bin Laden, represented a clear and present danger.
Margaret Henoch, then a counter-intelligence officer with little knowledge of terrorism, recalls confusion, chaos and an initial lack of direction from senior leadership as staff struggled to process what seemed like a bolt from a clear blue sky on that balmy late summer day.
“One of my officers came in and said to me: ‘A plane just ran into the World Trade Center,’” she said. To this day, Henoch – who had previously been stationed in Vienna, where she focused on the International Atomic Energy Agency and nuclear threats – is haunted by the apparent vacuum that followed.
About 40 minutes after the first attack, with no clear direction from the top of CIA, she decided to go up to the seventh floor, which accommodated the agency’s senior figures, including its then director, George Tenet.
To her surprise, the area was deserted, apart from three assistants.
“It was reasonable that they would have moved those guys someplace else,” said Henoch. “What was unreasonable, in my humble opinion, was that no one thought about all those people sitting in that building. Because if the Pentagon was hit, there was a chance that we, too, were a target – and it would be nice to believe that the people who left the building rapidly had a thought for all those who worked for them.
“It was not clear that they did.”
The Guardian contacted Tenet, now working in the private sector, for comment. In an emailed response, Bill Harlow, the CIA’s public affairs director at the time of the attacks, cited details in the 2007 memoir, At the Center of the Storm, which he co-wrote with Tenet, and said orders were issued for the majority of the staff to leave the building at “about 10am” – nearly an hour after the second plane struck at 9.03am.
Harlow added: “We were aware at the time of intelligence gathered around 1995-96 of terrorist desires to attack CIA HQ with an airplane.
“Director Tenet and the senior leadership moved to another building on the compound that presented a lower profile and would have a greater chance of survival if we were hit by a plane.
“Notably, a decision was made that the personnel of the counter-terrorism center remained in the original headquarters building throughout that day … accepting the risk. The senior leadership team returned to the headquarters in the middle of the afternoon on 9/11.”
‘I had a briefing on who the hell al-Qaida was’
Some time afterwards, an order was given for the thousands of personnel in the building to evacuate. Some, including Henoch, were told to relocate to alternative sites to address the emergency.
But by the time of that instruction, nearby roads were choked with traffic as commuters returned home from Washington DC after being released from work early. That prevented agency staff from departing, and triggered fears that they could be sitting ducks for the doomed fourth plane, which was already known to be in the air.
“Large segments of the CIA operating staff were trapped,” Henoch said. “One guy, who was senior to me, was standing next to me in the car park and he said, ‘I have served in multiple war zones. I was a combat soldier in Vietnam and I’m going to die in the parking lot of the CIA.’”
The dysfunctional scene was soon replaced by one of much greater conviction – leading to permanent changes in US intelligence.
“I just remember loads of cable traffic coming in that said: it’s got to be al-Qaida,” said Henoch. “It wasn’t my world, so I had to have a quick briefing on who the hell al-Qaida was, because I just didn’t know anything about it.
“The change was immediate. The next morning, everybody at the Central Intelligence Agency had to know who they were, and how it intersected with everything you were doing.”
Steven Cash, a former CIA counter-terrorism officer who had left the agency to join the staff of the US Senate intelligence committee six months beforehand, faults the CIA’s pre-9/11 terrorism strategy as being too narrowly focused “looking to find bad guys” while neglecting the “political dimension”.
“There was an emphasis on looking at terrorists as if they were a motorcycle gang,” said Cash, who had specialized on the Lebanese Shia group Hezbollah, a close ally of Iran. “A decision was made in the first [George HW] Bush administration to take terrorism away from the people who looked at geographic areas and separate it out. [It was] illustrative of a mistaken way of looking at the world, because terrorists don’t exist in a vacuum.”
Cash moved on to focus on the Balkans before leaving the agency, but still harboured guilt after the attacks. “Was this our fault? Did we fail? That kind of guilt felt, at least for me, really personal.”
Cash had been on Capitol Hill, attending a committee meeting, when news of the attacks filtered through. “Somebody said, put on the TV and we saw the second plane hit,” he said. “And then they started evacuating the building.
“It was a mess. People were in the hall screaming, running around. The third plane had hit the Pentagon by that point, because we could see smoke across the National Mall.”
The following day, Cash and his then boss, the late Democratic senator Dianne Feinstein, visited CIA headquarters and found a mood of determined resolve. “It was all hands on deck. The people I knew were getting deployed very quickly to Afghanistan,” he recalled. “These people are pros. They didn’t care whether they were blamed or not. They wanted to do something.
“I have a little bit of survivor guilt here. Maybe I should have been shipped out to Afghanistan.”
Political pressure
On their visit to CIA headquarters on 12 September, senators asked agency operatives what legislation and resources they would need to respond to the attacks of the previous day, according to Cash.
Two early – and controversial – results were the USA Patriot Act of 2001, which expanded law enforcement and surveillance powers, and the Homeland Security Act of the following year, creating the US Department of Homeland Security, which houses agencies including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
Later changes established the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, with the goal of coordinating 18 different intelligence bodies and eliminating the lack of coordination widely held to blame for warning signs of the 9/11 plot going unheeded.
“DNI was formed to make sure that we actually share everything with everybody. We don’t just keep it inside CIA,” said Susan Miller, a retired CIA counter-intelligence officer.
“What’s really cool is we’ve changed how we do things across the board, not just for terrorism. It’s really improved things. There was no coordination before.”
Yet the reaction to the attacks changed intelligence in another way – by making it more susceptible to political pressure, as President George W Bush’s administration searched for information that could be used to justify an invasion of Iraq to topple Saddam Hussein.
In September 2002, Henoch – who had previously studied Russian weapons capabilities working at the Stanford Research Institute – was asked to assess intelligence provided by an Iraqi defector codenamed Curveball, who had sought asylum in Germany, and provided its intelligence agency with what he said was proof of Saddam’s biological weapons program.
She quickly concluded the claims were fabricated, and passed her conclusions up the chain of command. They were not well received. When Colin Powell, the then US secretary of state, visited the CIA months later to review the agency’s intelligence on Iraq, Henoch and her fellow doubters were not informed. Powell’s subsequent speech to the United Nations security council in February 2003, in which he made the case for war, relied heavily on Curveball’s testimony – despite Henoch’s insistence when the address was checked with her and other officers beforehand that his assertions were not credible.
“We took a look at the Powell speech and I said: ‘You can’t use this. We think this is garbage,” she said. “I did write somewhere – I can’t remember on what page – ‘How can you send someone to die for something like this? No one ever answered that for me.
“The next thing I heard was, ‘Well, when we get in there, we’ll find something.’”
After the invasion, inspectors found no evidence of biological weapons. Curveball was later debunked as a fraud.
Miller, too, encountered the administration’s zeal for intelligence that could justify invading Iraq when she was posted to Prague as CIA station chief in 2002. Czech intelligence had investigated – and, initially, tentatively confirmed – a claim that one of the 9/11 ringleaders, Mohammed Atta, had travelled to Prague the previous year and met an Iraqi embassy official, Ahmad Samir al-Ani, months before the attacks.
The report was seized on by the hawkish US vice-president, Dick Cheney, as evidence of Saddam’s possible links to the attacks, thus providing another justification for war. But Czech intelligence officials retreated from their earlier stance, and the CIA concluded there was no evidence that the meeting happened.
Nevertheless, Donald Rumsfeld, then the US defense secretary, brazenly tried to revive it when Miller briefed him – along with George W Bush and Condoleezza Rice, the national security adviser – when they visited the Czech capital for a Nato summit in 2002.
“‘Young lady, you forgot about this other thing’,” Rumsfeld told Miller, she said. “I played dumb and said: ‘What other thing?’ He replied: ‘Mohammed Atta was here in Prague meeting the Iraqi consul.’
“Bush was looking really uncomfortable and Condi was looking straight ahead. I simply said, ‘Mr President, Madam Secretary, and Mr Rumsfeld, the CIA, the Czech service and I don’t make things up. We give you the facts, and the fact is that he was not here.’
“Bush and Rice nodded in acceptance and the ambassador supported me. But Rumsfeld threw his pen down in disgust.”
The invasion the neocons craved
Whether the supposed meeting happened or not, Rumsfeld and his neoconservative allies got the invasion they craved – leading to a protracted conflict that tarnished the CIA’s reputation and whose length, along with the coinciding US-led military campaign in Afghanistan, spurred popular opposition to “forever wars”.
Despite the blow to the agency’s standing, Cash insisted that its intelligence-gathering and functioning radically improved, thanks to the changes instituted after the attacks. “We have improved our intelligence capabilities significantly from what they were before 9/11,” he said, citing the success in preventing repeat attacks on US soil.
But with the Trump administration now engaged in a war with Iran, roiling the Middle East, such security could no longer be guaranteed, he believes.
“I’m not saying it was a great time,” Cash said, of the CIA’s record in the months and years after September 2001. “But the sense of purpose of being at a place in history where we – as a group, as a society – can do something, was pretty intoxicating.
“I was very proud to have been part of it. It sucked – but proud to have been part of it. And I think everything we’re seeing now is the antithesis of that.”

articles.title: Ukraine and Canada signed a declaration on a 100-year partnership
articles.body:
Ukraine and Canada signed a declaration on a 100-year partnership
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine and Canada agreed to jointly produce drones, electronic warfare systems, and ammunition. The parties are also preparing a Drone Deal and defense supplies.
Prime Minister of Canada Mark Carney and President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed the "Declaration on a 100-Year Partnership," which provides for a long-term partnership in the defense industry to jointly produce unmanned systems, counter-drone and electronic-warfare capabilities, as well as ammunition. The parties are also working on the Drone Deal. This was reported by the Government of Canada, according to UNN.
"On September 10, 2026, Prime Minister of Canada Mark Carney and President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy met in Calgary and signed the "Declaration on a 100-Year Partnership," in which they expressed their intention to elevate relations between their countries to the level of a comprehensive strategic partnership and confirmed their alignment," the statement said.
It is noted that, based on the Letter of Intent on joint production signed in Kyiv on August 24, 2025, Canada and Ukraine will establish a long-term partnership in the defense industry to jointly produce unmanned systems, counter-drone and electronic-warfare capabilities, as well as ammunition, supported by scientific research and technology transfers.
"They will promote predictable procurement of jointly produced equipment and work with partners to establish a Defense, Security and Resilience Bank. Canada and Ukraine will expand trade and investment under a modernized Free Trade Agreement, promote the development of public-private partnerships, and mobilize the capital and risk-mitigation solutions necessary to support Ukraine's recovery and reconstruction. Canada will cooperate with the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development to support macroeconomic stability and mobilize private capital," the Canadian government said.
It is also noted that both countries will deepen cooperation in the areas of energy security and critical minerals, industry and sustainable forest-resource management, as well as strengthen ties between innovators and researchers in the fields of artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, space, biotechnology, and digital governance.
Zelenskyy said that, together with Prime Minister Carney, they had discussed opportunities to ensure Ukraine's financial resilience for this year and the next.
"Thank you for your willingness to help find the funding necessary for the needs of the budget and our soldiers. I also spoke about Russia's virtually constant ballistic missile and drone strikes. Mark assured me that Canada is ready to join our European FREYJA anti-ballistic program with its technologies. This is a necessary and timely step. There will also be additional defense supplies. Of course, we also had a substantive discussion of promising bilateral projects in defense and the economy. In particular, our teams are currently working on the Drone Deal. We expect that in the near future we will be able to reach a full-fledged agreement," Zelenskyy said.
It should be recalled
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that Canada had decided on a "very important package of assistance for air defense".

articles.title: India Welcomes Russia, Iran Leaders for BRICS Summit Overshadowed by War
articles.body:
Leaders from Russia and Iran were in India for talks on Friday, ahead of a BRICS summit dominated by conflict and economic challenges, which Chinese President Xi Jinping will also attend.
Wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, as well as global trade turbulence and oil are expected on the agenda at the two-day annual summit that opens on Saturday, when Xi is set to arrive.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
It will be Xi’s first visit to India since 2019, and marks the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the rival neighbours, six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Tibetan border.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming again, with flights, visas and high-level contacts gradually being restored.
“China stands ready to work with India... by strengthening communication, enhancing cooperation, and properly handling differences,” Beijing’s foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said Friday.
Deep mistrust remains, with their contested Himalayan frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.
Dozens of Tibetans protested in New Delhi on Friday -- exiles, like their Buddhist leader the Dalai Lama, who has lived in India since fleeing a Chinese crackdown in 1959 -- waving placards against Xi’s visit.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is due to hold talks on Friday with President Vladimir Putin, who last visited India in December 2025. Moscow is one of New Delhi’s most important strategic partners.
Russian Chemical Giant’s Plant in Perm Targeted in Ukrainian Drone Strike
“One should engage in debate and friendship only with the virtuous, and nothing whatsoever with the unvirtuous,” Modi wrote Friday, in a social media message in Sanskrit to welcome leaders to the 11-nation summit.
Posters of a beaming Modi line streets across New Delhi, with heavy deployments of security forces across the capital and widespread traffic restrictions.
BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who arrived in New Delhi on Friday and will hold talks with Modi, said that “BRICS was established to counter unilateralism”, according to Tehran’s IRNA news agency.
- ‘Fault line’ -
As well as Iran, BRICS includes Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates -- countries with sharply differing positions on the war launched by the United States and Israel in February.
All three have been admitted to the group in recent years, joining founding member states that include India, China and Russia.
“The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the BRICS summit,” said Harsh V. Pant of India’s Observer Research Foundation.
“What was seen until last year as an achievement -- the expansion of BRICS -- today looks like a big constraint on BRICS,” Pant said.
Pezeshkian’s participation -- his first visit to India as Iranian president -- will put the Middle East conflict firmly on the agenda.
“The war in Iran will provide a stern test of the group’s cohesion,” said Shilan Shah of Capital Economics, noting the failure of the BRICS foreign ministers to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May.
UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is also expected, as is Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan, and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi.
India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.
New Delhi has navigated the energy crisis sparked by the US-Iran war in part by turning to Russia for fuel despite Western sanctions as the war against Ukraine drags on.
Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar visited Kyiv this month, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he was “grateful to India for its commitment to ending this unjust war”.

articles.title: Russia Issues Nuclear Threats to Lithuania Over Vilnius’s Plan to Lift Nuke Ban
articles.body:
Russia has threatened Lithuania with nuclear weapons as the Baltic nation is eyeing a lift of its nuclear weapons ban.
Lithuania’s parliamentary parties provisionally agreed to the constitutional amendments in July, and the parliamentary Committee on Legal Affairs voted 7-2 on the proposal on Wednesday, Sept. 9, paving the way for a final decision in early 2027.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The lifting of the ban would allow NATO, of which Lithuania has been a member of since 2004, to deploy nuclear forces on its territory.
On Friday, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov threatened Vilnius over the plan by saying the Baltic nation – once under Soviet occupation – will be “in the sights of our nuclear weapons.”
“And if there are nuclear weapons on the territory that are aimed at us, then the territory of this country will also be in the sights of our nuclear weapons,” Peskov told Russia’s Channel One on Friday, as reported by state media RIA Novosti.
Lithuania, one of Ukraine’s strongest backers in Europe, borders Russia’s exclave of Kaliningrad to the west and staunch Moscow ally Belarus to the south, with Vilnius a mere two-hour drive from Minsk, Belarus’s capital.
Russia began deploying nuclear weapons to Belarus, a non-nuclear nation, in June 2023. In December 2025, Russia also deployed its nuclear-capable Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missile (IRBM) to Belarus, whose combat use in Ukraine marked the first combat use of its kind in history.
St. Petersburg Metro Prepares 9 Stations as Civil Defense Shelters
In May, Belarus conducted a nuclear war drill with Russia, involving Belarusian military units tasked with the combat use of nuclear weapons and nuclear support operations.
In July, when discussions over the nuke ban gained traction in Vilnius’s parliament, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda attributed the need to changing geopolitical circumstances.
“The geopolitical situation is getting worse… Our constitution was written when geopolitical circumstances were totally different,” Nauseda said.

articles.title: Kremlin spokesman says Lithuania would be ‘in the crosshairs of our nuclear weapons’ if it deploys a nuclear arsenal on its own territory
articles.body:
Kremlin spokesman says Lithuania would be ‘in the crosshairs of our nuclear weapons’ if it deploys a nuclear arsenal on its own territory
Kremlin Press Secretary Dmitry Peskov said Russia would aim its nuclear weapons at Lithuania if the country deploys nuclear arsenals on its own territory, speaking in an interview with the Russian state-controlled television channel Channel One.
“Obviously, these weapons will not be aimed westward: they will be aimed eastward, that is, at us,” Peskov was quoted as saying by the Russian news agency Interfax.
And if there is nuclear weaponry on that territory aimed at us, then that country’s territory will also be in the crosshairs of our nuclear weapons.
Peskov called that scenario “a very serious round of escalation and tension.”
Lithuanian authorities confirmed in June 2026 that they were negotiating the deployment of nuclear weapons on their territory. The British newspaper the Financial Times reported that the talks involve American bombers capable of carrying nuclear warheads. Lithuania’s current constitution bans deploying weapons of mass destruction or hosting foreign military bases in the country, and Lithuanian authorities said they are ready to begin discussing amendments to lift that ban.
Under a 1997 agreement between Russia and NATO, the North Atlantic Alliance pledged it has “no intention, no plan and no reason to deploy nuclear weapons on the territory of new members.”
After the full-scale war between Russia and Ukraine began, Moscow deployed tactical nuclear weapons in Belarus.
