articles.title: GA-ASI’s Uncrewed Combat Aviation Portfolio Answers Call for High-End Warfare Capability
articles.body:
General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, Inc. (GA-ASI), the company that introduced the world to unmanned warfare, has systematically transformed its aircraft lineup to address the defining requirements of modern high-technology warfare: range, persistence, payload, survivability, and scale against advanced adversaries.
The portfolio now spans from the company’s enhanced MQ-9B SkyGuardian and SeaGuardian platforms capable of long-range maritime strike, to the expeditionary Mojave STOL, to the Air Force’s newly selected FQ-42A Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) — its first uncrewed fighter — and, most recently, to the Wildfire Massed Modular Aircraft (MMA), a theater-range platform engineered for affordable, attrition-tolerant combat mass.
According to GA-ASI President David Alexander, the United States has entered an era where winning demands large, capable Uncrewed Aircraft Systems (UAS) that can operate from friendly airspace into contested environments affordably, without risking aircrews.
“We’ve never been a company that rested on its laurels,” said Alexander. “The conversation around uncrewed systems has changed, and frankly, it should. The battlefield has evolved, threats have evolved, and so have we.
“We’re keeping ahead of the game, and, in the case of our FQ-42A and Wildfire aircraft, we’ve designed them from the start to overmatch threats today and into the future.”
Physics Demands Large Airframes
Losses in contested environments have prompted some observers to suggest moving away from large UAS platforms. Alexander sees those same operations as validation for continued investment in evolved large UAS.
“Yes, we’ve seen combat losses,” he said. “We’ve also heard Pentagon leaders call our Reaper the ‘MVP’ of the campaign. That tells you something important. When a system consistently delivers decisive effects, you modernize it and build on it. And I believe that’s where the Department of War is headed.”
Alexander emphasized that Reaper was purpose-built to provide persistent surveillance, long endurance, and precision strike. MQ-9A delivers these capabilities at scale and at a fraction of the cost of manned platforms that put pilots’ lives at risk, he added.
The proliferation of small drones — quadcopters, gliders, and short-range rockets — doesn’t change fundamental operational requirements, he said.
Despite the hype, smaller platforms “can’t change physics,” Alexander noted.
“Long-range, high-payload, high-endurance missions require large, hefty airframes with significant wingspan, fuel capacity, and payload volume,” he continued. “If we are serious about surveilling and targeting across wide ocean areas, tracking mobile missile units, and holding adversary assets at risk from standoff distances, large UAS modernized for contested environments are the decisive advantage.”
Wildfire: Delivering Attritable Mass at Theater Range
Wildfire represents GA-ASI’s answer to a critical requirement: affordable combat mass that can sustain losses while maintaining operational pressure across contested theaters.
This theater-range, high-production UAS is designed specifically for high-threat environments:
Combat payload and range: Wildfire can carry two Long Range Anti-Ship Missiles (LRASM) or four Joint Strike Missiles (JSM) for meaningful combat distances and has a ferry range that exceeds 8,000 nautical miles. This enables delivery of weapons, sensors, electronic warfare capabilities, or communications relay deep into contested battlespace.
Modular architecture: Open interfaces and modular payload hard points enable modularity to support rapid mission reconfiguration, allowing commanders to adapt as threats and priorities shift during operations.
Volume production: Leveraging more than 5 million square feet of manufacturing capacity and advanced production processes, Wildfire is engineered to be built and fielded in numbers sufficient to absorb attrition while maintaining persistent theater-wide pressure.
Combined with Gambit Series capabilities, Wildfire delivers what defense leaders call “attritable mass”— large numbers of capable systems whose loss does not constitute strategic setback because they are affordable, uncrewed, and replaceable.
Gambit Series: Autonomous Combat Jets for Peer Threats
The Gambit Series represents GA-ASI’s family of autonomous jets for high-end contested operations. Built around a common core comprising roughly 70 percent of key components, the platform’s modular architecture drives down costs while simplifying production, logistics, and sustainment.
Recently selected by the U.S. Air Force for its CCA program, the FQ-42A — designed to fly alongside fighters like the F-22 — is a variant of GA-ASI’s Gambit 2.
Across six missionized Gambit variants, the architecture supports:
- Long-endurance ISR in contested airspace
- Air-to-air combat
- Adversary training for advanced threat replication
- Stealth reconnaissance in denied areas
- Carrier-based naval operations
- Penetrating air-to-ground strike and suppression of enemy air defenses
All Gambit aircraft are designed for human-machine teaming with advanced fighters and other UAS, extending sensors, adding weapons capacity, and imposing complex targeting dilemmas on adversary defenses — precisely the type of effects envisioned in modern Air Force operational concepts.
Mojave STOL: Airpower, Hold the Tarmac
Built on GA-ASI’s other pioneering aircraft, Mojave STOL addresses a critical vulnerability in modern combat: dependence on large runways.
Short Takeoff and Landing (STOL) capability: Mojave STOL operates from austere, unprepared locations — open fields, dry riverbeds, even amphibious assault ship decks — generating uncrewed combat airpower from sites adversaries cannot easily target or predict.
Advanced sensor integration: Controllable via human-portable, laptop-based ground control systems, Mojave STOL carries cutting-edge radar, electro-optical/infrared, and signals intelligence payloads, providing a comprehensive operational picture for precise targeting and situational awareness to support dispersed forces.
In a combat environment where large runways are vulnerable to adversary strikes, Mojave STOL establishes airfields without airports. Its rugged construction enables persistent ISR and strike capability sourced from improvised mobile launch and recovery sites.
MQ-9B: Evolved Flagship Platform for Standoff Operations
MQ-9B SkyGuardian and SeaGuardian remain GA-ASI’s flagship multi-mission ISR platforms, now upgraded for long-range contested operations and integration into distributed kill chains.
Long-range weapons integration: New pylons with 30-inch lug spacing accommodate larger standoff munitions, including LRASM and JSM. Combined with MQ-9B’s advanced ISR suite, this transforms the aircraft into a long-range strike and maritime interdiction platform capable of engaging far outside adversary standoff ranges.
Resilient communications: Integration with proliferated Low Earth Orbit (pLEO) satellite constellations provides low-latency, high-bandwidth, jam-resistant connectivity. In combination with DoD-standard cybersecurity, MQ-9B maintains secure command-and-control and sensor links globally, even under electronic attack.
For Air Force and joint planners, MQ-9B has evolved beyond counterinsurgency roots into a standoff sensor-shooter that functions as a resilient node in distributed operations.
Urgency Driven by Evolving Threats
Alexander noted that changing battlefield conditions have continually driven the company to advance its technology and operational concepts.
“When you look at the threats we’re seeing in Ukraine and Iran, we already knew our aircraft would need to evolve, and we’ve been pushing ahead there for years now,” he said. “But it seems like every morning the news puts fresh urgency behind delivering that vital combat capability while finding ways to strip out some of what drives up costs.”
That urgency is backed by unmatched operational experience. To date, GA-ASI has accumulated nearly 10 million flight hours, the vast majority in combat operations.
Taken as a whole, Alexander said, the aircraft portfolio shows that GA-ASI is serious about retaining its position as the leading provider of UAS to the United States and its allies.
“We know, to our core, what it takes to deliver relevant systems,” he said. “We have the people, infrastructure, and capacity in place, today, to do it at scale.
“GA-ASI is ready to answer the call.”

articles.title: EU Approves €6.1 Billion Ukraine Defense Package, Unlocking PAC-3 Patriot Purchases
articles.body:
The European Commission approved a €6.1 billion ($7.1 billion) tranche of defense funding for Ukraine on Sept. 11, including exemptions allowing Kyiv to use the money to purchase US-made PAC-3 interceptor missiles for Patriot air defense systems.
The approval allows Ukraine to draw on the EU’s €90 billion ($104 billion) support loan to purchase PAC-3 interceptors, among the few weapons capable of intercepting Russian ballistic missiles.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The decision does not, however, mean the missiles will be delivered immediately. Ukraine faces a global shortage of Patriot interceptors as it prepares for another winter of Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure.
European Commissioner for Defense and Space Andrius Kubilius confirmed the decision at a press conference in Brussels on Friday, according to a Ukrinform report, the Commission had formally approved the package after EU member states backed the measures earlier this week.
“Today, the Commission officially approved €6.1 billion for Ukraine for air defense, drones and missiles from the Ukraine Support Loan,” Kubilius said.
The latest approval means the EU has now allocated all €28.3 billion ($32.9 billion) earmarked for Ukraine’s defense under the sprogram.So far, €8.4 billion ($9.7 billion) has been disbursed. Kubilius said another €4.7 billion ($5.5 billion) is currently being processed.
Fires, Explosions Reported Across Russia as Ukrainian Drones Target Refineries, Ozon Hubs
The €90 billion support loan, approved by EU countries in April, is intended to cover around two-thirds of Ukraine’s defense and budgetary needs in 2026 and 2027 and will be delivered in tranches.
PAC-3 missiles global shortage
This latest decision allows Ukraine to bypass some of the loan’s standard procurement requirements.
Under the rules, weapons purchased with the loan are generally required to come from the EU or Ukraine sources, with equipment containing more than 35% of components sourced from third countries requires explicit approval.
Kubilius said the Commission had granted five such exemptions: three for Ukrainian companies to source drone components from outside the bloc and two for US-made equipment, including PAC-3 interceptor missiles.
“Ukraine’s military edge depends on the rapid availability of critical products in the required quantities and within very short time frames,” Kubilius said.
The commissioner said speed is particularly important for air defense, given Ukraine’s immediate needs and the limited global supply of Patriot interceptors.
The European Commission estimates that Ukraine needs around 2,000 PAC-3 interceptors annually to defend against Russian ballistic missile attacks, while global production is only gradually increasing.
Kubilius said allies are exploring ways to provide Ukraine with missiles from existing stockpiles while waiting for new production.
One option under discussion is for EU member states that already have PAC-3 missiles to transfer them to Ukraine immediately and receive replacement missiles under agreements planned for 2027.
EU relaxes sourcing rules for Ukrainian drones
Three of the five exemptions approved by the Commission relate to Ukrainian drone manufacturers.
The Commission did not specify from which countries the components covered by the exemptions would be supplied. However, an earlier exemption approved in April allowed Ukraine to source drone components from China.
The remaining two exemptions cover US-made equipment, including PAC-3 missiles, with purchases potentially coordinated through NATO.
The decision comes as Ukraine and its allies seek to strengthen air defenses before winter, when Russia is expected to again target Ukraine’s energy infrastructure with large-scale missile and drone attacks.

articles.title: Anthropic details bad actors’ efforts to misuse its AI for bioweapons
articles.body:
Criminals, state-sponsored groups, spyware vendors, scientists and propagandists have attempted to use Anthropic’s powerful artificial intelligence models to design missiles and bombs, create deadly pathogens and surveil dissidents, according to a threat intelligence report the company published on Thursday.
“The cases we share here aren’t typical misuse, but rather examples of the most notable and novel threat activity we’ve identified to date,” Anthropic wrote in its 154-page report. “We’re publishing this work because we believe we have a responsibility to disclose malicious misuse of our services.”
In particular, the company detailed five case studies of scientists using its AI models in biological research. In these examples, Anthropic said the researchers circumvented its safeguards meant to prevent users from “unsupported regions”, as well as worked to hide the purpose of their work.
“Biological misuse is one of the most serious risks of frontier AI models,” Anthropic wrote. “Without the correct safeguards, such capabilities could have catastrophic consequences.”
Anthropic said it banned these accounts. The company did not reveal the names of the research institutions or the countries where the misuse took place, saying it was uncertain of the researchers’ intent.
Anthropic gave dozens of other examples of threat actors using its AI models. Those included cyber operations such as Russian espionage and “smash-and-grab” cyberhacks; surveillance operations, including a China-based program targeting Uyghurs in Syria and another targeting internal dissidents; propaganda campaigns in Russia, Malaysia, Iran and Bangladesh; and the use of its Claude AI model in Yemen, China and Russia to develop software for conventional weapons, including firearms, missiles, armed drones, bombs and other munitions.
In one of the examples of biological research, Anthropic found a scientist using Claude to work on a state-sponsored grant application to study the virus chikungunya. The virus is a mosquito-borne disease, similar to dengue and malaria, that can cause months of severe pain, fever and other debilitating symptoms.
Such research could be used to develop vaccines, but could also be used to create biological weapons. Anthropic told the New York Times this case was especially concerning because it could see the study was to be done at a military research institute.
The report comes just two days after an Anthropic employee, Jacob Coxon, set off a media firestorm with his resignation. He stated that he quit the company because it was not acting responsibly in creating its technology. Coxon said Anthropic and its rival, OpenAI, were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence” that would cause human extinction by 2030. Current Anthropic employees posted public agreements with him.
Many AI experts say the real-world threats, like those detailed in Anthropic’s intelligence report, are far more concerning within the next three years than an apocalypse brought on by an omnipotent intelligence.
“AI accelerationism and AI doomerism are two sides of the same coin: they both enforce the notion that an AGI superbeing will come into existence,” said Heidy Khlaaf, the chief AI scientist at the AI Now Institute. Khlaaf said AI labs creating technology that can be used for cybersecurity exploitation and weapons of war could be exceedingly more deadly.
In its report, Anthropic said that the potential real-world misuse from AI models is not typically in public view, instead, it’s investigated internally and by academics, governments and international organizations.
The company said that the entire AI industry needs to work together, alongside governments, to address these harms and create defenses.
“As models become increasingly capable, their risks will increase, unless AI developers and society’s defenders act to make them safer,” Anthropic wrote.

articles.body:
The United States used more than 60 anti-aircraft missiles during Iran’s missile strike on a U.S. base in Jordan.
OSINTtechnical published footage of the massive deployment of Patriot missiles.
On September 9, a spokesperson for the Jordanian Armed Forces stated that air defense systems intercepted 18 of the 20 Iranian missiles, while two munitions fell in uninhabited areas.
Given that each PAC-3 MSE interceptor costs approximately $4 million, the missiles used during this operation likely cost between $240 million and over $400 million.

Given current rates of stockpile depletion, repeated attacks could quickly deplete the stockpiles, which would take years of production to replenish.

India has navigated the energy crisis sparked by the Iran war in part by turning to Russia, its most controversial fuel supplier in recent years.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is also expected on Friday, and is due to hold talks with Modi.

articles.title: Turkish combat drone gets a longer-range strike weapon
articles.body:
- Baykar has integrated Roketsan's new 300-ER air-launched ballistic missile onto its Akıncı combat drone, with a test launch expected soon.
- The missile can strike targets more than 500 km away and extends a family of shorter-range weapons already fired from the Akıncı.
Turkish drone maker Baykar has fitted its Akıncı unmanned combat aircraft with Roketsan’s new 300-ER air-launched ballistic missile, with a first launch from the drone expected soon, according to Ulusavunma.
Roketsan first showed the 300-ER publicly at the IDEF defense show in Istanbul in July 2025, presenting it as the longest-range weapon yet in a family of air-launched missiles that began with the shorter İHA-122 and İHA-230. The missile can hit targets more than 500 km (310 miles) away, depending on the altitude it is launched from.
The 300-ER measures about 5 meters (16 feet) long, weighs 900 kg (1,980 lb) and carries a warhead of more than 150 kg (330 lb) inside a 370 mm-diameter body. It navigates using GNSS and inertial guidance and switches to a TV camera seeker for the final approach to the target, a setup Roketsan says is built for precision strikes on radars, armored vehicles, air defense systems and command centers.
The missile extends a lineage Roketsan built from its ground-launched artillery rockets. The company adapted its 122 mm and 230 mm-class rockets into the air-launched İHA-122 and İHA-230, both of which Baykar has already test-fired from the Akıncı, hitting targets roughly 55 km and 100 km away in past trials. The 300-ER carries that same approach out to a much longer range, inside a larger airframe.
That range matters because it lets a large drone like the Akıncı release a weapon and turn away before coming within reach of many surface-to-air missile systems built to intercept aircraft rather than incoming ballistic threats. Roketsan has said the missile is also intended for use on fighter jets and on Baykar’s jet-powered Kızılelma combat drone.
Roketsan told Turkish media in April 2026 that it expected to complete initial test firings of the 300-ER and deliver the missile to the Turkish Armed Forces within the year. Baykar’s September 10 statement does not say whether that test launch has already taken place or specify a date for it, and neither company has disclosed when the missile might enter regular service.

articles.title: Why Yemen government forces collapsed ahead of Houthi offensive
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Why Yemen government forces collapsed ahead of Houthi offensive
Yemen's Houthi movement has taken control of the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait after seizing Mayyun Island and government forces withdrew from Perim Island, following a rapid collapse of positions held by forces aligned with the internationally recognised government.
The developments came a day after the Houthis took control of the Red Sea city of Mokha, following about a week of heavy fighting.
The speed of the reversal has raised questions over the state of government forces on Yemen's western coast. Until shortly before the withdrawals, reports from the area had pointed to government advances. Their lines then collapsed within hours.
A Houthi official told The New Arab on Friday that the group had taken control of Mayyun Island and completed its control of Bab al-Mandab.
Reuters, citing two government sources, reported that Yemeni government forces had withdrawn from Perim Island.
The strait is one of the world's most important maritime chokepoints, connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean.
The latest reversal followed a series of withdrawals by government forces along Yemen's western coast.
On Thursday, forces loyal to the internationally recognised government withdrew from Mokha, near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, after earlier withdrawals from the districts of Hays and al-Wazi'iyah.
Government sources told The New Arab that orders had been issued on Wednesday evening for troops to leave Mokha, without an explanation being given for the immediate reason.
The withdrawal was described to the troops as part of a "redeployment".
Government forces then began leaving the headquarters of the Joint Forces formations in the city.
On Thursday morning, Presidential Leadership Council member Lieutenant General Tareq Saleh said forces on the western coast had been ordered to "reorganise their ranks".
He said the Joint Forces had established a command centre south of Mokha after what he described as "Houthi forces breaking through the various fighting fronts under intense fire pressure in which the Houthis used various types of weapons".
Saleh added that "the armed forces on the western coast, the National Resistance, Giants and Nation's Shield forces, in addition to units of the Taiz axis west of the governorate, have paid a heavy price, in martyrs and wounded, throughout the past days as they confronted the Houthi attack".
"We directed the formation of an alternative command centre in a safe location that would regroup the forces in consultation with the leadership of the Arab coalition and the Leadership Council," he said.
No official clarification followed about Saleh's location, the status of the forces under his command or the site of the command centre he said had been established south of Mokha.
Unconfirmed reports suggested it could be in the Dhubab area.
The Presidential Leadership Council, Joint Forces command and defence ministry also issued no further statements explaining the fate of the forces after the announcement that they were reorganising.
The lack of clarity has prompted widespread questions in Yemen about what happened, particularly after the government forces had announced advances before the balance on the ground changed rapidly.
Why Mokha matters
Mokha had been under heavy pressure in the days before the withdrawal.
The city was struck by dozens of missiles and explosive drones, while the Houthi advance accelerated after the movement deployed thousands of fighters to fronts west of Taiz.
Mokha lies in the far south-west of Taiz governorate, about 90km from the provincial capital and roughly 60 to 70km south of the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Its proximity to one of the world's main maritime routes for energy trade and oil tankers gives it major strategic importance and links its security directly to shipping through the Red Sea.
The city had also housed the headquarters of the Joint Forces, one of the most important military groupings aligned with Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council.
The formations include the National Resistance led by Tareq Saleh, the Southern Giants Brigades led by Presidential Leadership Council member Abu Zara'a al-Muharrami, and the Tihama Resistance Brigades.
The Joint Forces comprise about 30 military brigades.
They were reorganised and restructured at the beginning of 2026 into five main divisions and forces under direct Saudi supervision. These include the Guardians of the Republic, Tihama Brigades, Zaraniq Brigades and Giants Brigades, as well as a naval formation and specialised security forces.
Observers had regarded the formations as a major strike force and an integrated military institution protecting the southern gateway to the Red Sea.
Houthis say navigation remains safe
Hizam al-Assad, a member of the Houthi political bureau, told The New Arab that "what our Yemeni armed forces have carried out in some coastal areas is an internal national operation within the framework of imposing Yemeni sovereignty and dealing with the challenges and ambitions that threaten civil peace".
He added that "freedom of navigation and the movement of international trade in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab are safe and regular, and there is no need for any international concern about them, as there is no danger to them from the Yemeni side".
"The operations currently taking place have specific objectives in accordance with what was previously announced and come within the defensive framework," Assad said.
Asked whether the movement intended to impose fees at Bab al-Mandab after taking control of it, he said: "We have no such intention."
Yasmine al-Eryani, executive director for knowledge production at the Sana'a Center for Strategic Studies, said government forces had remained largely defensive in the previous period, with the exception of counter-operations in al-Jawf intended to disperse Houthi forces and ease pressure on Mokha.
She said the Houthis' determination to advance towards the city and their willingness to sustain heavy losses suggested they were seeking a rapid operation rather than a prolonged battle.
Eryani said the timing of the attack was significant in the context of regional escalation, arguing that Houthi moves appeared to coincide with "Iran's escalation ladder".
She warned that any attempt to impose fees or service arrangements at Bab al-Mandab could set a dangerous precedent and reshape the rules governing global maritime navigation.
Saudi calculations remain unclear
On the performance of government forces, Eryani said that despite some relative improvement in their capabilities and cohesion, the battle had tested whether the government had succeeded in unifying its military command.
"And it is clear that it has not done so yet," she said.
She said confronting an experienced fighting force such as the Houthis required a flexible military strategy, unified command and a disciplined defensive doctrine.
The growing use of drones and air power had altered the nature of the confrontation, she said, but was not sufficient on its own to determine the outcome.
Eryani also pointed to fragile military morale during the fighting.
She said the Houthis had invested in an information campaign that deepened doubts over whether reinforcements would arrive from other units.
Any military advance against the Houthis required simultaneous and coordinated mobilisation across multiple fronts, she said, something that did not happen during this confrontation.
Despite the setback, Eryani said the fighting reflected expectations among broad sections of Yemenis that advancing towards Sanaa and restoring state institutions could once again be possible, at least at a psychological level.
She cautioned, however, that it was too early to draw final conclusions from a battle taking place in a highly volatile environment where all scenarios remained open.
Eryani said Saudi Arabia's calculations remained unclear.
Riyadh had not indicated full support for a broad military operation and continued to stress that diplomatic channels remained open, despite what she described as Houthi provocations.
At the same time, Saudi Arabia had continued to provide the Yemeni government with relatively high levels of support and was likely to have been part of the calculations preceding the decision to respond militarily.
Eryani said no outside state could ultimately decide the conflict on behalf of the Yemeni side.
Regional and international interests in maritime security and deterring cross-border attacks could provide the government with allies, she said, but could not substitute for unified Yemeni political will to build a stable state.
"No one will put their full weight behind a weak link," she added.

articles.title: Iran nuclear file is back at the UN Security Council. What now?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran's nuclear file is back at the UN Security Council. What will happen next?
The International Atomic Energy Agency's Board of Governors has referred Iran to the UN Security Council over its alleged failure to comply with nuclear non-proliferation obligations, marking the first such referral in 20 years.
The 35-member board adopted the resolution on Wednesday by 23 votes in favour, with Russia, China and Niger voting against and eight countries abstaining.
Submitted by the United States, Britain, France and Germany, the resolution follows an earlier decision in June 2025 that found Iran to be in "non-compliance" with its obligations.
The latest move represents a significant diplomatic escalation between Tehran and Western powers, but with Russia and China holding veto power at the Security Council, it remains unclear whether it will result in any concrete action against Iran.
So why has Iran been referred, what could happen next, and what does it mean for Tehran's nuclear programme?
Why has Iran been referred to the Security Council?
The referral stems from the IAEA's previous finding that Iran had failed to comply with its nuclear non-proliferation obligations.
The agency's concerns predate the latest US-Iran war and centre partly on Tehran's failure to provide satisfactory explanations for traces of uranium found at undeclared Iranian sites that the IAEA had spent years investigating.
The Board of Governors ruled in June 2025 that Iran was in "non-compliance", but referring the matter to the Security Council on that basis required a separate resolution.
Wednesday's resolution also builds on a more recent decision calling on Iran to declare its remaining enriched uranium stockpile and allow IAEA inspectors to verify it.
What exactly does the new resolution do?
The resolution asks IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi to report on the latest decision and previous resolutions to all IAEA members, as well as to the UN Security Council and General Assembly.
Unlike a consensus decision, the resolution was put to a vote. Twenty-three countries backed it; Russia, China and Niger opposed it; and eight abstained.
It was submitted by four Western states: the US, Britain, France and Germany.
The referral itself does not impose new sanctions or other penalties on Iran. Instead, it formally brings the issue before the Security Council and increases diplomatic pressure on Tehran.
Why is the decision significant?
It is the first time Iran's nuclear file has been referred to the Security Council on non-compliance grounds in two decades.
It also comes during a vastly different political and military environment.
The June 2025 non-compliance finding was adopted just one day before Israel began bombing Iranian nuclear facilities, with the United States subsequently joining the attacks.
Iranian nuclear sites have also been targeted during the latest US-Israel war with Iran, while the IAEA has been unable to regain access to key facilities that were struck.
That has left the agency facing significant gaps in its knowledge about Iran's nuclear activities, including the fate of its highly enriched uranium.
How has Iran responded?
Iran has rejected the resolution as politically motivated.
Its mission to the IAEA said that "once again, a political resolution on Iran was adopted without consensus" by the agency's Board of Governors.
Tehran blamed the current situation entirely on what it described as the "criminal acts of aggression" committed by the United States and Israel, adding that Washington's objective of forcing Iran to surrender "will never be achieved".
Iran had warned before the vote that it would respond if the resolution was adopted, although its initial reaction did not specify what measures it might take.
Could the UN Security Council impose new measures on Iran?
In theory, bringing the issue before the Security Council opens another arena for international action against Tehran.
In practice, however, significant measures are considered unlikely.
Russia and China, both allies of Iran, are permanent members of the Security Council and possess veto power.
Both countries voted against Wednesday's IAEA resolution, meaning they could block attempts to impose measures against Tehran at the UN.
The immediate significance of the referral is therefore largely diplomatic: it further escalates the confrontation between Iran and Western powers and places the nuclear dispute formally before the Security Council.
What happened to Iran's enriched uranium?
This remains one of the biggest unanswered questions surrounding Iran's nuclear programme.
Iran has not allowed IAEA inspectors to return to bombed nuclear facilities, including the country's three uranium enrichment sites, which were destroyed or severely damaged in US-Israeli attacks.
Tehran has also not provided an account of its enriched uranium stockpile.
Before the strikes, the IAEA estimated that Iran possessed 440.9kg of uranium enriched to as much as 60 percent purity.
That is significantly above the levels normally associated with civilian nuclear energy and relatively close to the roughly 90 percent enrichment associated with weapons-grade material.
According to the IAEA's benchmark, the stockpile would have been sufficient, if further enriched, for around 10 nuclear weapons.
The agency believes more than 200kg of the stockpile remains at one site, although it is unclear how much survived the attacks undamaged.
Grossi has described the uncertainty surrounding the material as a "serious proliferation concern" and called for the situation to be addressed urgently.
Does this mean Iran is building a nuclear weapon?
No. The IAEA's non-compliance finding and the referral to the Security Council do not in themselves establish that Iran is building a nuclear weapon.
The dispute concerns Iran's compliance with its safeguards and reporting obligations, unanswered questions surrounding nuclear material and the IAEA's inability to verify the status of its enriched uranium stockpile.
Iran has consistently maintained that its nuclear programme is intended for peaceful purposes.
The immediate question is therefore not whether the Security Council will determine that Iran has decided to build a bomb, but whether the referral can increase pressure on Tehran to restore cooperation with inspectors and account for its nuclear material.
With Russia and China likely to oppose punitive Security Council action, the referral may ultimately have greater diplomatic significance than immediate practical consequences.

articles.title: Putin and Xi in India for BRICS summit as Ukraine, Middle East wars loom
articles.body:
Putin arrives in India for BRICS summit set to be dominated by Middle East, Ukraine wars
Russian President Vladimir Putin arrived in New Delhi on Friday for a two-day BRICS summit expected to focus on wars in Ukraine and the Middle East and economic challenges. Putin and Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian are due to meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi, while China’s Xi Jinping is also expected to hold talks.
Russian President Vladimir Putin arrived in the Indian capital on Friday ahead of an 11-member BRICS summit set to be dominated by wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, as well as economic challenges.
Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian were due to hold talks with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, while Chinese President Xi Jinping was also expected to meet him on the sidelines of the two-day meeting, according to Indian diplomatic sources.
Putin arrived at Palam Air Force Station in New Delhi, where he was greeted by India's Minister of State for External Affairs Kirti Vardhan Singh, according to footage broadcast by Russia's Ria Novosti news agency.
For China's Xi, it will be his first visit to India since 2019 and marks the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the rival neighbours, six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Himalayan border.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming again recently, with flights, visas and high-level contacts gradually being restored.
However, deep mistrust remains, with their contested frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.
Read moreChina, Russia conclude BRICS+ naval drills in South Africa amid controversy
'Fault line'
Posters of a beaming Modi line streets across New Delhi to welcome leaders, with heavy deployments of security forces across the capital and widespread traffic restrictions in central districts. Delhi police have urged people to be patient and cooperative.
BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.
It has since expanded and now includes Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates – three countries with sharply differing positions on the war launched by the United States and Israel in February.
"The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the BRICS summit," said Harsh V. Pant of India's Observer Research Foundation.
"What was seen until last year as an achievement – the expansion of BRICS – today looks like a big constraint on BRICS," Pant said.
Read moreXi calls on Mideast nations to be ‘masters of their own affairs’ in rare Egypt visit
It will be Pezeshkian's first visit to India as Iranian president, and will put the Middle East conflict firmly on the agenda.
"The war in Iran will provide a stern test of the (expanded) group's cohesion," said Shilan Shah of Capital Economics, noting the failure of the BRICS foreign ministers to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May.
India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the Iran war in part by turning to Russia, one of its most important strategic partners and its most controversial fuel supplier in recent years as the war against Ukraine drags on.
Putin last visited India in December 2025, but he also met Modi in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, this month.
Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar visited Kyiv this month, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he was "grateful to India for its commitment to ending this unjust war".
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: GUR: Around 25,000 DPRK troops already rotate through Russian army ranks
articles.body:
Approximately 25,000 North Korean troops have already rotated through the Russian armed forces, Lieutenant General Oleh Ivaschenko, Chief of the Main Intelligence Agency (GUR) of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, said in an interview with The Times.
Currently, according to Ivaschenko, about 8,000 DPRK troops are present in Russia's Kursk region.
"Today, there are approximately 8,000 DPRK troops in Russia's Kursk region. Our intelligence indicates that their numbers could rise to around 50,000," he said.
Overall, the GUR estimates that Russia has already recruited more than 28,000 foreign fighters—including individuals from African nations drawn by promises of high pay. However, the GUR believes the number of North Korean troops within Russian forces could increase sharply.
North Korea is also supplying ballistic missiles to Russia.
As of August last year, the GUR estimated that Pyongyang had supplied at least 150 KN-23 or KN-24 missiles, with another 120 promised.
As previously reported, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy noted that Russia plans to deploy between 30,000 and 50,000 troops from the DPRK on its territory.

Russia’s New Jet-Powered Drones Hitting Ukraine Packed With Nearly 100 Foreign Components
Nearly 100 foreign-made parts have been recovered from jet-powered strike drones used during attacks on Kyiv and other regions, according to Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Ukraine's presidential commissioner for sanctions policy.
The identified parts include hardware produced in the United States, China, Taiwan, European countries, Germany, and Japan, as reported by Unian.

Ukrainian specialists document every recovered part by its individual serial number to build tracking databases and expose evade-and-supply routes.
Once cataloged, the evidence is passed to international allies to help enforce stricter trade controls.
During the overnight assault on July 2, Russia launched hundreds of strike drones and dozens of missiles targeting Ukraine, concentrating its heaviest strikes on Kyiv and causing extensive destruction across multiple districts.
Ukrainian specialists examining the recovered wreckage identified approximately 35,000 foreign-manufactured components embedded within the weapons systems.
These dual-use and civilian microelectronics originated from prominent global technology firms, including Texas Instruments, Analog Devices, Intel, AMD, STMicroelectronics, Infineon, NXP, Murata, Bosch, Toshiba, and Raspberry Pi, alongside various Chinese producers.
Vladyslav Vlasiuk explained that Moscow acquired these items through complex networks of international intermediaries to supply its military production facilities.
He stressed that Ukraine regularly shares detailed findings with its foreign partners, urging international governments and manufacturers to strengthen export controls and thoroughly audit distribution chains supplying high-risk customers.
Russian Geran-2 attack drones were constructed almost entirely from foreign-made components despite international sanctions, according to an investigation published by the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP) on February 18. Journalists identified hundreds of Western and Eastern parts, including microchips, receivers, transistors, and fuel pumps, while finding only a few dozen components of Russian origin.
Although European and American authorities prohibited direct high-tech exports to Moscow, trade data revealed that hundreds of shipments of sanctioned European components reached Russia through intermediary procurement networks based primarily in China and Hong Kong. European manufacturers confirmed their compliance with export restrictions and noted that their parts were likely acquired through third-party brokers, pre-sanction inventory, or illicit smuggling routes.

articles.title: How the U.S. Treasury's New Aviation Sanctions on Iran Extend Beyond Tehran
articles.body:
The U.S. Treasury issued sweeping new sanctions against Iran on Tuesday, targeting the country’s airlines and their international service providers as it ramps up its effort to isolate Tehran from the global economy.
The aviation sanctions form a significant part of the Trump Administration's ”Operation Economic Outcast,” which the White House has described as “an unprecedented campaign to sever every remaining economic lifeline sustaining the Islamic Republic of Iran.” As negotiations have stalled, and with the U.S. and Iran engaged in active hostilities once more, the economic pressure is intended to push Tehran into a deal to end the war.
The U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned 27 Iranian airlines, accusing them of having “long supported the Iranian regime’s destabilizing activities.” The sweeping measures were largely focused on grounding Mahan Air, which was first sanctioned by the U.S. in 2011 and is also subject to E.U. sanctions. The carrier has long been accused of transporting personnel, equipment, and funds for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC).
The measures build on OFAC’s April and July actions “targeting persons servicing Mahan Air’s domestic and international flights,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.
The U.S. also designated firms based outside of Iran that it said had helped Mahan Air maintain operations by providing goods or services. This action specifically targets “covert front companies, foreign intermediaries, and deceptive transshipment routes that Iran relies on to obtain U.S.-origin aircraft and sensitive technology,” according to the Treasury.
The OFAC also suspended three Iran-related aviation authorizations that “allowed for overflights, and for non-U.S. airlines to fly U.S.-origin or U.S.-controlled commercial aircraft into Iran.”
The sanctions, and their international reach, are intended to "intensify Iran's economic isolation, to further degrade their military capability, and push them to some kind of a concession or settlement that favors the United States,” Jack Roush, a PhD candidate affiliated with the Iranian History Initiative at the London School of Economics, tells TIME.
Here’s what to know about the latest sanctions, how they extend beyond the borders of Iran, and the economic pressure mounting against Tehran.
Aviation sanctions target Kazakhstan, Malaysia, Turkey, and UAE-based firms
The U.S. Treasury has accused Iran of using front companies and other pass-through entities in third countries in an attempt to evade aviation links back to Tehran and has extended sanctions to nine internationally-based entities it alleges have aided these efforts.
Measures were imposed on two UAE-based commercial entities and a UAE-based individual, as well as one Turkish-based and one U.K.-based firm.
Four cargo providers and general sales agents were also sanctioned, accused of servicing Mahan Air and coordinating shipments on behalf of the airline. Two are based in Turkey, one in Kazakhstan, and one in Malaysia.
The new sweeping sanctions “will exacerbate challenges that Iran already faces in maintaining its fleet,” says Sanam Vakil, director of the Middle East and North Africa programme at Chatham House.
With the reliance on foreign entities to maintain Iran’s aging fleet, the measures targeting companies outside of Iran will likely damage Tehran’s aviation capabilities, she says, as it will “restrict Iran's ability to rely on those regional hubs” and could prompt “international carriers [to] further reduce or suspend Iranian services.”
“If that happens, then this becomes a blockade of Iran's aviation infrastructure, which is quite serious,” says Vakil.
U.S. issues warning to anyone doing business with Iran amid effort to choke Tehran off from global economy
The U.S. Treasury has vowed to isolate any international entity that continues to show support to Mahan Air. “Let this be a warning to anyone doing business with Iran’s remaining airlines, all of which we sanctioned,” Bessent said. “You are at risk of being cut off from the global financial system.”
In recent weeks, the U.S. has imposed sanctions on banking institutions in other countries, accusing the lenders of enabling Iran.
On. Aug. 28, the U.S. moved to cut off Egyptian Banque Misr's UAE-located branches from the dollar-based financial system. Banque Misr said it is reviewing the notice from the U.S. Treasury and will communicate with the department “to obtain further information and maintain ongoing cooperation.”
Days later, the U.S. Treasury sanctioned Turkey's Golden Global investment bank and two subsidiaries, accusing it of enabling the transfer of oil revenues from China to Iran. Golden Global rejected the allegations, calling them “entirely unfounded and inconsistent.”
The sanctions were significant, marking the first time a bank in a NATO ally had been hit under the current economic campaign, experts told Reuters.
These recent U.S. sanctions on Turkish firms are the latest points of tension between the two countries. In 2019, Turkish state-run lender Halkbank was charged in a Manhattan federal court, accused of participating in a “multibillion-dollar Iranian sanctions evasion scheme.”
The charges—referred to by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan as “ugly”—dragged on for years, before a settlement was reached in March. Halkbank was barred from entering transactions that benefit Iran and had to hire a compliance monitor to review its sanctions and anti-money-laundering programs.
The two NATO allies have also clashed in their differences of opinion related to Israel's operations in Gaza, Trump’s tariff policies, and Washington’s maintained block on F-35 fighter jet sales to Turkey while Ankara still holds Russian-made S-400 air defense systems.
Republican Sen. Rick Scott of Florida earlier this week said “Turkey is not our friend” as he showed support for the sanctions targeting firms in the country. “Bessent had to crack down on them for actively funding Iranian terrorists,” he claimed.
How corporations in other countries respond to the U.S. measures “is an important test” for the Trump Administration, Roush says, noting that despite Washington’s crackdown on international entities supporting the Iranian economy, some have shown they’re willing to continue doing business with Tehran.
"A lot of these smaller, more boutique firms… They're more informal. They tend to continue their trade ties or banking ties with Iran. The UAE has done, or well, they're trying to do a good job of severing these ties with Iran, but other states in the region, like Iraq and Azerbaijan and Turkey, are continuing to trade with Iran,” says Roush. “Iran is an important trading partner for them, and I think it's going to take a significant amount of diplomatic pressure to impose some kind of a full blockade of Iran.”
How Iran has responded to the aviation sanctions
Iran’s ambassador to the United Nations Gholamhossein Darzi on Wednesday argued that Washington’s sanctions amount to “economic terrorism” and “collective punishment,” according to Iran's Mehr news agency.
Abbas Araghchi, Iran’s Foreign Minister, dismissed the effectiveness of the “economic D-Day” campaign.
“After 47 years of sanctions, the U.S. went to war with Iran on behalf of Israel. The fallout has been disastrous for America, including its standing worldwide,” he said Tuesday. “After failing to achieve its aims through sanctions or war, Washington’s ‘novel’ solution is… more sanctions. Seriously?”
But experts say the ramped up economic pressure campaign will undoubtedly impact Iran in some way.
The aviation-related measures alone will “make it harder to transport materiel to keep Mahan Air going, and it'll contribute to regional isolation,” says Roush.
Furthermore, Iran is already feeling the economic impact of the conflict and the U.S. naval blockade on its ports in the Strait of Hormuz.
On Sep. 10, Iran’s Rial currency plummeted in value, hitting a record low open-market rate of 2.34 million rials to the dollar. Inflation has also climbed significantly, with reports indicating rural communities and low-income households are carrying the burden. The country lost around 630,000 manufacturing jobs in the first quarter of 2026, according to the Statistical Center of Iran.
“Ultimately, the Iranian people are likely to suffer, because the regime will continue its predatory practice of absorbing the economic resources of the country and channeling it toward its military efforts,” concludes Roush.

articles.title: Ukraine hits key Russia-Iran logistics hub in Caspian Sea, damages three Russian warships
articles.body:
Ukraine says its forces struck Russia’s Makhachkala port on the Caspian Sea and confirmed damage to three Russian warships in the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk in a series of long-range attacks.
Ukraine’s General Staff said the Makhachkala Sea Commercial Port in Russia’s Dagestan was hit overnight on 10 September, with a fire recorded at the site. The extent of the damage is still being assessed.
The Special Operations Forces (SSO) said Ukrainian units struck oil infrastructure at the port in a joint operation with other Defense Forces. The port’s oil terminal handles tankers with a capacity of up to 10,000 tonnes, while an oil depot is located nearby, according to the SSO.
Makhachkala is Russia’s only ice-free deepwater port on the Caspian Sea and operates year-round. The General Staff said it is an important link in the Russia-Iran logistics corridor, which Moscow uses to bypass Western sanctions.
According to the General Staff, the route is used to transport military-related cargo in both directions, including components and Shahed-type attack drones from Iran to Russia, and explosives, drone components, and ammunition from Russia to Iran. A base of Russia’s Caspian Flotilla is also located near the port.
The SSO said damaging the port’s oil infrastructure could reduce Russia’s ability to use the Caspian Sea to transport and transship energy resources.
Fire Point, a Ukrainian drone manufacturer, said Ukrainian forces used its FP-1 drones in the attack. The company said Makhachkala had been used as a transit point for Iranian attack drones delivered to Russia by sea before being moved onward for use against Ukraine.
Fire Point also said the port handled more than 2.9 million tonnes of cargo in the first eight months of 2026, including more than 2.08 million tonnes of oil.
Three Russian warships hit in Novorossiysk
Ukraine’s General Staff also said further analysis of data confirmed damage inflicted on three Russian warships in the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk on 9 September, along with fuel-oil storage facilities at the port.
The General Staff identified the vessels as the small sea minesweeper Zheleznyakov, the frigate Admiral Essen, and the Project 11711 landing ship Pyotr Morgunov.
Visual analysis published by Exilenova+ reported strikes on another Russian warship, the Buyan-M-class corvette, as well as confirming strikes on the frigates Admiral Essen and Admiral Makarov. The outlet said the Essen was hit in its superstructure and caught fire.
The Buyan-M class is capable of carrying Kalibr and Oniks cruise missiles. Russia has used such ships to launch strikes against Ukraine.
The Ukrainian General Staff said operations against key Russian military targets are continuing.

articles.title: Putin lands in India for BRICs summit, shadowed by Iran and Ukraine wars
articles.body:
Putin lands in India for BRICS summit, shadowed by Iran and Ukraine wars
Russian, Iranian leaders due to hold talks with India’s Modi at summit dominated by wars in the Middle East and Ukraine.
Russian President Vladimir Putin arrived in the Indian capital on Friday ahead of an 11-member BRICS summit set to be dominated by wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, as well as economic challenges.
Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian are due to hold talks with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, while Chinese President Xi Jinping is also expected to meet Modi on the sidelines of the two-day meeting.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Trump says Putin wants to make a deal to end Ukraine war
- list 2 of 4Europe’s far right: Putin’s best friend?
- list 3 of 4UN envoy warns Security Council Yemen’s war has entered ‘dangerous phase’
- list 4 of 4Iran claims to have captured a US ‘sail drone’ near Hormuz Strait
Putin arrived at Palam Air Force Station in New Delhi, where he was greeted by India’s Minister of State for External Affairs Kirti Vardhan Singh, according to footage broadcast by Russia’s Ria Novosti news agency.
Posters of a beaming Modi lined streets across New Delhi to welcome leaders, with heavy deployments of security forces across the capital and widespread traffic restrictions in central districts. Delhi police have urged people to be patient and cooperative.
BRICS, which stands for the original members of the grouping – Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa – was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.
It has since expanded, and now includes Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates – three countries with sharply differing positions on the US-Israel war on Iran launched in February.
“The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the BRICS summit,” Harsh V Pant of India’s Observer Research Foundation told the AFP news agency.
“What was seen until last year as an achievement – the expansion of BRICS – today looks like a big constraint on BRICS,” Pant said.
It will be Pezeshkian’s first visit to India as Iranian president, and will put the Middle East conflict firmly on the agenda. The Iranian president’s visit marks the first in eight years for the role.
“The war in Iran will provide a stern test of the (expanded) group’s cohesion,” Shilan Shah of Capital Economics told AFP, noting the failure of the BRICS foreign ministers to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May.
India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the war on Iran in part by turning to Russia, one of its most important strategic partners and its most controversial fuel supplier in recent years, as Moscow’s war against Ukraine drags on.
Putin last visited India in December 2025, but he also met Modi in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, this month.
Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar visited Kyiv this month, where Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he was “grateful to India for its commitment to ending this unjust war”.
For China’s Xi, it will be his first visit to India since 2019, and marks the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the rival neighbours, six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Himalayan border.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming again recently, with flights, visas and high-level contacts gradually being restored.
However, deep mistrust remains, with their contested frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.

Russian forces strike two dry cargo ships, motor boat at Chernomorsk port

The U.S. government announced new sanctions on Thursday against firms and individuals that it says are aiding Hezbollah and other Iranian proxies in the Middle East as it intensified its campaign to isolate Iran economically.
The latest sanctions are part of the Treasury Department's "Operation Economic Outcast," first announced 24 August, which aim to cut off the revenues that Tehran is using to fund the war, build missiles, conduct cyberattacks and support the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, or IRGC.

OFAC also issued a bulletin making clear that it would deny most Iran-related licensing requests, except in exceptional circumstances, and said its licensing division had immediately begun denying "the vast majority" of outstanding Iran-related specific license requests.

articles.body:

Ukrainian FP-1 Drones Fly Record 3,200 km to Strike Russian Gas Processing Plant
Ukrainian FP-1 long-range drones traveled more than 3,200 kilometers to strike a gas condensate processing facility in Russia’s Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug, setting a new reported distance record for the drone, according to Ukrainian defense company Fire Point and the CyberBoroshno OSINT project.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Fire Point said the target was the Novy Urengoy Condensate Preparation for Transport Plant, one of Russia’s largest facilities for processing gas condensate.
The strike also marks a significant increase in the FP-1’s reported reach. The drone initially had a maximum range of about 700 kilometers, compared with the more than 3,200 kilometers covered in the latest operation, substantially expanding the depth at which targets inside Russia can potentially be reached.
“We are erasing the deep rear doctrine from the Russian military vocabulary,” Fire Point CEO Iryna Terekh said at MSPO 2026 according to a UNITED24 Media correspondent.
CyberBoroshno reported that the drones specifically struck a de-ethanization gas treatment unit at the facility, operated by Gazprom Pererabotka and located about 18 kilometers from Novy Urengoy.
According to the OSINT project, FP-1 drones reached the Yamalo-Nenets region for the first time, making the facility the most distant target from Ukraine’s state border to have been struck since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Unlike oil refineries frequently targeted in Ukrainian long-range operations, the Novy Urengoy facility is part of Russia’s gas-processing industry. It handles the initial processing of unstable gas condensate into marketable products and receives feedstock from fields in the Nadym-Pur-Taz region, Russia’s largest gas-condensate basin. The plant has a design capacity of approximately 19.5 million tons of feedstock annually.
The unit targeted in the strike processes gases released during the de-ethanization of condensate. These gases contain ethane, a key feedstock for producing ethylene and polyethylene, and are intended to supply the Novy Urengoy Gas Chemical Complex.
The gas chemical complex has a planned production capacity of up to 400,000 tons of low-density polyethylene per year. CyberBoroshno estimated that this represents roughly 10% of Russia’s combined polyethylene and polypropylene production capacity.
According to the OSINT project, damage to the de-ethanization gas treatment unit could disrupt the broader production chain from gas condensate to polyethylene. Without gas treatment, ethane supplies to the Novy Urengoy Gas Chemical Complex could be interrupted, potentially affecting the production of ethylene and polyethylene.
CyberBoroshno noted that even if the plant’s condensate de-ethanization units remain operational, disruption to the gas treatment infrastructure could prevent the resulting gases from being processed and transferred further along the production chain.
The record-range FP-1 strike comes as Fire Point continues to expand its portfolio of domestically developed long-range weapons. The company has also advanced its FP-7 ballistic missile to military trials after completing two earlier rounds of testing, moving the system closer to potential operational deployment.

articles.title: EU approves funding for Patriot missiles for Ukraine
articles.body:
EU approves funding for Patriot missiles for Ukraine
EU Commissioner for Defense and Space Andrius Kubilius said this at a press conference in Brussels on Friday, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
"Today, the Commission officially also approved EUR 6.1 billion for Ukraine air defense drones and missiles from the Ukraine Support Loan. This is really a very important step forward. We worked a lot with member states and Ukraine to this goal," the commissioner said.
He stressed that the decision is a crucial step toward ensuring the Ukrainian military's combat capability and protecting critical infrastructure from Russian attacks.
According to the official, the decision will allow Ukraine to urgently address shortages of precision weapons and missiles for Patriot air defense systems through exemptions from the general procurement rules.
"The decision officially enables Ukraine to procure PAC-3 missiles for Patriots. Funded under the Ukraine Support Loan, the package includes five derogations from standard eligibility conditions – three for Ukrainian-made drones and components exceeding cost thresholds and two for U.S.-made equipment, in particular PAC-3 missiles, including we as a NATO-coordinated portal mechanism," Kubilius said.
The EU commissioner noted that the speed of deliveries is now a decisive factor, and that the partnership between the EU and Ukraine should ensure a steady supply of the weapons needed on the battlefield.
"Ukraine's military edge depends on the rapid availability of critical products in the required quantities and within very short time frames. Accelerating EU deliveries through desk stocking, reprioritizing orders, and ramping up the production remains crucial," he said.
Asked about the timeline for the delivery of PAC-3 missiles, Kubilius stressed that allies are looking for flexible solutions to immediately meet Ukraine's needs until new batches leave the factory.
He said the question now was whether it is possible to reach agreements with member states that already have PAC-3 missiles in their stockpiles to transfer these missiles from their stocks to Ukraine now and then receive replacements under Ukraine's agreements for 2027.
As reported, under the approved decision, the European Union has fully allocated the EUR 28.3 billion planned for this year to finance Ukraine's defense under the Ukraine Support Loan.
The European Commission is currently processing a request for the disbursement of another EUR 4.7 billion tranche, after EUR 8.3 billion had already been transferred.
According to European Commission estimates, Ukraine's annual needs to defend against ballistic attacks amount to around 2,000 PAC-3 interceptor missiles for Patriot systems, while global production capacity is only gradually increasing, requiring flexible solutions from NATO and EU allies.
