articles.title: Western partners should treat Ukraine's defense industry as extension of their own – ex-Google chief
articles.body:
Western countries should treat Ukraine's defense industry as an extension of their own, jointly producing weapons, resolving supply chain bottlenecks, and guaranteeing Ukrainian troops the quantities of strike capability they need, former Google CEO and chairman Eric Schmidt argues.
According to a column by Schmidt published in the Washington Post, the U.S. needs to recognize that Russia is pursuing a total-war strategy, mobilizing its factories and manpower.
He said that for most of the full-scale invasion, Ukraine's great advantage was its ability to adapt and innovate, while the enemy had greater numbers of troops, funding and industrial capacity.
"That advantage is rapidly shrinking. When Ukraine developed interceptors capable of destroying Russian Shahed drone swarms, Russia adapted by fielding faster, jet-powered Shaheds that are much harder to intercept," the former Google CEO said.
He said Russia is now deploying a satellite constellation that could rival Starlink, which Ukrainian drone units use to strike Russian forces in occupied Ukrainian territory.
He said that for years the enemy's strategy was to counter Ukrainian innovation with its own industrial scale, but Russia is now combining scale of production with its own innovation as well.
Schmidt also pointed to the rapid pace of technological competition in the war, in which a drone can be effective the moment it appears but lose its edge within a few months as the adversary adapts.
He said Ukraine is successfully adapting to such changes, but that innovation alone is not enough to scale production and meet the demands of a full-scale, high-intensity war.
"A brilliant drone built in the hundreds is interesting, but a good drone built in the hundreds of thousands can change the course of a war," Schmidt said.
He stressed that Russia is preparing for total war, considering a large-scale mobilization and building up industrial capacity for weapons production.
According to Schmidt, Ukraine cannot withstand these Russian capabilities on its own.
"The coming winter will be decisive. Russia is already exploiting Ukraine's lack of defenses against ballistic missiles to strike power plants and substations, aiming to soon plunge Ukrainians into darkness, cold and suffering," the former Google CEO said.
He said Ukraine now needs more interceptors, ammunition and long-range strike capability, as well as investment to expand its own production capacity.
"Closer engagement with them (Ukraine's military — Interfax-Ukraine) would let Western militaries help secure Ukraine's victory, absorb hard-won lessons about modern warfare, and strengthen the international order against the threats that will shape events in the decades ahead," he wrote in the column.
At the same time, he said that praising Ukrainian resilience cannot be a strategy, since courage alone cannot defend cities or win a war.
"We cannot allow it to face another winter alone under Russian bombs," Schmidt added.

articles.title: EU urging Kiev to mobilize women – Moscow
articles.body:
EU urging Kiev to mobilize women – Moscow
The EU is encouraging Ukraine to start mobilizing women amid chronic manpower shortages and has demanded that Kiev immediately make “a political decision” on the matter, the Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) has said.
Kiev launched its mobilization campaign soon after the conflict with Russia escalated in February 2022. Amid mounting frontline losses and desertions, the mobilization drive has grown increasingly violent. Recruitment officers have repeatedly been filmed chasing, beating, and forcibly detaining reluctant conscripts before bundling them into vehicles in what in Ukraine has become known as ‘busification’.
The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, described the idea of expanding the campaign to include women as “a step in the right direction” at a recent informal EU foreign ministers’ meeting, the SVR said on Thursday, citing information it had obtained. She allegedly warned that Kiev could soon run out of manpower due to a growing shortage of men fit for military service and said that Ukraine should use Israel as a “model to follow.”
The mobilization of women has long been a subject of debate in Ukraine. MP Mariana Bezuglaya argued as early as 2024 that it was time Kiev started targeting women to meet its conscription quota. Last year, the Ukrainian presidential administration’s deputy head, Brigadier General Pavel Palisa, also voiced support for mandatory conscription of women.
According to the SVR, Brussels demanded that Kiev immediately “move from words to action” and make a formal decision to start mobilizing women.
Under current Ukrainian law, men aged 25 to 60 are subject to mobilization, while those aged 23 to 60 are generally barred from leaving the country. Women can serve voluntarily.
Kiev’s brutal mobilization campaign has encountered large-scale draft-dodging and desertion. According to Euronews, around 1.15 million fighting-age Ukrainian men had ended up in the EU as of summer 2026, despite the ban on travelling abroad. According to the SVR, up to 5.6 million Ukrainians are currently residing in other European nations, with women accounting for 43.4% of them.
Many men have proven ready to risk their lives to flee the country illegally through forests, rivers, and mountainous terrain. In February, the head of the Ukrainian border agency, Andrey Demchenko, reported that over 70 apparent draft dodgers had died since 2022, most while trying to cross the Tisza River along Ukraine’s border with Hungary and Romania.
Brussels has reportedly urged EU governments to devise legal mechanisms for sending back Ukrainian refugees residing in the bloc, the Russian intelligence service said, adding that the European Commission sees them as a reason behind the “rise of far-right sentiment” in countries such as Germany or Poland.
Some Western officials have also voiced support for the mobilization of Ukrainian women.
Last year, former UK Defense Secretary Ben Wallace said Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky should have launched a truly mass mobilization.
“Zelensky took a view that he was going to preserve the 18 to 28-year-olds, so it’s not a mass conscription,” Wallace said at the time, adding that the Ukrainian leader should have mobilized everyone and “asked Europe to train them because that is not a hard ask.”
Ben Hodges, a former top commander of US forces in Europe, argued earlier that Kiev should consider both drafting women and lowering the mobilization age to 18. “I also think that there is enough work for women in the army,” he said.
Moscow has slammed Ukraine’s NATO backers as pushing the nation into a war “to the last Ukrainian,” describing the conflict as a Western proxy war against Russia fought through Ukraine.

articles.title: Permanent 5 members clash in UN Security Council over Iran sanctions snapback
articles.body:
Yasin Gungor
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
The five permanent members of the UN Security Council clashed Thursday during a high-stakes session about the legal validity of international sanctions against Iran and the reimposition of UN sanctions under the 2015 nuclear accord's "snapback" provision.
The snapback clause, established under the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), was designed to automatically reinstate UN Chapter VII sanctions if Iran breached the deal, intentionally bypassing the veto power of permanent council members.
"The mechanism for reinstating previously adopted Security Council resolutions on Iran, a mechanism set forth in Resolution 2231, was not activated, and this for a whole host of legal and procedural reasons," said the Russian representative, demanding a procedural vote to block a scheduled briefing on the 1737 Sanctions Committee.
Moscow argued that UN Resolution 2231, which endorsed the nuclear deal, expired Oct. 18, 2025, and insisted that the non-proliferation agenda item was struck off the council's list of active matters that day. The Russian envoy maintained that the 1737 Committee ceased to exist in 2015 and that no legal grounds remain to discuss its “so-called work.”
The Chinese representative supported the move, asserting that the council presidency lacks the mandate to draft or deliver a 90-day report. Warning against unilateral action, Beijing stressed, "A few members, in disregard of differences, insist on forcibly reimposing the Council sanctions against Iran and convening Council meetings under a removed agenda item." The envoy warned that the steps deepen institutional division and impede a political settlement, expressing "grave concern" and “strong opposition" against the moves.
Western delegations firmly rejected the challenge, arguing that the sanctions regime had been legally revived following Iranian breaches.
"The United Kingdom, with France and Germany, initiated the snapback mechanism in full accordance with Security Council Resolution 2231," said the British representative, explaining that European powers acted because of Iran's "significant non-performance" under the 2015 nuclear pact. London noted that the process concluded Sept. 28, 2025, leaving six Chapter VII resolutions in effect for nearly a year.
The French representative affirmed that council resolutions were restored alongside the committee's mandate to report every 90 days.
"Regardless of such politically driven matters, the facts are the facts. The 1737 Committee exists," said the US representative, accusing Russia and China of attempting to undermine council decisions to protect Tehran. The American diplomat noted that the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) confirmed Iran remains non-compliant with its Comprehensive Safeguards Agreement.
The council voted 11-2 in favor of adopting the provisional agenda, with two abstentions, defeating the Russian and Chinese bid to halt the meeting. Under UN Security Council rules, procedural votes cannot be blocked by a permanent member's veto and require a minimum of nine affirmative votes to pass.
Permanent members trade accusations after vote
Moscow denounced the briefing as an illegitimate exercise and an "inefficient use" of council resources, with the Russian representative describing it as a “flagrant procedural breach.”
The Russian envoy accused Washington and Israel of conducting strikes on "peaceful" facilities under IAEA safeguards, warning that the "illegal and reckless actions" risked provoking a wider regional catastrophe, while dismissing a new IAEA Board of Governors resolution referring Iran to the council as “politicized.”
Beijing maintained that lasting solutions require addressing the root causes of regional tensions. The "United States’ unilateral withdrawal from the JCPOA, its use of force against Iran twice during the negotiation process, and its pursuit of a policy of maximum pressure against Iran are the primary causes of the current complex and intractable situation in the Middle East and the Iranian nuclear issue," argued the Chinese envoy. China defended lran's "legitimate right to the peaceful use of nuclear energy," and said it acknowledges “Iran's repeated commitments not to develop nuclear weapons.”
"Iran is the only country without nuclear weapons to enrich uranium to this level," said the British envoy, criticizing Tehran for reportedly stockpiling more than 400 kilograms (882 pounds) of uranium enriched to 60% without "any credible civilian justification." London accused Iran of barring UN inspectors from all nuclear facilities since June 2025, sparing only the Bushehr plant, reiterating that a negotiated settlement remains the only durable path.
Rejecting safety arguments raised by Tehran for barring inspectors, the US representative said UN personnel continue to operate safely inside war-torn Ukraine, which IAEA director Rafael Grossi noted as a "worse and more constant war zone." The American diplomat accused Moscow and Beijing of trying to shield a state whose nuclear program is progressing “in the dark.”
France underlined Tehran's stockpile, warning that the amount is potentially sufficient for about 10 explosive nuclear devices.

articles.title: NATO member risking nuclear standoff – Kremlin
articles.body:
NATO member risking nuclear standoff – Kremlin
Russia will respond to any deployment in Lithuania of nuclear weapons aimed at the country by adjusting its own posture accordingly, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has warned.
The Baltic NATO state is currently moving to abolish a constitutional ban on hosting weapons of mass destruction, which President Gitanas Nauseda described as outdated in July. Speaking to Russian TV on Friday, Peskov said Vilnius would cause another rise in tensions with the proposed move.
“If you host nuclear weapons, they are aimed at somebody. Those won’t be aimed to the west. They will be aimed to the east, i.e. at us,” Peskov said. Consequently, “our nuclear weapons will be aimed at” the hosting nation.
Lithuanian media has described the proposed constitutional reform, which could be approved as soon as this winter, as creating a legal framework for a proposed EU nuclear-sharing scheme. France, the only nuclear power in the economic bloc, is considering moving some of its weapons to other member states.
NATO already has a nuclear-sharing arrangement under which US nuclear bombs are stored in non-nuclear countries, including Belgium, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Türkiye, and the UK.
Earlier this week, a Lithuanian parliamentary committee on legal affairs approved a proposal to amend the constitution, with two MPs voting against. The opposition argued that the change should be put to a referendum, while Nauseda’s government said approval by parliament is sufficient. Constitutional amendments in Lithuania require two separate votes in parliament at least three months apart.
The provision outlawing weapons of mass destruction also bans foreign military bases and was included in the basic law to safeguard the post-Soviet republic’s neutrality. Lithuania joined NATO in 2004 along with Latvia and Estonia. Germany is currently working to deploy a heavy tank brigade in the country.
Russia has described NATO’s expansion in Europe as a key cause of current tensions with the US-led military bloc. Moscow views the forward deployment of nuclear-capable weapons near Russia’s borders as a major risk because it significantly reduces the time available to determine whether a detected attack is a false alarm or an actual strike warranting nuclear retaliation.

articles.title: Iran destroys US spy Saildrone in Hormuz (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Iran destroys US spy Saildrone in Hormuz (VIDEO)
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it has destroyed a US Saildrone Explorer reconnaissance vessel at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz, releasing footage showing the unmanned craft burning in the water.
The IRGC Navy said on Thursday that the vessel, identified by hull number 5838, was struck while operating near the strategic waterway. Iranian state media described it as an American surveillance drone, but the US military has not confirmed the loss.
“The American terrorist and aggressor army, over the past few days, out of fear of approaching and confronting the fighters of Islam, has dispatched its unmanned vessels to the Strait of Hormuz,” the IRGC said.
The Iranian Navy: We have struck a US unmanned vessel, with hull number 5838, at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz. pic.twitter.com/WyesLWXI47
— IRIB (Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting) (@iribnews_irib) September 10, 2026
The strategic waterway remains under Tehran’s control and “intelligence surveillance,” the IRGC added, warning that “any hostile presence in this strategic strait will be targeted.”
The roughly seven-meter Saildrone Explorer is an unmanned surface vessel equipped with cameras, sensors, and communications systems for maritime surveillance and reconnaissance. The US Navy previously deployed the platform with the Bahrain-based 5th Fleet’s Task Force 59, which integrates unmanned systems and AI into regional operations.
The latest incident comes just two days after the IRGC captured a US underwater drone at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz. Footage released by Tehran shows what appears to be an Anduril-built Dive-LD autonomous underwater vehicle commissioned in 2025. The Pentagon acknowledged that it lost the submersible, but said it was old and broken and carried no sensitive data or classified equipment.
The incidents come amid an escalating maritime standoff between the US and Iran.
The US has destroyed several Iranian oil tankers after accusing the IRGC of firing ballistic missiles at US warships. Iran has attacked US vessels and commercial tankers it accused of violating restrictions regarding the Strait of Hormuz.
The confrontation has severely disrupted traffic through one of the world’s most important energy corridors and pushed Brent crude above $107 a barrel, while farther west, Iran-aligned Houthi forces are tightening their grip on Bab al-Mandeb, another vital chokepoint linking the Red Sea and Indian Ocean.

articles.title: Russian forces kill 9, injure 145 across Ukraine over past day as Moscow expands gas station strikes to Kyiv
articles.body:
Russian forces kill 9, injure 145 across Ukraine over past day as Moscow expands gas station strikes to Kyiv
At least nine people were killed and 145 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day, local authorities said.
The Ukrainian Air Force reported that Russia launched 161 attack drones of various types overnight, including jet-powered drones, as well as one S-8000 "Banderol" low-cost cruise missile. According to the Air Force, Ukrainian forces shot down or suppressed 138 drones using electronic warfare, with hits recorded at 19 locations, while falling debris from downed drones struck three additional sites.
During the Russian attack on Odesa early on Sept. 11, Romania scrambled F-16 fighter jets to monitor drones or missiles approaching the Romanian border. No violations of Romanian airspace were ultimately recorded, the Romanian Defense Ministry said.
In Pavlohrad, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, a Russian strike on a shopping center in the middle of the day caused a mass-casualty incident, according to Ukrainian authorities. At least five people were killed and 67 others injured, including at least three children.
Across the rest of the region, two people were killed in Russian attacks on the regional capital, Dnipro, on Sept. 10, while five others, including a 6-year-old girl, were injured, local authorities reported.
Two more men were injured in overnight attacks in Dnipro, while one person was injured in the Nikopol district, according to Governor Oleksandr Hanzha.
In Donetsk Oblast, Russian attacks killed one resident of Kramatorsk and injured 29 other residents of the region over the past day, according to Governor Vadym Filashkin.
In Kyiv, Russian jet-powered drone strikes continued, hitting several civilian targets, including a gas station. Four people were injured in attacks on Sept. 10, while eight more were injured in an overnight drone strike on a residential building, city authorities reported.
The Sept. 10 strike marked the first time Russian forces targeted a gas station in Kyiv, after similar attacks had largely been concentrated in frontline regions. The expanding campaign is complicating fuel distribution, with potential consequences for both civilians and military personnel who depend on passenger vehicles to get around.
The attacks continued as Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski arrived in the Ukrainian capital by train.
A woman was also killed in a Russian drone strike in Kyiv Oblast's Vyshhorod district on Sept. 11, according to Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Regional State Administration.
In Kharkiv Oblast, a 49-year-old man was wounded by Russian shelling in the settlement of Zolochiv, according to local authorities.
In Kherson Oblast, nine people were injured in various Russian attacks, local authorities reported.
In Odesa, a Russian attack damaged a warehouse containing humanitarian aid and injured two people, Governor Oleh Kiper said.
In Sumy Oblast, 12 people, including four children, were injured in Russian glide-bomb strikes, while a woman was wounded in a separate drone strike, local authorities reported.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, five people, including two children, were injured in Russian attacks on the city of Zaporizhzhia and the surrounding district, according to local authorities.

articles.title: Putin arrives in India for BRICS summit amid wars in Ukraine and Iran
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has arrived in the Indian capital ahead of an 11-member BRICS summit set to be dominated by wars in the Middle East and Europe, as well as economic challenges.
Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian were due to hold talks with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, while Chinese President Xi Jinping was also expected to meet him on the sidelines of the two-day meeting beginning on Friday, Indian diplomatic sources said.
Putin arrived at Palam Air Force Station in New Delhi, where he was greeted by India's Minister of State for External Affairs Kirti Vardhan Singh, according to footage broadcast by Russia's RIA Novosti news agency.
For China's Xi, it will be his first visit to India since 2019 and marks the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the rival neighbours, six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Himalayan border in India-administered Kashmir.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming again recently, with flights, visas and high-level contacts gradually being restored.
'Fault line'
Posters of a beaming Modi line streets across New Delhi to welcome leaders, with heavy deployments of security forces across the capital and widespread traffic restrictions in central districts. Delhi police have urged people to be patient and cooperative.
BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.
It has since expanded and now includes Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates — three countries with sharply differing positions on the war launched by the United States and Israel in February.
It will be Pezeshkian's first visit to India as Iranian president, and will put the Middle East conflict firmly on the agenda.
"The war in Iran will provide a stern test of the (expanded) group's cohesion," said Shilan Shah of Capital Economics, noting the failure of the BRICS foreign ministers to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the Iran war in part by turning to Russia, one of its most important strategic partners and its most controversial fuel supplier in recent years, as the war against Ukraine drags on.
Putin last visited India in December 2025, but he also met Modi in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, this month.

articles.title: Iran has resumed production of ballistic missiles, which the US called "effectively destroyed"
articles.body:
Iran has resumed production of ballistic missiles, which the US called "effectively destroyed"
Kyiv • UNN
Iran has resumed limited assembly of ballistic missiles following the ceasefire with the US. Production is continuing at underground facilities despite damage to the plants.
Iran has resumed production of ballistic missiles, using components stockpiled before the war and underground production facilities. The Wall Street Journal reports this, citing U.S. and Middle Eastern officials, writes UNN.
Details
According to U.S. intelligence, active missile assembly resumed around mid-June following the ceasefire with the United States. Iran is producing both liquid- and solid-fuel missiles.
The activity was detected at several underground facilities, including the Khodjir missile complex in the southeast of the country. Tehran is also attempting to establish new underground production sites.
Production remains limited
According to WSJ sources, Iran is currently producing significantly fewer missiles than before the war. Some factories and infrastructure were damaged by U.S. and Israeli strikes, while the naval blockade has complicated the import of necessary components.
In the spring, U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said that Iran’s missile program had been "effectively destroyed" and that the country had no ability to produce new missiles.
The White House did not directly answer the WSJ’s question about the resumption of production, instead stating that Iran’s armed forces had been seriously weakened.

articles.title: Ukrainian drones strike Makhachkala port and Sochi waterfront, satellite data points to new damage in Russia’s Arctic gas region
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones attacked the commercial seaport in the city of Makhachkala in Russia’s Dagestan overnight into Sept. 10. At around 3 a.m., local residents began reporting explosions and air defense activity near the port. Before the authorities issued any official statements, the independent outlet Astra analyzed witness footage and determined that the commercial seaport was the likely target.
Astra also geolocated one of the explosions to the area of Pushkin Street where the Avar Theater is located.
Ukrainian monitoring channels Exilenova+ and Supernova+ published several videos showing drones flying overhead and exploding. Other footage showed smoke rising in the port area and damage in the city. Exilenova+ also published what it said was the apparent moment of a strike on the port’s infrastructure.
Acting Dagestan head Fyodor Shchukin confirmed that fires broke out at the port and at the Avarsky Theater. He said all aerial targets had been destroyed and that the fires were caused by falling debris. However, the theater’s director, Magomed Bisavaliyev, reported that a drone fell directly onto the building’s roof, blowing out windows before a fire started. Shchukin said the fires had been extinguished, no one was killed or injured, and the theater’s damaged roof would be repaired. Airports in Makhachkala, Vladikavkaz, and Grozny suspended operations for three and a half hours.
The Makhachkala Commercial Seaport is Russia’s only ice-free, deep-water port on the Caspian Sea. It is used for the shipment of oil, petroleum products, grain, containers, and other cargo moving between Russia, Iran, and countries in Central Asia and the South Caucasus. From January through August 2026, it handled a record 2.9 million metric tons of cargo, according to its own data, up 42.5% from a year earlier. More than 2 million metric tons of that volume was oil.
In addition to the strikes on Makhachkala, the Russian Black Sea city of Sochi was attacked by maritime drones on the evening of Sept. 9. Supernova+ published a full video of one part of the attack, while another clip captured a strike on a pier. Footage posted on social media also appeared to show a cafe building burning near a beach.
Twenty-eight people were injured in the attack, including two children.
Beach infrastructure and a nearby section of the Primorskaya Embankment were damaged. A concert by Russian singer Tatyana Bulanova at the Festivalny concert hall was also interrupted due to the threat of an attack, and performers and audience members were sent to shelter.
Russia’s Defense Ministry reported that it had intercepted more than 440 fixed-wing drones in the south of the country and over the Black Sea.
New data also emerged about the consequences of yesterday’s Ukrainian drone attack on gas infrastructure in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous District, located more than 2,000 kilometers from the border between the two countries.
The open-source intelligence channel Falcon Insight noted that NASA’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) detected several thermal anomalies at the Urengoyskaya compressor station near the Novy Urengoy Condensate Preparation Plant, which was attacked on Sept. 9.
Falcon Insight said such heat signatures are not typical for the compressor station.
The station supports several major gas pipelines, including the Urengoy-Center and Urengoy-Novopskov systems, which transport gas from the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous District to other parts of Russia. There had been no previous reports of an attack on the compressor station, and there is still no separate confirmation that the facility was damaged. Satellite monitoring data only shows sources of intense heat and cannot by itself establish what caused them.
Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces claimed responsibility for strikes on two other facilities in the region: the Novy Urengoy and Purovsky gas condensate processing plants. The Novy Urengoy plant has a design capacity of 19.5 million metric tons of feedstock a year, while the Purovsky plant processed 13.4 million metric tons in 2025. Ukraine’s military did not list the Urengoyskaya compressor station among the targets it said had been hit.

articles.title: Iran attack on base in Jordan damaged American military aircraft
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran attack on base in Jordan damaged American military aircraft, US official says
Iranian strikes damaged multiple American military aircraft this week on the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, a U.S. official told Reuters.
The U.S. military, the highest-funded in the world, suffered material damage even before Iran's strikes on Tuesday. This includes the destruction of more than two dozen drones, Iran striking fighter jets, and aircraft being lost to accidents.
According to a May report from the Congressional Research Service, 42 U.S. military aircraft had already been lost or damaged in the conflict.
Since the Iran war started in February, 18 U.S. service members have been killed and over 800 injured.
A U.S. official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said Iran's attack hit one A-10 Thunderbolt II, known as the Warthog, leaving it with a missing wing, while roughly eight F-15s sustained light damage and were returned to service.
Iran's strike on the U.S. base in Jordan came after U.S. forces said they destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers. The U.S. said its strikes were in response to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targeting a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the previous two days.
The Iranian attack required U.S. forces to fire roughly 30 Patriot interceptors to counter the missiles, the U.S. official said, amid increasing concern about the inventory of U.S. air defence interceptors and other missiles.
While specific inventory numbers are classified, the Center for Strategic and International Studies has estimated that about 65% of U.S. Patriot interceptors were expended between February and July, with fewer than 850 left on hand, down from 2,330 before the Iran war began.

articles.title: Ukraine almost ran out of F-16 missiles — Zelensky’s former spokeswoman
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 10. /TASS/. The armed forces of Ukraine have almost run out of AIM-120 and AIM-9 air-to-air missiles for F-16 fighter jets, Vladimir Zelensky’s former press secretary Yulia Mendel said.
"In Ukraine, the missiles F-16s use <…> are almost gone. AIM-120s and AIM-9s are running out. Patriot batteries are also critically short of PAC-3 interceptors needed to stop ballistic missiles," she wrote on the X social network.
"І keep coming back to the same thought: without a move toward peace, there is just no way to stop the destruction and keep people alive," Mendel added.

articles.title: Russian air defence stocks significantly depleted
articles.body:
Russian long-range air defence interceptor stocks have been depleted to the point where Moscow is having to make serious decisions about where it deploys them, a Western official has told the UK Defence Journal.
We asked whether the assessment is that Russian air defence stocks are genuinely running down to a point that would leave Russian cities and infrastructure more vulnerable than they have been, or whether the decline reported by Ukrainian intelligence in S-300 and S-400 interceptor reserves is being offset by external supplies.
“No, absolutely, 100 per cent. They’ve been depleted,” the official said.
The explanation offered was that the stockpiles were never intended for this. Those reserves existed “for defence of Russia in a campaign from NATO, not some sort of regional conflict with Ukraine”, the official said, with the consequence that “absolutely those numbers are dwindling, and Russia is having to make some really serious prioritisation decisions about where they employ those air defence assets.”
The depletion was explained by reference to a series of Ukrainian operations that Russian planning had not anticipated. Reflecting on how much has changed, the official said an intelligence officer five years ago would not have thought the present situation realistic, and that the same applies looking at it from the Russian side. Ukrainian drone strikes reaching the vicinity of the St Petersburg International Economic Forum, and Russian oil refining capacity down by 40 per cent at its peak, were described as completely unforeseeable by Moscow.
One measure of how acute the problem became was legislative as Russia introduced a law to mobilise reservists specifically for the air defence of oil refineries, the official said, a step taken late last year in response to the success Ukraine was having against those targets.
On whether a point of exhaustion can be identified, the official was careful, telling me “I don’t think we’ll be in a position yet to say what that pivot point is,” they said, declining to predict a date by which reserves might run out while maintaining that Russia faces very difficult choices.
Officials described Russian use of North Korean KN-23 ballistic missiles as significant in itself. “The fact that Russia is having to use North Korean missiles is quite significant. It says a lot about Russia’s ability to resource its own conflict,” one official said, declining to give numbers.

articles.title: This Is What Ukraine’s Novorossiysk Strike Did to Russia’s Kalibr Fleet
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
This Is What Ukraine’s Novorossiysk Strike Did to Russia’s Kalibr Fleet
Satellite imagery and new visual evidence are revealing the aftermath of Ukraine’s September 9 strike on Novorossiysk, with at least three Russian Black Sea Fleet vessels now confirmed hit and additional missile-carrying warships appearing to have sustained damage.
Ukraine has confirmed that at least three Russian Black Sea Fleet vessels were hit during the September 9 missile-and-drone strike on Novorossiysk, with new imagery providing a clearer picture of the damage inflicted inside one of Russia’s most important naval hubs.
Ukraine’s General Staff said on September 10 that additional analysis confirmed strikes on the minesweeper Zheleznyakov, the missile frigate Admiral Essen and the Project 11711 large landing ship Pyotr Morgunov.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The updated assessment significantly expands the confirmed results of the overnight operation, which targeted both military and port infrastructure in Novorossiysk.
Fuel-oil storage facilities at the port were also confirmed hit.
The most striking evidence, however, comes from imagery showing the vessels after the attack, published by the OSINT community Exilenova+.
Visual analysis indicates that Admiral Essen, a Russian missile-carrying frigate capable of launching Kalibr cruise missiles, was struck in its superstructure. A fire subsequently broke out on the ship, an effect also reported by Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence.
Separate imagery also appears to show another strike on the superstructure of the missile frigate Admiral Makarov. The full extent of damage to that vessel is still being assessed.
A Buyan-M-class small missile ship was also identified among the vessels apparently hit during the operation. Ships of this class are used by Russia as platforms for long-range cruise missiles and have participated in strikes against Ukraine.
One Buyan-M vessel linked to the latest visual evidence had reportedly taken part in a recent Russian missile strike on Kyiv before subsequently coming under Ukrainian attack in Novorossiysk, Exilenova+ noted.
The September 9 operation combined missiles and drones against the port, where Russia has concentrated significant elements of its Black Sea Fleet after Ukrainian strikes made operations from occupied Crimea increasingly dangerous.
Novorossiysk has consequently become particularly important for Moscow as both a naval base and a logistical hub.
Damage assessments remain underway, and Ukrainian authorities have not yet disclosed the full results of every strike recorded during the operation.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces struck a Russian high-speed Mangust patrol boat in temporarily occupied Crimea, along with drone facilities, reconnaissance systems, and ammunition depots across several temporarily occupied regions.

articles.title: Houthis seize strategic Red Sea port near key shipping route – media
articles.body:
Houthis claim control of strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait (VIDEOS)
Yemen’s Houthis have seized the crucial Red Sea city of al-Makha (Mocha), tightening their grip on the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the organisation’s spokesperson told RT on Thursday.
The Houthis pushed Saudi-backed government forces out of Mocha after several days of fierce fighting, reportedly capturing both the city and its port. Videos circulated by OSINT accounts online appear to show Houthi forces entering the strategic port city as the group continues its advance toward full control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast.
The organisation’s spokesperson, Mohammed Al-Bukhaiti, told RT that while it is fighting directly against Saudi forces, it is prepared for a potential expansion of the conflict if any other country “becomes embroiled in the aggression against Yemen.”
“Of course, we now control Bab al-Mandeb, but the goal of our battle remains liberating Yemen and restoring its sovereignty and independence by ending the Saudi aggression and ending the blockade that has caused great suffering to Yemen,” Al-Bukhaiti said.
The Houthis are committed to protecting the freedom of maritime navigation in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and the Red Sea, and “do not target any country except the Saudi enemy,” the spokesman added.
Houthi forces captured the key coastal city of Mokha overnight after Saudi/UAE backed forces retreated.
Seen here, Houthi fighters pose with an abandoned M-ATV MRAP at the city’s critical seaport. pic.twitter.com/1WD6l08MVc
“This is one of the most important objectives of our military operations, because the one infringing upon maritime navigation is Saudi Arabia and its allies, as they prevent commercial vessels from travelling to and from Yemen,” he said.
Houthi convoys have reportedly entered the city of Mokha. https://t.co/nKrIOyt0Zypic.twitter.com/wFjvGPzg3H
— Open Source Intel (@Osint613) September 10, 2026
The Houthis have also reportedly landed forces on the strategic Hanish islands after pushing government troops further south. An unnamed military source told Reuters the group seized Zuqar Island after rocket attacks and an amphibious assault. Control of the area would further strengthen the Houthis’ position, potentially cutting government supply routes and depriving Saudi-backed forces of a key logistics hub, sources said.
Yemen’s internationally recognized government has not confirmed Mocha’s capture. However, Lt. Gen. Tareq Saleh, whose forces controlled the city, said earlier Thursday he had ordered them to “reorganize their ranks and establish an alternative command center in a secure location.”
The reported advance marks a sharp escalation after roughly four years of relative calm following a UN-brokered truce in 2022. The Houthis had previously fought Yemen’s internationally recognized government since seizing Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene.
Tensions flared again in July after, according to Yemen’s internationally recognized government, its forces struck Sanaa airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft carrying a Houthi delegation from landing. The Houthis blamed Saudi Arabia, declared the de-escalation phase over and subsequently announced a naval blockade of the kingdom. By mid-August, the group was launching coordinated missile and drone strikes on camps belonging to Yemen’s Saudi-backed government, which in turn launched counteroffensives across several provinces.
The fighting sharply escalated earlier this week. On Tuesday, the Houthis targeted energy and other infrastructure in Saudi Arabia’s south, including facilities belonging to Saudi Aramco, the country’s largest oil producer. The Houthis called the operation retaliation for Saudi strikes in Yemen, claiming Riyadh had carried out 121 airstrikes over the previous three days. Saudi aircraft carried out another 40 strikes across four Yemeni provinces on Thursday, according to the Houthi-run Saba news agency.
What is the significance of the Houthis’ advance?
The battle for Yemen’s Red Sea coast has implications far beyond the country. Bab al-Mandeb links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and Indian Ocean and carries roughly 10% of global seaborne trade. Its importance to energy markets has surged since the US-Israeli war on Iran erupted on February 28 and the Strait of Hormuz came under a de facto blockade, forcing Saudi Arabia, one of the world’s largest oil exporters, to rely more heavily on Red Sea exports.
Saudi Aramco has increasingly diverted crude through its cross-country pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu. Loadings have averaged more than 4 million barrels per day since June, more than four times last year’s level. Saudi crude shipments through Bab al-Mandeb between March and mid-July were eight times higher than in the same period of 2025, making disruption to the strait a growing threat to the kingdom’s oil exports.
The Houthis have disrupted the waterway before, repeatedly attacking Red Sea shipping in 2023 in what they said was support for Palestinians during Israel’s war in Gaza.
Despite the renewed hostilities, Riyadh says diplomacy remains possible. Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud earlier this week accused the Houthis of prioritizing “their narrow interests” over the interests of Yemen, but insisted that “the road to diplomacy is not closed.”

articles.title: Yemen’s Houthis Capture Red Sea Port City, Threatening New Front in War
articles.body:
Iran-aligned Houthi rebels have captured Yemen’s port city of Mokha from Saudi-backed government forces, potentially opening up a second theater in the war between the U.S. and Iran.
The capture of Mokha marks the Houthis’ largest territorial gain since a 2022 cease-fire in Yemen that paused major fighting between the group and Yemen’s government. The Houthis also disrupted shipping in 2024 in response to Israel’s occupation and bombardment of Gaza, which prompted the U.S. and U.K. to carry out deadly strikes on Yemen.
The Houthis swept south along the Red Sea coast before taking Mokha on Thursday and subsequently reached the Hanish archipelago, Yemeni government sources told Reuters. A Yemeni commander and a member of the Houthis’ political bureau separately confirmed the Houthi capture of Mokha to the Associated Press.
Government forces retreated south toward Dhubab, which overlooks Bab el-Mandeb. Yemen’s government has reportedly launched airstrikes west of Taiz and warned civilians to avoid roads between Taiz and Mokha. Houthi-owned Al-Masirah TV reported that Saudi-backed forces launched 40 airstrikes on the provinces of Taiz, Jawf, Hodeida, and Marib.
Observers and Yemeni residents fear the escalation could renew an all-out civil war in Yemen. “This renewed war should alarm us all,” Hans Grundberg, the U.N. special envoy for Yemen, said at an emergency meeting of the U.N. Security Council on Thursday. “It effectively marks the end of the relative calm that Yemen has experienced for over four years since the U.N.-brokered truce.”
Capturing the southwestern port also strengthens the Houthis’ ability to threaten shipping through Bab el-Mandeb, a waterway through which around 12% of global trade normally passes. The strait, which lies between Yemen, Djibouti and Eritrea and links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, has become more important since Iran militarized the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation for the U.S. and Israel’s Feb. 28 strikes.
Iran’s involvement
The Houthis reportedly received direct guidance and weapons from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Iran reportedly told the Houthis last week to escalate their attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Iran publicly maintains that the Houthis are “not a proxy.” The country’s foreign ministry said in a statement on Friday that the conflict in Yemen must be resolved through dialogue instead of military action. It also invoked what it called the “expansionism of the Israeli regime with U.S. complicity.”
Mohammed Abdulsalam, a spokesperson for the Houthis, posted on social media that the group will stop targeting Saudi ships when the “aggression” against Yemen ends.
A Houthi-run body in Yemen that communicates with commercial shipping companies said navigation through Bab el-Mandeb remained safe, except for Saudi vessels.
The advance comes as Tehran has sought new ways to counter Washington’s economic pressure campaign and military attacks. A stronger Houthi position along the Red Sea coast could further constrain global energy supplies, raise shipping and insurance costs, and push up oil prices. Even if the Houthis are acting in their own interest, Iran could gain significant leverage over Washington in conjunction with continued pressure on traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
The capture of Mokha came hours after President Donald Trump on Wednesday suggested that Iran’s government was prolonging the war in an attempt to affect Republican prospects in the U.S. midterm elections in November. He nevertheless insisted Iran is on the verge of collapse and that the war will end “immediately after” the vote.
More shipping disruptions
From Mokha, which lies around 80 km north of Bab el-Mandeb, the Houthis have a stronger position to disrupt shipping, particularly targeting vessels travelling to and from Saudi Arabia, which is the world’s biggest crude exporter and a close U.S. ally.
Saudi Arabia has routed more oil to its Red Sea port of Yanbu after the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz. But the Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia on July 20 and began attacking Saudi shipping and energy infrastructure. Saudi crude exports have fallen to their lowest level in 13 years, with production dropping 23% from July to August. Overall vessel traffic through Bab el-Mandeb fell around 24% in the week following the July blockade.
The kingdom has responded with airstrikes in Yemen’s north and warned Iran to rein in the group. It has supplied its Yemeni allies with arms, intelligence, and logistical assistance. The Saudi government is reportedly reticent to escalate its fight with the Houthis and has so far resisted requests for a broader air campaign in the south of Yemen and along the Red Sea coast.
The advance could also force the U.S. to devote military resources towards protecting a second maritime chokepoint and assisting its ally, potentially complicating efforts to limit or swiftly end U.S. involvement in the Middle East.

articles.title: Russia strikes data center in Kiev – MOD
articles.body:
Russia strikes data center in Kiev – MOD
Russia has struck a commercial data center in Kiev and infrastructure in the Ukrainian port of Odessa, the Defense Ministry in Moscow has said.
The 4,500-square-meter Be Mobile facility in the Ukrainian capital was among a string of military-linked industrial, logistics, and port targets hit overnight with precision weapons and attack drones, according to the ministry’s morning update on Friday.
In Kiev Region, Russian forces struck a site near the town of Gostomel that the ministry said was used to store components for long-range drones. 
Kiev deploys kamikaze drones for strikes deep inside Russia on a daily basis.
Multiple videos circulated by Ukrainian media show a fire reportedly caused by a jet-powered drone strike.
Footage shows bright sparks and apparent secondary explosions, fueling speculation that munitions may have been stored at the site.
The incident comes amid growing tensions in Ukraine over the military’s use of facilities close to residential areas to store explosives.
In late August, a Russian strike on an ammunition depot in the village of Milaya northwest of Kiev triggered a massive detonation that killed 35 people and damaged hundreds of nearby homes. This week, a security official responsible for setting up and operating the depot was formally accused of negligence.
Russia’s latest operation also reportedly targeted two logistics hubs in Khmelnitsky Region and Dnepropetrovsk Region, both of which the ministry said were used to store drone parts.
In Odessa Region, the ministry said multiple targets were struck, including a repair shop servicing Ukrainian military hardware, another storage facility for drone components, as well as several cargo ships and fuel depots linked to the Ukrainian military.
Ukraine made attacks on Russian civilian ships a key part of its attempted “pressure campaign” during the summer. Russian retaliation has since virtually paralyzed shipping through ports in Odessa Region.

articles.title: EU approves EUR 6.1 bln support loan for drones, Patriot air defense missiles
articles.body:
The European Commission has officially approved providing Ukraine with a EUR 6.1 billion support loan to purchase drones and missiles for Patriot air defense systems, EU Commissioner for Defense and Space Andrius Kubilius said.
"Today I'll share news about our decisions under the Ukraine support loan. Today the European Commission officially approved allocating EUR 6.1 billion from this loan for the purchase of drones and missiles for Ukraine's air defense systems," he told reporters in Brussels on Friday.
Kubilius called this a genuinely important step forward, saying the Commission had worked hard with member states and Ukraine to reach this point, and that the decision formally allows Ukraine to purchase PAC-3 missiles for Patriot systems.
He explained that for EU funding to be used to purchase weapons from third countries, member states must adopt a separate decision. This package, financed under the Ukraine support loan, involves five departures from standard procurement eligibility rules, he said: three concern drones and components of Ukrainian manufacture whose cost exceeds set limits, and two concern equipment made in the United States, including PAC-3 missiles, among them procurement carried out through a joint purchasing mechanism coordinated by NATO.
The commissioner said Ukraine's military edge depends on the rapid availability of critical equipment in the necessary volumes and on very short timelines. Speeding up the delivery of needed equipment by drawing on existing stockpiles, reprioritizing orders and scaling up production remains a decisive task, he stressed, adding that today's decision means the full EUR 28.3 billion allocated this year from the Ukraine support loan has now been assigned to the country's defense needs.
He said the European Commission is currently processing payment requests worth EUR 4.7 billion, in addition to the EUR 8.3 billion already disbursed earlier. The disbursement process is therefore also moving forward, he said, noting that before transferring funds, the Commission verifies contracts to ensure they comply with the terms of the Ukraine support loan and with procurement rules agreed with member states.

articles.title: Pro-Palestine groups 'blockade' UK insurers over Elbit ties
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Pro-Palestine groups 'blockade' UK insurers over ties to Israeli arms firm Elbit
Pro-Palestine activists have carried out protests outside five UK offices belonging to two of the world's largest commercial insurance and reinsurance providers over their alleged links to Israeli arms manufacturer Elbit Systems.
Chubb and Sompo offices in Manchester, Glasgow, London and Maidstone faced disruption from campaigners who say that the insurers have provided underwriting for Elbit Systems and its subsidiary, UAV Engines, in Britain, as well as Elbit's US operations.
Elbit, Israel's largest arms manufacturer, supplies drones, surveillance systems and other weapons to the Israeli military, including during Israel's genocidal war on Gaza, which began on 7 October 2023.
According to the groups involved in the direct action, including Manchester-based Palestine Resistance Collective (PRC), Mothers Against Genocide Scotland and Boycott Bloody Insurance, protesters gathered outside Chubb's Glasgow office carrying banners and formed a 'red line' around the building while distributing leaflets to passers-by and office workers.
A speech was delivered inside the building's lobby, and a letter was handed to Chubb's management calling on the insurer to sever its relationship with Elbit.
In Manchester and London, protesters blockaded office entrances while making the same demand.
In a statement, Andrew Taylor, a member of Boycott Bloody Insurance, a campaign group calling on insurance companies to end their support for "destructive companies",, said: "Israel relies on Elbit’s weapons and technology to enact its genocide and occupation in Palestine – and Elbit wouldn’t be able to operate without insurance from Chubb."
He added: "People of conscience all over Britain will continue to reject Chubb’s complicity in war crimes until they see it come to an end."
Boycott Bloody Insurance has also accused Chubb of having significant exposure to companies it considers destructive, ranking it among the worst-performing insurers for underwriting weapons, fossil fuel and border detention and surveillance companies.
The group says this includes providing insurance to Lockheed Martin and several UK suppliers of components for F-35 fighter jets, which are also used by Israeli forces in military operations in the occupied Palestinian territories.
The latest action follows moves by two other insurance firms, Allianz and Aviva, to end underwriting for Israel's largest arms manufacturer following sustained direct action by banned activist group Palestine Action.
Allianz's coverage of Elbit Systems UK ended last November, while Aviva's employment liability insurance coverage for UAV Engines Ltd, an Elbit subsidiary, ended in last September.
Elbit Systems UK is now reportedly receiving employer's liability insurance from Aspen Insurance, while UAV Engines is insured by Chubb.

articles.title: Ukrainian Flamingo missiles strike chemical plant in Russia's Volgograd, Fire Point says
articles.body:
Ukrainian Flamingo missiles strike chemical plant in Russia's Volgograd, Fire Point says
Ukraine carried out an FP-5 "Flamingo" missile strike on Russian military-industrial facilities in Volgograd overnight on Sept. 11, according to Ukrainian missile manufacturer Fire Point.
"Flamingos paid a little visit to Volgograd last night," Fire Point said in a social media statement. "Ukrainian sanctions, as always, proved to be the most effective."
The company said direct hits on the facilities sparked a "massive fire."
The FP-5 Flamingo is a Ukrainian heavy cruise missile manufactured by Fire Point that first entered service in August 2025. While early versions were relatively inaccurate, the missile has since undergone modifications and upgrades and has been used in several attacks on Russian military-industrial facilities.
"The Flamingo was fairly inaccurate in the beginning," Fabian Hoffmann, a senior research fellow at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, told the Kyiv Independent, explaining that Fire Point has since modified and upgraded the missile. "The missile is now operationally more useful," he said.
Footage posted by monitoring channels on social media showed fires apparently coming from the facility, although the extent of the damage remained unclear.
Volgograd Region Governor Andrey Bocharov acknowledged that a Ukrainian missile strike had taken place in the city, claiming that "an industrial facility in southern Volgograd" was damaged by "falling debris."
Volgogradpromproekt LLC is a chemical company based in Volgograd that is under U.S. sanctions for supporting Russia's military. According to the U.S. sanctions designation, the company "produces ferrocene-containing combustion catalysts and technology for the production of chemicals."

articles.title: Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels seize strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha
articles.body:
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels seize strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha
Yemen’s Houthis seized the strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha on Thursday as their offensive against Saudi-backed government forces intensified. Saudi Arabia launched dozens of airstrikes over the past 24 hours, the Houthis said, after the Iran-backed group carried out attacks on Saudi territory that wounded dozens of people.
Yemen's Houthis seized control of the strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha on Thursday, with witnesses telling AFP of fighters marching on the area chanting "death to America, death to Israel".
Saudi Arabia meanwhile launched dozens of airstrikes in the last 24 hours, according to the military spokesman for the Houthis, who control large parts of northwest Yemen and launched a large-scale offensive last week against Riyadh-backed Yemeni government forces.
The Houthis launched attacks on Saudi territory that left dozens of people wounded, in a conflict that has reignited during the Middle East war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February.
A Yemeni military source told AFP on Thursday that the Iran-backed Houthis were advancing towards the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait "after having taken control of Mocha".
The waterway, which links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez Canal, has gained importance as a transit route since the start of the wider Middle East war, which saw Iran blockade the Strait of Hormuz.
The regional war has disrupted maritime traffic in the Gulf, causing oil prices to soar.
On Thursday, the US oil contract WTI surpassed $100, after Brent North Sea crude -- the main international benchmark -- already did so on Wednesday.
After Mocha's capture, the leader of Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, said the protection of the country's coasts and restoring state control of them was an "Arab and international interest".
The military source said the Houthis also seized Zuqar Island in the southern Red Sea, "after rocket attacks and a ground assault carried out using boats transporting fighters".
In a statement, Tarek Saleh, who heads the Yemeni National Resistance Forces that controlled Mocha, said he moved his command centre "to a safe location" to regroup.
Government forces have paid "a heavy price in recent days in the face of a Houthi offensive that was planned and supported by Iran", he added.

'Maritime coercion'
Before the offensive, the Houthis already controlled a large part of Yemen's north, including the capital Sanaa, as well as the major port city of Hodeidah on the Red Sea.
But they did not yet hold any areas directly overlooking Bab al-Mandab.
With their drones and missiles, the Houthis have been able to disrupt traffic in the Red Sea.
But "controlling the coast would strengthen Houthi maritime coercion", said Andreas Krieg, a security expert at King's College London.
The advance of the Houthis in Mocha, as well as in the nearby areas of Khokha and Hays, has driven many people to flee to Aden, where the internationally recognised government is based.
Mohamed, 46, who left Mocha in the middle of the night, told AFP there was an "apocalyptic" atmosphere in the port city.
Mujahid Tahami, who also set off for Aden, said some families had fallen victim to "looting by gangs as they tried to flee".

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Hundreds dead
Yemen relapsed into war in July after years of relative calm punctured by sporadic violence and deepening poverty.
Since last week, the fighting in Yemen has left more than 500 dead, mostly combatants, according to an AFP tally compiled from several sources.
It has also forced nearly 20,000 people to flee their homes, the International Organization for Migration said on Tuesday.
On Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition battling the Houthis said the group fired ballistic missiles and drones at several cities in southern Saudi Arabia.
On Thursday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Saudi Arabia had launched 64 strikes on Yemenover the previous 24 hours.
Their Al-Masirah TV channel reported 10 strikes on Taiz province in western Yemen.
The United Nations Security Council met Thursday to discuss the conflict with its Yemen envoy, Hans Grundberg, who called for "the active investment of every member of this body to contain what could be the precipice for a far more dangerous conflict".
The emergency meeting was brought together by the United Kingdom, which called on the Security Council to "send a clear and consistent message: the Houthis must de-escalate, cease their attacks, and return to a path towards peace".
The hostilities kicked off in July when the Houthis let an Iranian plane land in defiance of Saudi control of Yemeni airspace.
The government retaliated by striking Sanaa airport, an attack the Houthis blamed on Saudi Arabia.
The ongoing exchanges risk returning Yemen to a conflict that left hundreds of thousands of people dead and sparked one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
The Houthis, after seizing Yemen's capital and forcing out the government, fought the Saudi-led coalition from 2015 until a United Nations-brokered ceasefire in 2022.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Iran arms, advice helped Yemen's Houthis seize key Red Sea city
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iranian arms and advice helped Yemen's Houthis seize key Red Sea city, sources say
The lightning Houthi advance down Yemen's Red Sea coast this week came with direct guidance from Iran's Revolutionary Guards seeking to open a new front in Iran's war with the U.S., according to Yemeni government, Iranian and regional sources.
By seizing the southwestern port city of Mocha, the Houthis have strengthened their chokehold on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key waterway whose disruption further constricts global energy supplies after Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
Six months into the wider regional conflict between the Houthis' Iranian allies and the United States, the group now looks focused on consolidating that grip on the strait even as opposing government forces backed by Saudi Arabia focus on an offensive in the north.
Iran told the Houthis last week to escalate their attacks on Saudi Arabia, a close U.S. ally, and promised more funding, weapons and senior officers to help them do so, two Iranian sources said.
While Iran describes the Houthis as an ally, it publicly denies giving them military direction, saying they are "not a proxy".
Several senior Revolutionary Guards commanders had already travelled to Yemen to oversee and command Houthi attacks directed against Saudi Arabia after weeks of discussions over military strategy, a regional diplomat briefed by Tehran said.
A third Iranian source, an official, said Iran had held several meetings with allies including the Houthis and that the move on Mocha was a Houthi rather than Iranian decision. However, it had helped Iran by putting upward pressure on oil prices and hurting the United States and Saudi Arabia, the official added.
Inside Yemen, five military sources from the Saudi-backed and internationally recognised government said the Revolutionary Guards had directed the new Houthi campaign along the Red Sea coast, a flat, narrow plain known as the Tihama, starting with a blitz of rocket fire.
Citing communications intercepts and the accounts of captured Houthi prisoners, the Yemeni military sources said they believed the Iranian effort was being directed by Abdolreza Shahlaei, a top Revolutionary Guards commander.
Iranian sources were not immediately able to confirm that, though they had previously described Shahlaei, who is in the Guards' specialist Quds Force unit, as having spent time in Yemen in recent years.
The Guards were still able to move weapons and personnel in and out of Yemen despite an aerial and maritime blockade of Houthi areas, the Iranian sources said without elaborating on how they did so.
"If we look at their offensive on the west coast, it's not something prepared just last week or last month," said Ahmed Nagi, Yemen analyst at International Crisis Group, describing the seizure of Mocha as a significant milestone in the war.
"The evolution of the Houthis was basically because of the new weapons they gained, either through the Iranians directly or through the different smuggling networks that they are counting on," Nagi said, pointing specifically at their use of drones in the latest offensive.
As the Houthis began an advance towards Mocha last week, Yemen's government requested more air support and other help from the Saudis, two more Yemeni officials said.
It was seeking a Saudi air campaign against Houthi targets in the Houthi heartland including Sanaa and key strategic assets such as oil depots, they said.
However, the kingdom stuck to providing logistical, armament and intelligence support with only limited air strikes that were focused on northern battlefronts in Jawf and Marib provinces, areas the government regarded as less important.
The officials' own assessment was that Riyadh was anxious to avoid a major escalation with the Houthis for fear of provoking heavier drone strikes on Saudi territory.
Saudi officials did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment on Riyadh's military focus on the northern front rather than the Red Sea coast and other big Houthi targets.
The overall military situation in Yemen is hard to gauge after a years-long pause in major warfare since a ceasefire was agreed in 2022. Both Iran and Saudi Arabia have invested in forces they back there. But the pro-government coalition has suffered from internal splits.
Although previous rounds of warfare in the Tihama had produced sudden advances and retreats, it remains unclear if Saudi-backed forces can easily dislodge the Houthis this time, Nagi said.
"Maybe we can see some advances from the government if they get the necessary support from the Saudis. But that could be a bit difficult this time," he said.

articles.title: Ukrainian air defense shoot down 138 of 161 enemy targets; hits recorded at 19 locations
articles.body:
Ukrainian defense forces destroyed 138 enemy targets overnight into Friday, with enemy aerial assets striking 19 locations, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
"According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense units had shot down or suppressed 138 enemy UAVs—including Shahed and Gerbera types, as well as other drone models," the message reads.
In total, overnight into September 11 (starting from 18:00 on September 10), the enemy launched an attack involving 161 strike UAVs—including Shahed (including jet-powered versions), Gerbera, and Parodiya-type decoy drones—from the following directions: Orel, Kursk, and Primorsko-Akhtarsk (Russian Federation), as well as occupied Donetsk and Hvardiyske (occupied Autonomous Republic of Crimea).
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Ukrainian defense forces.
Meanwhile, impacts by enemy aerial assets were recorded at 19 locations, while debris from shot-down targets fell at three locations.

articles.title: Ukrainian drones reportedly strike Russian oil refinery, Ozon warehouse in Saratov
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones launched an attack on the Russian city of Saratov overnight on Sept. 11, reportedly striking oil and logistics infrastructure, Russian Telegram media channels reported.
Independent Russian outlet ASTRA said its OSINT analysis identified a fire at the Rosneft-owned refinery in Saratov. Videos circulating on social media also appeared to show drones and Russian air defenses in operation in the region.
The Saratov Oil Refinery has been repeatedly targeted during Ukraine’s long-range strike campaign against Russia’s energy infrastructure. The facility, which is part of state oil company Rosneft, has an annual processing capacity of roughly 4.8 million metric tons of crude oil.
Saratov Oblast Governor Roman Busargin posted on Telegram around 2 a.m. local time about a threat from unmanned aerial vehicles, claiming that emergency services had been placed on full alert.
Soon after the strike on the refinery, a logistics hub belonging to Russian e-commerce giant Ozon was also reported to be set ablaze in Saratov. Video published by Exilenova+ appeared to show a major fire emanating from the facility shortly after explosions were heard.
Ozon is Russia’s second-largest e-commerce marketplace, behind Wildberries, and operates an extensive network of warehouses, fulfillment centers and delivery infrastructure across the country.
Elsewhere in Russia, explosions were also heard in the port city of Kaspiysk in the Dagestan Republic. No information was immediately known as to the outcome of the reported attack.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the reports or the extent of any damage. Ukraine’s military has not yet commented on the reported attack.
Saratov is located approximately 460 kilometers (285 miles) east of the Ukrainian border with Russia, near Luhansk Oblast in eastern Ukraine.
Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have emerged as one of the most economically significant aspects of Kyiv's long-range drone campaign, contributing to fuel shortages and pushing Russian production down sharply over the summer. Russian refinery throughput fell to about 3.8 million barrels per day in August, down from around 5 million barrels per day a year earlier, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing Energy Aspects.
Ukraine has increasingly targeted Russian refineries in an effort to disrupt fuel supplies and reduce energy revenues that help finance Moscow’s war.

articles.title: Ukrainian companies increasingly integrating AI into missiles
articles.body:
Ukrainian companies increasingly integrating AI into missiles
Several Ukrainian companies are working on missile systems that use artificial intelligence, Brave1 CEO Andrii Hrytseniuk told Business Insider.
Source: Business Insider
Details: According to Hrytseniuk, AI is now "increasingly being integrated into missile systems as well".
"...although this has not yet reached the scale of hundreds of solutions that we see in the drone sector, we are already seeing the first successes and many developments that are currently under way," the Brave1 chief said.
Ukrainian companies are already widely integrating artificial intelligence into drones and combat robots, including for decision-making, navigation and targeting.
"Initially, AI began to be used on a large scale in drones. It is not that fast – it is sufficient for drones, but missiles require significantly higher speeds," Hrytseniuk said.
In an interview in May, Hrytseniuk said that more than 200 Ukrainian companies were developing AI-powered components for missiles, drones, radars and other systems.
Efforts to integrate AI into missiles appear to have intensified as Ukraine invests in developing long-range strike weapons, which are frequently used to attack military and energy facilities in Russia.
It is currently unclear exactly how Ukrainian companies are using artificial intelligence in missiles or how far the relevant developments have progressed. Brave1 said the technology would expand Ukraine's capabilities but would not remove humans from the process entirely.
Background:
- Ukrainska Pravda reported that the Ruta Block 2 missile, developed with support from Brave1, is undergoing flight testing in Ukraine. For the prospective Ruta Block 3, the developers say it will feature autonomous navigation in degraded GNSS environments and a terminal guidance system.
- Ukraine is testing drones equipped with AI-based autonomous terminal guidance. According to the Defence Ministry, the number of strikes using AI-assisted guidance has increased tenfold since the beginning of 2026.
