articles.title: Trump's war cascades into a multifront battle for regional order
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump's war cascades into a multifront battle for regional order
Iran has widened its war in the Gulf. Israel, meanwhile, continues its war in the Arab Levant and is also preparing for a greater role in the Gulf.
Tel Aviv is openly declaring that it will continue its war against Iran and its regional axis, while Benjamin Netanyahu continues to speak of bringing down the Iranian regime. Tehran, weakened and in retreat across parts of the Levant, is seeking to expand its influence in the Gulf, not only through the Strait of Hormuz but also by opening a new front around the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
It has already laid the groundwork through a series of military operations against Gulf states and appears to be preparing for further action if the US blockade continues and military strikes persist.
The world is holding its breath. Donald Trump is threatening to strike Pickaxe Mountain, the heavily fortified nuclear facility near Natanz. Netanyahu, meanwhile, continues to say that Israel is ready to carry out further operations against Iran as Tehran seeks to restore its nuclear programme.
Israel is working to provoke Iran further and draw it into a renewed war. Netanyahu appears to see escalation as the main route through which to fight his electoral battle, and therefore prefers to continue military operations in pursuit of achievements that could improve his political standing.
What Netanyahu wants is a renewed war stretching from Lebanon to Syria, alongside renewed confrontation between the United States and Iran. He is also seeking a greater Israeli role in the Gulf, particularly in the Yemen war.
Israeli reports point to concern in Tel Aviv that the Houthis could consolidate control over Bab al-Mandab and gain greater influence over shipping in the Red Sea. The Israeli military has also conducted exercises in Eilat simulating naval warfare.
Redrawing West Asia for good?
What the United States is doing amounts to redrawing the map of the Middle East, and of a significant part of the wider region. Israel, for its part, repeatedly says that it has already changed the Middle East and intends to continue doing so.
The shared US-Israeli objective is to draw the states of the region further into Israel’s orbit and into the Abraham Accords. Israel will seek to impose this through military pressure, whether in Lebanon, Syria or later on other states, including Gulf countries.
Saudi Arabia is particularly important in this regard, as Trump continues to push for it to join the Abraham Accords.
Lebanon, meanwhile, remains under sustained military and political pressure aimed at pushing it in the same direction.
This cannot be separated from remarks by the Israeli president about his ambition to meet the Lebanese president, visit Beirut and announce a peace agreement. Nor is it different from US statements that openly point towards an eventual peace agreement between Lebanon and Israel.
The framework agreement between Lebanon and Israel is increasingly being presented as the basis for governing that relationship, with Hezbollah’s disarmament across Lebanese territory treated as a central condition.
In this way, Washington is effectively giving Israel political cover to remain militarily active until Hezbollah is disarmed.
The US position coincided with Israel’s destruction of tunnels at Ali al-Taher, north of the Litani River, a clear indication that Israeli military operations may continue in other areas.
Netanyahu himself said that the Israeli army had destroyed tunnels around Beaufort Castle and Ali al-Taher, adding that there would be further operations.
Against this backdrop, the region appears to be approaching another moment of explosion.
It may be delayed, or it may erupt at any moment, particularly as Iran studies the options available to it and considers how to respond to the tightening US blockade, the strikes it is facing and the escalation in Lebanon.
In Yemen, Iran has moved towards an escalation through its allies, with the aim of strengthening control over Bab al-Mandab.
This has come alongside advances by the Yemeni government in other provinces as it seeks to tighten pressure around Sanaa and weaken the Houthis.
Iran’s moves in Yemen therefore constitute one of the most important tests of the Mecca security arrangement between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey.
Dealing with the situation in Yemen will require renewed activation of the international coalition established by Saudi Arabia to protect navigation through Bab al-Mandab and the Red Sea.
Israel is likely to watch from the sidelines initially and wait for an opportunity to impose itself as a central player there, whether through security and intelligence cooperation or through direct military power.
But that would come at a high political price: first through a security agreement with Saudi Arabia, and then through a political agreement, peace deal or normalisation.
Israel as the region's policeman
What Israel wants is clear: to become the “policeman of the region” and the effective successor to US predominance from the Gulf to the Arab Levant.
Israel is presenting itself as a state capable of guaranteeing the security of regional governments and protecting them, on the basis that such protection requires alliance with Israel and acceptance of its conditions.
Israel also wants to demonstrate that the Mecca arrangement, or any other security or defence agreement, cannot provide Saudi Arabia or other regional states with an alternative source of military strength.
Turkey and Pakistan did not intervene militarily in support of Saudi Arabia in the past, have not done so now and may not do so in the future.
Israel, which is increasingly fighting over strategic routes, corridors and crossings, is also unlikely to accept a Turkish military presence around Bab al-Mandab or Turkish intervention in a campaign against the Houthis.
Israel is seeking to widen the war across the region.
It wants to show that it alone is capable of confronting Iran and its allies, and through that confrontation impose itself as an essential party in any regional equation involving the Arab Levant, the Gulf or the Eastern Mediterranean.
This is what Israel has been working towards for years.
It has built partnerships and strategic alignments around the Eastern Mediterranean, particularly with Cyprus and Greece, while also seeking to connect these arrangements to the Gulf.
The same logic is visible in the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor, or IMEC, which links India to Europe through the Gulf and the Eastern Mediterranean.
Israel wants Saudi Arabia and Egypt to become part of this wider strategic architecture, while gradually drawing Lebanon and Syria into it as well.

articles.title: Ukraine and Canada agree on 100-year partnership: declaration signed
articles.body:
Ukraine and Canada agree on 100-year partnership: declaration signed
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney have signed a declaration establishing a 100-year partnership, which sets out the two countries' intention to raise bilateral relations to the level of a comprehensive strategic partnership in various spheres, including defence and assistance to Ukraine's armed forces.
Source: European Pravda, with reference to a joint statement by Carney and Zelenskyy
Details: In the statement, the leaders condemned Russia's war in Ukraine and paid tribute to the courage of the Ukrainian people and their defenders.
Both leaders stressed the importance of continuing reforms in Ukraine on the path to full membership of the European Union and NATO.
"Canada remains a committed partner in supporting these efforts," the statement emphasised.
The statement stressed that Canada will continue to "meet Ukraine's most pressing military needs and sustain Operation UNIFIER, now extended until 2029".
Canada will also continue to strengthen the Armed Forces of Ukraine, paying particular attention to "urgently needed air defence capabilities and interceptors, while continuing to provide training, military equipment, ammunition and other critical military support".
"The two countries will deepen cooperation in the areas of intelligence, cyber defence, counter-drone and electronic disruption capabilities, and in countering hybrid threats and foreign information manipulation. Canada will continue to work with partners on a framework of politically and legally binding security guarantees to prevent any future aggression by the Russian Federation," the statement said.
The statement also notes that Canada and Ukraine will establish a long-term defence industry partnership for the joint production of unmanned systems, counter-drone and electronic jamming systems, as well as ammunition.
In addition, the countries will expand trade and investment under the modernised Free Trade Agreement, promote the development of public-private partnerships and mobilise capital and risk-mitigation solutions needed to support Ukraine's recovery and reconstruction.
Separately, Canada and Ukraine agreed to deepen cooperation in the areas of energy security and critical minerals, industry and sustainable forest resource management, and will strengthen ties between innovators and researchers in the fields of AI, cybersecurity, space, biotechnology and digital governance.
The countries will also cooperate to ensure reliable and safe navigation in the Black Sea, as well as to further disrupt and deter the activities of Russia's shadow fleet.
In addition, Canada has pledged to maintain and intensify economic pressure on Russia.
Background:
- Zelenskyy is on a three-day visit to Canada together with First Lady Olena Zelenska.
- On the same day, Zelenskyy stated that Canada had prepared a new aid package with air defence systems for Ukraine.

articles.title: EU gives final green light to 6 billion euros in defense aid for Ukraine, Patriot missiles purchase
articles.body:
EU gives final green light to 6 billion euros in defense aid for Ukraine, Patriot missiles purchase
BRUSSELS, Belgium — The European Commission approved a 6.1 billion euros ($7.1 billion) tranche of defense aid for Ukraine on Sept. 11, along with several requests for Ukraine to source weapons from outside the bloc, namely Patriot missiles.
The approval allows Ukraine to use funds from the EU's 90-billion-euro ($104-billion) support loan to purchase U.S.-made PAC-3 Patriot interceptors, one of the few weapons capable of intercepting Russian ballistic missiles.
This, however, does not mean an immediate delivery of the missiles. There is a global shortage of Patriot interceptors, while Ukraine is bracing for a new wave of Russian strikes against its energy grid in winter.
EU member states voiced support for the new defense tranche and the Patriot purchase earlier this week, but the steps still needed final approval from the European Commission.
EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius confirmed at a press conference in Brussels on Sept. 11 that the EU's executive arm has signed off on the measures.
With the latest package, the EU has approved all of the 28.3 billion euros ($32.9 billion) earmarked for Ukraine's defense under the support loan this year.
So far, 8.4 billion euros ($9.7 billion) of that defense money has been disbursed, a process that can only occur once Ukraine provides receipts for cross-checking. Kubilius said another 4.7 billion euros ($5.5 billion) is now being processed.
In April, EU countries approved the 90 billion euro support loan for Ukraine, intended to cover two-thirds of Kyiv's defense and budgetary needs in 2026 and 2027, to be delivered in tranches.
The loan also includes requirements to buy weapons from the EU and Ukraine. Any item where more than 35% of the value of its components comes from third countries requires explicit approval.
Kubilius mentioned that five such derogations had been granted: three for Ukrainian companies to source drone components, and two for U.S components, including the PAC-3 missile interceptors.
Justifying the decision to grant the exemptions, Kubilius said: "Ukraine's military edge depends on the rapid availability of critical products in the required quantities and within very short time frames."
The commissioner did not explain which countries would benefit from the exemption for drone components, but an earlier such exemption, made in April, allowed Kyiv to source components from China.

articles.title: Netanyahu vows Iran will not obtain nuclear weapons while he is prime minister
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Thursday vowed that Iran would not obtain nuclear weapons as long as he remains prime minister, after US President Donald Trump said that Tehran was attempting to rebuild its nuclear weapons capabilities.
“President Trump announced this evening that Iran is trying to arm itself again with nuclear weapons. That is true,” Netanyahu said.
“After we destroyed its immediate ability to produce nuclear bombs, both during Operation Rising Lion and Operation Roaring Lion, they are trying again.”
Speaking at the Western Wall ahead of Rosh Hashanah, Netanyahu pledged that Israel would prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.
"I pledge to you here at the Western Wall, ahead of the New Year: As long as I am prime minister, Iran will not have nuclear weapons," he said.
Netanyahu also announced that the IDF was "dealing with the Ali Taher Ridge" shortly before he announced that the IDF destroyed Hezbollah's underground infrastructure there.
Trump: US 'noticed there's a little activity at Pickaxe'
It is important to note that Trump never directly said that Tehran was attempting to rebuild nuclear weapons; rather, he stated that the US had "noticed there's a little activity at Pickaxe."
Trump also stressed that if US forces saw activity the president did not approve of, he would order CENTCOM to strike Pickaxe.
"We're leading in space. We know everybody that's moving at Pickaxe, we know everybody that's moving everywhere, all over Iran, and if anything goes bad, we hit them. We hit them hard," Trump said.
He also downplayed the situation, calling it a "military conflict" instead of a war.
"It's small potatoes for us. It's not a big thing," he added.

articles.title: How Russia Is Targeting Ukraine’s Food Chain, From Factories to Store Shelves
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
How Russia Is Targeting Ukraine’s Food Chain, From Factories to Store Shelves
Russian strikes on Ukraine's food production and logistics are increasingly reaching supermarket shelves, where shortages have begun to surface. What began as attacks on distant warehouses is now registering at the checkout, in thinner produce aisles and in new limits on how much shoppers can buy.
The retail chain ATB, among Ukraine's largest supermarket networks, has introduced temporary purchase limits on several categories of goods. Customers can buy no more than six units or kilograms of groceries, eggs, and bulk products in a single transaction, the company reported on Facebook.
It attributed the limit to the fallout from Russian strikes and a surge in speculative buying, describing resellers who make wholesale purchases in stores and pile additional pressure on already-stretched logistics. ATB stressed that the restrictions are temporary and that it is doing everything possible to keep shelves supplied.
The squeeze is visible in Kyiv, where fresh fruit, vegetables, sugar and dairy have intermittently vanished from some supermarkets as strikes disrupt the depots that feed them.
Ninety percent of food retail logistics is destroyed
The pressure on retailers follows weeks of intensifying attacks on warehousing and delivery infrastructure. Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi, cited by Reuters, told reporters in Kyiv that roughly 90% of the food logistics run by retail chains had been wiped out.
"As of today, roughly speaking, 90% of food logistics operated by retail chains have been destroyed, but that doesn't mean Ukrainians will be left without food," Vysotskyi noted.
Both sides have stepped up strikes on economic targets in recent weeks, with Russia concentrating on warehouses tied to Ukraine's leading supermarkets, its top postal service and home-goods stores. The blows have rippled beyond food: a wave of attacks delayed trains across several regions and left passengers stranded, while Kyiv spent close to 15 hours under air-raid alert on a single day.
Food producers are hit directly
The strikes have repeatedly struck food producers themselves. In Dnipro, Mayor Borys Filatov reported on Telegram that a recent attack had damaged, for the second time in the full-scale war, an oil-extraction plant belonging to the US agribusiness Bunge, maker of the Oleina cooking-oil brand.
Filatov emphasized that the plant stands in the city center and that US Senator Richard Blumenthal had visited it shortly before the strike.
On September 8, a Russian drone hit a food plant operated by Euro Food Service in Bila Tserkva, south of Kyiv. The company stated on LinkedIn that its production and storage facilities had been significantly damaged and that manufacturing and shipments were halted. No staff were injured, and the firm indicated it was working to keep its products on store shelves while it assessed the destruction.
American-owned plants in the crosshairs
American-owned facilities have featured prominently in the campaign. On September 3, Russian drones set fire to a Coca-Cola plant outside Kyiv, near Brovary, an attack President Volodymyr Zelenskyy framed as a message to Washington.
"It's a clear Russian signal to America. The Russians cannot be unaware that this is an American facility," Zelenskyy declared in his nightly video address. The strikes on Bunge and Coca-Cola, together with the senator's earlier visit, have sharpened Ukrainian appeals for a firmer US response.
The disruption now reaches ordinary consumers. McDonald's reported on September 10 that frequent, prolonged air-raid alerts and delivery delays had forced some Ukrainian outlets to reduce their menus, with items to be restored as supply stabilizes.
Couriers, retailers and aid stockpiles
The wider wave has swept up couriers, retailers and humanitarian stockpiles alike. Reuters reported that recent strikes destroyed Nova Poshta sorting centers near Kyiv and in Sumy, wounded at least four people at an Epicenter home-improvement store in Zaporizhzhia, and gutted a warehouse shipping thousands of book titles a day.
A shopping center in Kharkiv was struck for the second time in two days, while drone attacks on the Kyiv region damaged more than a dozen warehouses and killed one person.
Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi wrote on Telegram that 16 people had been killed across Ukraine in a single day of attacks. "They are hitting civilian businesses, food warehouses, hypermarkets, postal terminals, warehouses where books are stored," he added.
The World Health Organization (WHO), cited by Reuters, confirmed that one of its main medical-supply warehouses in the Kyiv region was struck overnight in early September.
Spokesperson Christian Lindmeier told reporters in Geneva that at least 20 attacks had hit warehouses storing humanitarian supplies during 2026, 15 of them holding health-related goods. An earlier August strike on a WHO depot in Dnipro destroyed half the supplies intended for an estimated 225,000 people in front-line areas.
A deliberate strategy, officials contend
Ukrainian officials have characterized the campaign as a deliberate effort to grind down daily life rather than a run of stray hits. Andriyy Kovalenko, who heads Ukraine's Center for Countering Disinformation, described waves of jet-powered drones aimed at paralyzing the capital and exhausting its defenders and residents.
"The aim—to wear down the air defenses and the population," he indicated. The choice of food depots, hypermarkets and postal terminals, in Vyhivskyi's account, points to civilian supply as the intended pressure point.
What shoppers are being told
Authorities are also advising residents to prepare for potential supply and utility disruptions. Kyiv has begun stockpiling essential food and drinking water ahead of possible prolonged winter blackouts, while maintaining emergency reserves for vulnerable residents and Points of Invincibility.
The city can currently provide hot meals for up to 25,000 people and plans to purchase another 20,000 emergency food kits as Russia continues targeting critical infrastructure.
Vysotskyi has urged households to keep a modest one-week food reserve while ruling out any need for month-long stockpiling, warning that wartime disruptions could recur. Even so, he maintained that goods that are interrupted on the shelf tend to reappear once logistics adapt.

articles.title: Building Brics: PM Modi-Putin talks, a Thirukkural gift and Xi's big return - key points
articles.body:
With the 18th Brics Summit under way in New Delhi, key developments have already emerged from the high-level engagements. Prime Minister Narendra Modi held talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, gifting him a Russian translation of the Thirukkural, while Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian arrived in Delhi and is set to meet PM Modi. Chinese President Xi Jinping is also due to arrive on Saturday for the summit and bilateral talks.India is hosting the September 12-13 summit under its 2026 chairship theme, “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability”. The expanded Brics grouping, which now has 11 members, is expected to focus on development, trade, technology, sustainability and strengthening cooperation among emerging economies and the Global South.
PM Modi-Putin talks, Thirukkural gift & carpooling
Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin held bilateral talks, with trade, industrial cooperation, civil nuclear energy and other areas of strategic partnership being prominent in the discussions ahead of the 18th Brics Summit.They reviewed progress in bilateral cooperation across political, economic, defence, energy, space, skill mobility and people-to-people ties. They welcomed Russia’s INNOPROM India exhibition, held for the first time in India, and stressed its role in expanding trade and industrial cooperation, according to an MEA statement.
The leaders also visited the exhibition and interacted with participants.The two leaders also discussed India-Russia engagement in Brics under India’s 2026 chairship, along with key regional and global issues, including the conflicts in West Asia and the Black Sea region and their impact on maritime trade and the safety of Indian seafarers. PM Modi reiterated that dialogue and diplomacy were the way forward in resolving conflicts and said India was ready to assist in peace efforts."They also exchanged views on issues of mutual interest in the regional and global sphere, including conflicts in West Asia and the Black Sea region. PM reiterated that dialogue and diplomacy remains the way forward in resolving conflicts and India stands ready to assist in peace efforts," MEA said in a statement.Moreover, Putin invited PM Modi to visit Russia for the 24th India-Russia annual summit, and Modi accepted the invitation, the MEA said.During the meeting, PM Modi gifted Putin a Russian translation of the Thirukkural, the classical Tamil work attributed to poet-saint Thiruvalluvar. The 1,330 couplets deal with virtue, wealth and statecraft, and love. Modi said the translation would carry Thiruvalluvar’s “eternal wisdom” across languages and borders.
"Presented President Putin with a Russian translation of the Thirukkural, which carries the eternal wisdom of the great Thiruvalluvar across languages and borders," PM Modi said in a post on X.After the bilateral meeting, PM Modi and Putin shared a car as they travelled to an exhibition at Bharat Mandapam.
Pezeshkian arrives in Delhi, PM Modi meeting on cards
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian arrived in New Delhi for the 18th Brics Summit. The MEA said India and Iran, as Brics partners, are working towards “shared progress and prosperity”.Pezeshkian is scheduled to meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi later in the day. Ahead of his visit, he said Brics aims to confront unilateralism and reduce dependence on the US dollar.“A special bank has been formed within the BRICS framework, and we are going to see investment from countries so that interactions between countries and members can be carried out without dependence on the dollar, thus reducing America's totalitarianism with the dollar,” he said.
India and Iran had earlier discussed expanding and diversifying bilateral trade channels during Modi’s meeting with Pezeshkian at the SCO Summit in Bishkek.
Xi’s visit, PM Modi talks and Beijing’s message on managing differences
Chinese President Xi Jinping will arrive in New Delhi on Saturday for the Brics Summit and a bilateral meeting with PM Modi, his first visit to India in nearly seven years. Beijing said the two countries should view ties from a strategic and long-term perspective, strengthen communication, enhance cooperation and properly handle their differences.The PM Modi-Xi meeting comes as India and China work to stabilise ties following the 2020 Eastern Ladakh standoff. The two sides have held talks on the boundary issue and agreed to advance discussions on an “Early and Substantial Harvest” of boundary delimitation and border management. Xi’s visit is expected to offer fresh indications of the future direction of bilateral relations.
Aastha Jha is a writer at The Times of India, covering politics. She also writes on business, global affairs, social issues, with a focus on policy, governance and their impact on everyday lives. Her work brings together reportage and analysis, tracking developments in India and abroad while examining the broader social and economic currents shaping public discourse.

articles.title: Russia and Vietnam to strengthen military cooperation and intelligence sharing on “hostile” countries
articles.body:
Russia and Vietnam have agreed to deepen cooperation in defense, security, and military technology, as well as to exchange information on the activities of “hostile forces and foreign special agencies,” according to a joint statement issued following talks between Vladimir Putin and Vietnamese President To Lam in Moscow on Sept. 9. Additionally, Putin announced that Russia will soon introduce a visa-free regime for Vietnamese nationals.
The two sides agreed to “enhance cooperation between military branches” and cooperate in maritime security, military personnel training, science, technology, and engineering. After the talks, To Lam stated that Russia and Vietnam intend to “deepen defence, security, and military technical cooperation as a strategic pillar of our ties.”
A separate clause in the joint statement addresses cooperation in the field of information security. Russia and Vietnam agreed to intensify the exchange of information and expertise “in countering the conspiracies, intentions, and activities of hostile forces and foreign special agencies,” which, in the document’s wording, are aimed at interfering in internal affairs and influencing state, political, and legislative institutions. The two sides also stated their readiness to expand cooperation “in combating crime in all its forms and manifestations, including cybercrime” and to continue cooperation between law enforcement agencies.
In addition, Moscow and Hanoi intend to expand cooperation in the oil and gas sector. The joint statement describes energy and fossil fuels as areas of “strategic breakthrough in Vietnam-Russia relations.” The two sides agreed to speed up work on possible supplies of Russian oil and liquefied natural gas to Vietnam and on building infrastructure on the Vietnamese side for receiving, processing, and storing hydrocarbons.
Putin said the Russian side had even proposed creating strategic fuel reserves in Vietnam. “Our companies are also interested in establishing transit deliveries of energy resources through Vietnamese territory to neighboring states,” he said. During the visit, the two sides signed agreements on oil and gas projects on the Vietnamese shelf and a framework agreement between Zarubezhneft and Petrovietnam regarding the strategic oil reserve.
Nuclear energy remains another area of cooperation. This past March, Russia and Vietnam signed an intergovernmental agreement on building a Russian-designed nuclear power plant in Vietnam. Putin called the initiative “a truly flagship project.” The two sides also intend to build a Nuclear Science and Technology Center in Vietnam.
In the context of expanding political and security cooperation, Putin announced the potential liberalization of Russia’s visa regime for Vietnamese citizens. “For our part, we are working to introduce reciprocal visa-free travel for our Vietnamese friends in the near future,” he said. Russians no longer need a visa for short trips to Vietnam, and according to Putin, almost 700,000 Russians visited the country in 2025, and another 800,000 in the first half of 2026.
In the final statement, Moscow and Hanoi called their development a “long-term strategic choice and one of the priorities in the foreign policy of each country.” During the meeting with Putin, To Lam called the Russian leader “a great friend of our country and a close brother to the Vietnamese people.” The joint statement also says that Russia “highly appreciates” Vietnam’s position regarding the war in Ukraine.

articles.title: F-16s That Defended Capital on 9/11 Preserved for History
articles.body:
Three F-16s that flew in defense of Washington, D.C., on Sept. 11, 2001, will be retired and preserved as museum artifacts.
The three planes all flew on 9/11: two were among the first three jets to scramble in defense of the capital and the third escorted Air Force One as it returned to Washington later in the day.
On Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist groups hijacked four U.S. airliners, with two striking the twin World Trade Center towers in New York City and the third slamming into the Pentagon near Washington, D.C. The fourth plane was the one that would eventually crash in Shanksville, Pa.
This week, on the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, the National Guard Bureau confirmed that the three planes would be saved:
- Tail number 85-1438, flown by now-Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine, will go to the National Museum of the U.S. Air Force in Dayton, Ohio. His plane was the third to scramble on 9/11.
- Tail number 85-1461, flown by now-retired Lt. Gen. Marc Sasseville, will become a static display at Joint Base Andrews. He was the first to scramble, but this was the jet he flew as escort for Air Force One at the end of the day.
- Tail number 86-0255, flown by Heather Penney, now director of research at AFA’s Mitchell Institute of Aerospace Studies, will go to the American Heritage Museum in Hudson, Mass. Penney’s was the second plane to scramble, flying with Sasseville.
Saving the Vipers
Members of the wing began research more than a year ago to figure what had happened to the jets flown on that fateful day, tracking down old paperwork to figure out who signed out which aircraft and then to discover where those tails were today.
Working with the National Guard Association of the United States, a nonprofit association that advocates for the Guard, they reached out to the Air Force, the Air National Guard, the White House, and others, offering ideas for preserving the historic aircraft under the National Museum of the United States Air Force Heritage Program.
Among the D.C. National Guard F-16s flown on 9/11, one remains in regular flying status with the Air National Guard’s 162nd Wing in Tucson, Ariz. That was the plane Caine flew, which will eventually go to the Air Force Museum.
Guard advocates learned three other planes flown on 9/11 had been converted into QF-16 Full-Scale Aerial Target drones. One—the jet Sasseville scrambled in—was destroyed at the end of its flying life in a missile test. The remaining two were headed for a similar fate when the issue of saving the planes was raised with the Air Force and others.
Jon “Ice” Eisberg, vice president at NGAUS, said once the issues were clear, the challenge was getting the attention of the right people.
“This was a team effort,” Eisberg said. “We just reached out to some of our normal contacts. We went to the National Security Council. We went to Office of Public Liaison in the White House. We went to the Pentagon, and we alerted some folks up on Capitol Hill to this issue.”
The challenge in saving the planes was that QF-16s are a limited resource. The conversions are expensive, about $5 million apiece. The last of 127 conversions was delivered to the Air Force by contractor Boeing in April 2025, according to Air & Space Forces Magazine’s 2026 USAF & USSF Almanac.
QF-16 drones are used for targeting, and once their available flying hours are used up, they can be used in destructive live ordnance tests. One program that would benefit from such tests is the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile, which the Air Force is developing to extend the range of air-to-air combat capabilities beyond visual range.
Still, saving the planes was a priority, and the Air Force came up with a solution: Run down the clock on the QF-16s available flying time, and when their flying hours were all used up, transfer the planes for preservation.
The 9/11 Mission
In a National Guard Bureau video created for the 25th anniversary, Caine recounted his 9/11 experience. “I was running our flying program” that day, Caine recalled. When he saw the second plane hit the World Trade Center on TV, “it was clear that the United States was at war.”
Caine, a major and the wing’s weapons officer at the time, called for live weapons to be readied on the flightline, but getting weapons ready takes time. Soon after, the White House called, he said, “telling us to get airborne.”
Joining Sasseville, a major and the wing’s operations director, and two junior pilots, Penney and Brandon “Igor” Rasmussen, Caine said the group formulated “a hasty, quickly constructed gameplan.”
The clock was ticking as they waited for official authority to launch, and once they had that, weapons were still not ready. Sasseville, who would eventually rise to become Vice Chief of the National Guard Bureau, told Penney as they headed to their plane that they would have to ram the airliner.
“We had an entire wing of support behind us, getting things moving that day, reacting to that terrible attack,” he said. “The White House communicated with us because we were one of the few units in a position to actually do something. … We took off as soon as we could.”
Penney, a young lieutenant and the daughter of an experienced fighter pilot, has wondered why she got the nod that day. “I like to think it was because I was a good pilot,” she said in a recent conversation. “But I think it was because I was single. It was just me and a dog.”
Everyone was operating on adrenaline, Sassevile said. “No one asked any questions.”
Once on the flightline, they dispensed with the routine pilot’s precheck, climbing directly into their planes, trusting their maintainers to have gotten everything ready. Penney had never scrambled an aircraft before—or even trained to.
They took off without clear rules of engagement—these were arranged once they were airborne—and headed out in search of what would later become known as Flight 93, which crashed in a field in Shanksville, Pa., after the passengers stormed the cockpit to stop the terrorists inside.
In fact, they had already done so when Sasseville and Penney took off, but no one knew that at the time.
“We understood what the threat was,” Penney said, recalling their flight up the Potomac River to the northwest of Andrews. “We were looking for a rogue airliner, flying low. We knew they had turned off their transponders.”
Without missiles or bullets—the F-16 has a gun, but they were loaded only with training rounds—the objective target would have to come down with brute force.
“Our only choice,” Penney said, “was going to be to ram the airliner.”
But first they’d have to find it. Unsure of its location or even what vector it was taking to the capital, they headed up the Potomac, then circled back to defend the city. The plan, Sasseville told Penney, was that he would aim his jet at the cockpit and the terrorists, and Penney would take aim at the tail.
The Federal Aviation Administration had ordered all planes in U.S. airspacer to land, and it gradually became clear that Flight 93 had crashed short of the terrorists’ intended target.
Returning to Andrews, Penney recalled looking down at a base that had come alive, its parking lots full, and a line of cars backed up waiting to get on base. “Guardsman came to their units without needing orders, without waiting for paperwork,” she said. They got planes ready, set up cots in the operations area, brought in food. The Guardsman would fly air combat patrols over Washington for the next 90 days straight, and they were already on duty—before they’d ever received orders or even a call.
“They just told their employers, ‘You know, boss, my nation’s calling,’ and they went.”
Now their planes will endure as a reminder of that day and the clear sense of duty those Airmen displayed when the United States came under attack.

articles.title: Race for Xi-Modi meeting at Brics summit
articles.body:
Beijing and New Delhi are arranging for a bilateral meeting between President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a Foreign Ministry spokeswoman said in Beijing on Friday, as Xi is set to travel to India to attend a Brics summit this weekend.
A meeting would mark the third consecutive year in which Xi and Modi meet, following their talks in Kazan and Tianjin, said Mao Ning at a regular news briefing.
She said China stands ready to work with India to follow the strategic guidance of the two leaders, view bilateral relations from a strategic and long-term perspective, strengthen communication, expand cooperation and properly handle differences, so as to be good-neighbourly friends and partners helping each other succeed. 
Xi will attend the 11-member Brics summit, address the event and have in-depth exchanges with leaders on the current international situation, she said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin arrived in New Delhi on Friday and was followed hours later by his Iranian counterpart, Masoud Pezeshkian, for a summit set to be dominated by wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, as well as economic challenges.
Putin and Pezeshkian were due to hold talks with Modi.
For Xi, it will be his first visit to India since 2019 and marks the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the neighbours that has seen flights, visas and high-level contacts gradually being restored.
Brics, created in 2009, now includes Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates – three countries with sharply differing positions on the war launched by the United States and Israel in February.
"The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the Brics summit," said Harsh V Pant of India's Observer Research Foundation. "What was seen until last year as an achievement – the expansion of Brics – today looks like a big constraint on Brics." 
"The war in Iran will provide a stern test of the [expanded] group's cohesion," said Shilan Shah of Capital Economics, noting the failure of the Brics foreign ministers to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May.
The summit is being held on Saturday and Sunday at the capital's Bharat Mandapam convention centre amid heightened security measures.
   
Around 15,000 police personnel and 200 companies of paramilitary forces have been deployed, India's state-run broadcaster All India Radio quoted Manish Kumar Agrawal, special commissioner of police of the protective security division, as saying.
Traffic on key roads may be temporarily halted or diverted, and government and private schools have been shut. (Agencies)

articles.title: 25 years after 9/11: Did Osama bin Laden really win?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
25 years after 9/11: Did Osama bin Laden really win?
A quarter-century tends to sharpen questions that once sounded indecent to ask out loud. On the eve of the 25th anniversary of 11 September 2001, one of them refuses to go away: did Osama bin Laden win?
The instinctive answer is no. Bin Laden is dead. Al-Qaeda's core was hunted into irrelevance years before a US Navy SEAL team found him hiding, isolated and largely powerless, in a walled compound in Abbottabad, Pakistan. No caliphate rose from the ashes of the Arab autocracies he despised. When the region's people finally did rise, in 2011, they carried no black banners and quoted no jihadist scripture. They wanted bread, dignity and a vote - not a war with Rome.
And yet, a quarter-century out, with US troops gone from Kabul in humiliation and the region's old American-built order in open collapse, the honest answer is more uncomfortable than the instinctive one. It requires separating two projects that have been carelessly conflated for 25 years: bin Laden's theological ambition, and his strategic method. The first failed absolutely. The second worked - not as he designed it, but as an act of asymmetric provocation succeeds: by luring a far stronger adversary into destroying itself.
A miscalculation
Nothing has done more to correct the record on bin Laden's own thinking than Nelly Lahoud's forensic reading of the roughly 6,000 Arabic-language documents recovered from his compound. Her account of the archive demolishes a myth popular on both the jihadist and the neoconservative side: that bin Laden foresaw, and welcomed, a long American entanglement in Muslim lands. He didn't. His calculation was almost the opposite, and considerably cruder.
Bin Laden had watched Washington abandon Beirut after the 1983 barracks bombing, and flee Mogadishu after the 1993 firefight. He concluded, wrongly, that the American public had no stomach for casualties, and that one spectacular strike would do to Washington what a decade of Vietnam had done: force a humiliated retreat from the Muslim world. Strip away the US security umbrella, he reasoned, and the "apostate" Arab regimes propped up by it would collapse on their own, clearing the way for al-Qaeda to lead the masses into a restored caliphate.
It was, in the language of his own circle, a plan to strike the head of the snake rather than its tail. It was also a catastrophic misreading of American politics. Rather than withdraw, Washington rallied behind an open-ended global war. Al-Qaeda's core, by its own internal correspondence, spent the following decade not building a movement but simply surviving - hunted by drones, its own security committee called a calamity, cut off from the regional franchises that hijacked its brand for sectarian wars it privately regarded as disastrous for its image.
The organisation was reduced to watching the Arab Spring unfold on satellite television with a mixture of excitement and dread.
Bin Laden's own daughter, according to the documents, worried openly that a new generation might conclude that political change was possible without jihad. She was right. It was.
Judged on its own terms, bin Laden's project was a rout. He did not mobilise the Ummah. His own franchises did not obey him. He died in hiding, isolated even from the organisation that bore his name. This part of the story is genuinely worth putting to rest.
The trap sprung anyway
But grand strategy is not measured only by whether the plan worked as drafted. It is measured by what an adversary's reaction costs. And on that score, the story Andrew Bacevich tells in America's War for the Greater Middle East is not one of jihadist failure. It is one of imperial self-harm.
Convinced of its own indispensability, Washington treated 9/11 as a licence to remake the Islamic world by force, launching an open-ended "war on terror" that eventually touched some 85 countries. By the accounting of Brown University's Costs of War project, the bill has run past $6 trillion - closer to $8 trillion counting veterans' care - and has cost close to a million lives, including thousands of American service members.
The invasion of Iraq did not produce a client democracy. It produced a sectarian civil war, the rise of the Islamic State group, and a decisive strategic gift to Iran. Two decades spent chasing a stateless enemy through the mountains of the Hindu Kush were two decades China spent consolidating power in Asia largely undisturbed.
None of that was written into bin Laden's plan. He did not predict a multipolar 2026 any more than he predicted his own decade in hiding. But he understood something his adversary did not: a wounded superpower certain of its own righteousness can be goaded into wounding itself far more badly than any non-state actor ever could.
An order that cannot be rebuilt
This is usually where the anniversary essay stops, with irony and a shrug. It shouldn't. Because the structure 9/11 set in motion did not just cost blood and treasure - it broke the political architecture that made American primacy in the Middle East possible in the first place.
Marc Lynch has called this structure the "American Middle East": the post-1991 order built on Washington's protection of Israel, its access to Gulf oil, and its sponsorship of a network of compliant, heavily militarised Arab autocracies. As Lynch argues in Foreign Affairs, that order is now finished - and the recent war with Iran was only its final casualty, not its first.
Steven Cook's diagnosis in The End of Ambition supplies the mechanism. Throughout the Cold War, he argues, Washington succeeded precisely because its Middle East goals were modest and preventive: keep oil flowing, keep the Soviets out, keep Israel secure. Only after 1991, drunk on unipolar confidence, did the foreign policy establishment swap prevention for transformation - and transformation, in the Middle East, is where American power keeps going to die.
The invasion of Iraq was, in Cook's own reading, Washington's Suez moment: the self-inflicted blow that broke the back of its regional order, much as the 1956 Suez crisis broke Britain's and France's.
The bookends of that unravelling arrived a generation apart: the fall of Kabul to the Taliban in 2021, and the Saudi-Iran normalisation two years later, brokered not in Washington but in Beijing, with the United States pointedly absent. Riyadh, Abu Dhabi and Cairo no longer behave as client states. They hedge, openly, between Washington, Beijing and Moscow, having concluded, correctly, that American protection is no longer unconditional and American attention no longer reliable.
Add to this the moral cost. Unconditional US backing for Israel's campaign in Gaza finished off whatever remained of Washington's claim to defend a rules-based order, in full view of a generation across the Global South that will not forget what it watched happen, with American fingerprints on it.
Two ledgers, one verdict
So did he win? Only if the two ledgers are kept scrupulously separate.
On the ledger of political theology, bin Laden's account is bankrupt. No caliphate. No mobilised Ummah. A movement that outlived him mainly as a brand hijacked by local warlords for massacres he privately deplored. The region's people rejected his vision the moment they had a real choice, in favour of something more modest and more human: a job, a vote, an end to the torture chamber.
On the ledger of systemic consequence, the verdict runs the opposite way. Bin Laden did not need to build anything. He needed only to provoke a superpower certain of its own virtue into a two-decade campaign of overreach that would drain its treasury, fracture its domestic politics, distract it from its real strategic competitors, and ultimately dissolve the very regional order his 19 hijackers set out to attack. He got exactly that - more than he could have imagined from a cave in Tora Bora.
None of this vindicates him. But a quarter-century on, as Washington confronts a Middle East it can no longer arrange, referee or rebuild, the uncomfortable truth is that the man who lost the argument over what the region should become nonetheless helped determine, more than any other single actor, who no longer gets to decide.
Hesham Gaafar is a researcher specialising in Islamic thought and movements and conflict resolution. He served as editor-in-chief of the Arabic section of IslamOnline.net portal from 2000 to 2010. He co-founded the Regional Center for Mediation and Dialogue and serves as a consultant to a number of international institutions in the field of conflict resolution.

articles.title: South Lebanon trembles as Israel destroys Ali al-Taher tunnels
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Tremor recorded in southern Lebanon as Israel destroys Ali al-Taher tunnels
Israel said Thursday it demolished key tunnels built by the Iran-backed Hezbollah group beneath the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge in southern Lebanon, with a 4.1 magnitude tremor recorded in the area.
AFP journalists in the area heard several explosions. In a video shared by Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz, a huge fireball can be seen rising into the night sky.
The explosion comes a few days after Israeli authorities claimed to have taken control of the Ali al-Taher ridge, claiming that Hezbollah had dug numerous tunnels there.
Israeli troops occupy swathes of southern Lebanon, establishing a so-called "security zone" along the entire border region.
A joint statement by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Katz said the tunnels were strategic infrastructure "built over two decades, with Iranian funding and planning."
The destruction "completes the achievement of operational control over the Ali al-Taher ridge -- above and below ground", the statement added.
The United States Geological Survey meanwhile reported a 4.1 magnitude tremor in the area, after Lebanon's state-run National News Agency (NNA) reported that Israel carried out a "massive explosion" on the Ali al-Taher ridge in the Nabatiyeh region, "causing tremors and a powerful rumble".
AFP journalists in south Lebanon also said they heard "huge explosions" on Thursday evening.
"We were sitting there and everything shook," Joelle Fares, who recently moved to Marjaayoun, told AFP.
Israel announced last week that it had captured the Ali al-Taher ridge. Hezbollah has remained silent on the matter.
The Israeli army said the Hezbollah infrastructure extended for more than two kilometres (1.2 miles) and contained "dozens of Iranian-made rockets, missiles, and UAVs (unmanned aerial vehicles), as well as machine guns, dozens of anti-tank missiles, and hundreds of mines and explosive devices".
The underground compound also included a command centre of Hezbollah's "Badr" unit, the army added.
A military official told AFP that some of the militants that had operated in the area of the ridge had abandoned it, while others were "eliminated by aerial strikes and artillery fire".
The official said Hezbollah members had dug eight underground routes to move safely beneath the ridge, and several dozen explosive drones and hundreds of mines were seized by the Israeli army.
An all-out war resumed on 2 March when Hezbollah fired rockets into northern Israel in support of its backer Iran. Israel had already been violating a November 2024 ceasefire with daily attacks on Lebanese soil. The wider conflict between Hezbollah and Israel began in October 2023.
There had been a lull in violence after the agreement reached between Lebanon and Israel in June, and talks are set to resume next week. But Israeli strikes have increased in intensity in recent days, killing dozens of people.
During negotiations, the United States, which is sponsoring the talks, proposed that the Lebanese army take control of the Ali al-Taher ridge, but Hezbollah refused, a source close to the parties told AFP.
Beirut authorities say Israeli strikes have killed more than 4,300 people in total since March, and more than 8,500 since October 2023. Israeli forces continue to occupy a so-called "security zone" in the south and have wiped out dozens of towns and villages.

articles.title: Ukrainian Ballistic Missiles To Strike Russia in Just a Few Weeks — Fire Point CEO
articles.body:
Ballistic missiles manufactured by Fire Point will strike targets on Russian territory in just a few weeks.
Iryna Terekh, the company’s CEO, announced this on the sidelines of the “Photonics4Defense 2026: Technology Exchange & Matchmaking” event.
According to her, the FP-7 has already successfully completed two stages of testing. The company is now preparing to test the product under combat conditions. This stage is also part of the missile’s certification process.
“We expect it to be ready for deployment very soon. We’re talking about weeks, not months,” Terekh noted.
She explained that the initial stages of missile testing involve ground and laboratory tests, during which each system and subsystem—including the rocket engine and navigation equipment—is tested separately.
This is followed by flight tests, during which the company collects data on the missile’s performance and compares its actual characteristics with the calculated ones.
The third stage, which the company is currently preparing for, involves testing under combat conditions. In late November 2025, it was announced that the company planned to complete the codification process for the FP-7 tactical ballistic missile with the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense by the end of 2025.
In early February 2026, Denys Shtilierrman clarified in an interview with DW that, despite hopes that the missile would enter service by the end of 2025, a “series of events” had prevented this from happening—‘we hope to complete all tests in February’.
At the same time, the FP-9 is currently undergoing flight tests, meaning it is in the second phase.
The developers note that testing the FP-9 is harder to organize because of its long range. The missile has a minimum ballistic flight distance beyond which it can no longer be programmatically stopped.
Because of this, Ukraine’s territory is insufficient for a full-scale test of the FP-9. Therefore, once the current phase is complete, its military testing may immediately proceed to operations against Russian targets.
Militarnyi previously reported that in July 2026, Denys Shtilierman, Fire Point’s chief designer, stated that the only thing standing between the start of FP-9 ballistic missile tests—involving strikes on Russia—and their implementation is the testing of the solid-fuel engine.

articles.title: UAE might be the best way to solve S-400 saga: US congressman
articles.body:
A senior U.S. congressman has suggested that transferring Russian-made S-400 air defense systems to the United Arab Emirates could be the ideal solution to the ongoing rift between Türkiye and the United States, potentially allowing Ankara to reenter the F-35 fighter jet program.
“We have discussed this matter extensively. The core issue here is how this can be implemented. As you know, negotiations were held with the UAE. This might be the best solution,” U.S. Congressman Darrel Issa told the daily Hürriyet in an interview in Ankara on Sept. 10.
Issa paid a visit to Ankara, where he was hosted by President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan. He also attended the 250th anniversary reception of the U.S. at the Ankara Embassy along with U.S. Ambassador to Türkiye Tom Barrack.
Türkiye and the United States have long been negotiating the former’s return to the F-35 joint fighter program and the removal of all remaining sanctions stemming from its 2019 purchase and deployment of Russian S-400 air defense systems.
In July, U.S. President Donald Trump promised to lift the sanctions imposed on Türkiye under the Countering America’s Adversaries Through Sanctions Act (CAATSA), but that requires Türkiye to give up possession of the S-400s.
Issa recalled talks between Türkiye-U.S. and the UAE for the re-export of the air defense systems to the latter.
On sanctions, Issa recalled the promises voiced by Trump, saying “A decision has already been made from the President down to the lowest level; there are no sanctions against Türkiye.”
On Türkiye’s return to the F-35 program or sales of these jet fighters to Türkiye, the congressman underlined that there is a huge backlog of orders.
“Right now, in my opinion, the highest priority needs to be the modernization of the F-16s. The modernization of existing aircraft is a high priority for both Türkiye and the U.S.,” he stated.
Türkiye has agreed to buy 40 brand-new F-16 fighter jets from the U.S., but negotiations continue over pricing. It dropped the initial request for 79 modernization kits from the package and decided to assign Turkish Aerospace Industries (TUSAŞ) to upgrade the existing F-16 fleet.

articles.title: Ukraine's Fire Point confirms attack on Ozon in Russia's Saratov and reports Flamingo strike in Volgograd
articles.body:
Ukraine's Fire Point confirms attack on Ozon in Russia's Saratov and reports Flamingo strike in Volgograd
Ukraine's defence forces struck an Ozon warehouse complex in the Russian city of Saratov and the chemical plant Volgogradpromproekt on the night of 10-11 September.
Source: Fire Point; Andrei Bocharov, Governor of Russia's Volgograd Oblast
Quote from Fire Point: "Overnight, Ukraine's defence forces destroyed another Ozon warehouse complex using FP-1 drones – this time in Saratov. The area of the destroyed warehouse was 85,000 sq m. The complex was designed to store more than 30 million items of goods."
Details: It was also reported that FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles struck the Volgogradpromproekt plant in Volgograd overnight.
"Direct missile hits on the target were recorded, resulting in a fire… Ukrainian sanctions, as always, proved to be the most effective," Fire Point stated.
On the morning of 11 September, Volgograd Oblast Governor Andrei Bocharov reported a missile attack on the region, saying that "debris was recorded falling on the territory of an industrial facility in the south of Volgograd".
"Emergency services are working and dealing with the consequences. Emergency services and the municipality have been instructed to assess the damage, deal with the consequences and prepare temporary accommodation facilities," Bocharov stated.
For reference: Volgogradpromproekt LLC is under US sanctions for working with the Russian military-industrial complex. The company produces ferrocene-containing combustion catalysts and develops chemical production technologies.
Background: On the night of 10-11 September, drones struck the Saratov oil refinery in Russia. In addition to the refinery, a fire broke out at an Ozon logistics centre.
