articles.title: Gateway or outpost? Inside Israel's growing footprint in Cyprus
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Gateway or outpost? Inside Israel's growing footprint in Cyprus
On the southern coast of Cyprus, the signs of a growing Israeli presence are becoming harder to miss.
There are new housing developments marketed to Israeli buyers, large parcels of land changing hands, political posters, and a network of schools, synagogues, kosher businesses, and other institutions serving a community that is no longer made up solely of tourists and second-home owners.
The result is an increasingly visible Israeli footprint on an island that has long relied on foreign capital to drive its property market.
Yet the scale and concentration of some projects have prompted a debate on the island: is this simply another wave of foreign investment, or is something more permanent taking shape?
A new wave of foreign investment
Cyprus’s economy has long depended on third-state investment, with successive schemes – including the controversial “golden passports” and golden visas – designed to attract capital, particularly into property.
Historically dominated by the United Kingdom and Russia, capital has more recently come from Lebanon, Ukraine, and Israel.
The golden visa scheme enables non-European Union (EU) nationals to obtain residency by investing €300,000 in property or a company, raising concerns over transparency and regulation.
Direct investment vis-à-vis Israel stood at around €3.5 billion in stock in 2025, with €308 million in transactions, according to preliminary data from the Central Bank of Cyprus.
Recent Israeli investments have involved large land purchases and projects combining housing developments with resorts and gated communities. In 2023, liberal Israeli newspaper Haaretz wondered whether Cyprus was becoming the “second Israel?”
Israel's growing exodus
The trend coincides with rising Israeli emigration. Since 2023, political tensions surrounding judicial reforms proposed by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's far-right coalition government, followed by the Gaza war, have fuelled mounting insecurity and pessimism about the country’s future.
“The justice reform from January 2023 was the first turning point. Many lost hope in the future of Israel. October 2023 confirmed this trend, and many decided to move,” Michael Harari, Israel’s former ambassador in Cyprus, told The New Arab.
Between 2023 and 2025, 270,000 citizens left Israel, a recent study based on data from the Israel Central Bureau of Statistics (CBS) found, highlighting particularly substantial emigration among highly educated and economically strong groups.
In Cyprus, this movement has translated into both relocation and investment – helping turn what was once largely a tourism and property relationship into a more visible presence.
Cyprus as a haven
In this troubled landscape, removed from regional convulsions, Cyprus has become “Israel’s favourite island escape” – less than an hour away by plane, relatively affordable and safe.
“Cyprus offers the closest escape,” Louisa Varaclas, director of the Israel Office within the Cyprus Tourism Ministry, told The New Arab.
Israel was Cyprus’s second-largest tourism market in 2025, accounting for 13% of all arrivals, or 600,000 visitors. The Israeli Embassy estimates that around 15,000 to 20,000 Israelis currently live in Cyprus, compared with 6,500 in 2018, although the exact number is difficult to determine because many hold European Union (EU) passports.
Geographical proximity, political ties, a favourable tax regime, business opportunities, and a sense of security have helped make the island attractive for residence and investment.
“Cyprus is a security partner,” Roee Kibrik, Director of Research from the Israeli Institute for Regional Foreign Policies (Mitvim), told The New Arab. For Israel’s strategic logic, he argues, the island can almost be understood as an extension of Israel’s security space - while the partnership also serves Cyprus’s security interests.
“Given that political and economic relations between Israel and Cyprus deepen, there will also be growing Israeli interest in tourism, residence, and investment in Cyprus,” Zenonas Tziarras, a lecturer in the Department of Turkish and Middle Eastern Studies from the University of Cyprus, told The New Arab.
Cyprus also offers a “gateway” to the European Union (EU), its market, its electricity and gas infrastructures and sea routes, but also its institutional structures and political channels, Kibrik argues.
From property to communities
The growing Israeli presence is particularly visible in coastal areas around Larnaca, Limassol, and Paphos, where Israelis have purchased property and marketed dedicated housing complexes. Jewish institutions, kosher businesses, and Hebrew-language services have expanded alongside them.
“Some definitely left Israel. Some others live in Cyprus while continuing to work in Israel, while others are moving part of their assets or establishing companies in Cyprus,” Kibrik says.
This trend has also fueled concerns over housing affordability. Property prices rose by 11.7% in Larnaca and 10.7% in Limassol between 2025 and 2026, with the Central Bank of Cyprus attributing part of the inflation to stronger demand from third-country investors, alongside construction and labour costs.
Harari admits there are tensions. “This migration is a natural process and contributes largely to the local economy. But of course, for a small place as Cyprus, these numbers are substantial, and you can also understand concerns from local populations because there is influence on property prices.”
The island’s role as a refuge during crises has further deepened these connections. In October 2023, 5,000 Israelis landed in Cyprus. During the Israel-Iran conflict in June 2025, 15,000 Israelis were stranded after airspace closure.
Chabad centres provided accommodation, food, and emergency assistance, illustrating how a network initially serving religious and tourist needs has also become part of the infrastructure supporting a growing Israeli community.
Chabad, a global Hasidic Jewish movement, operates around 4,000 centres in 100 countries. Publicly apolitical, recent investigations have documented support from parts of the movement for Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power), the far-right party led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
In Cyprus, Chabad operates six centres, alongside a synagogue, kindergarten, mikvah, kosher certification agency, a cemetery, and summer programmes. Its founder and Cyprus’s chief rabbi, Zeev Raskin, also promotes the development of resorts and tourist complexes designed to comply with Jewish law.
Gated communities and contested projects
Several projects have sparked controversy over planning and environmental regulation, the role of national and local authorities, and the longer-term character of this presence.
In Latchi, a large hotel complex completed the final stages of construction while licensing issues remained unresolved. In Polemidia, a €50 million Jewish school designed for up to 1,500 students has generated concerns over traffic and planning, while the municipality had not been involved in the process.
Its slated director, Rabbi Yehoshua Smukler, has described the project as the future “cornerstone” of Cyprus’s Jewish community.
In Trozena and Gerovasa, Hungarian-Israeli businessman Uriel Kertesz has proposed redeveloping abandoned villages into an “ecotourism” project combining homes, vineyards, a wellness centre and restored ruins. The project has faced environmental scrutiny, as the area falls within the Natura network of protected natural areas.
In Zygi, a 60,000-square-metre luxury development is marketed as a gated complex of residences serving the Jewish community. When announced in 2024 by property entrepreneur Daniel Morris Goldberg and Rabbi Ziv Raskin, the project was promoted as a “kosher slice” of Cyprus.
“Do we have closed communities, rather than absorbing individuals into the local culture?” Kibrik asks, pointing to an emerging debate over housing, culture, and the transformation of some areas.
The speed and concentration of Israeli investments distinguish them from the longer-established Russian presence, notes Nasia Hadjigeorgiou, Assistant Professor in Transitional Justice and Human Rights from the University of Central Lancashire - Cyprus.
“Russians have had a very long-standing presence on the island, which developed gradually, whereas Israelis have been much more sudden and economically aggressive, with entire areas being purchased. Russians are primarily based in Limassol and live within the city, whereas some Israelis have begun constructing gated communities, separating themselves within exclusive areas," Hadjigeorgiou tells The New Arab.
"There is also an oversensitivity here because of what is happening in Israel and Palestine and the history of Israelis settling on land, accompanied by violence and displacement, while the local history of occupation vis-à-vis Türkiye adds another layer.”
Theodosis Pipis, a doctoral candidate in History from the University of Leiden, puts the question more bluntly.
“Given these projects and the high concentration of land purchases happening swiftly in coastal and port cities, could Cyprus be falling under the auspices of some form of permanent or semi-permanent Israeli expansionism?”
Growing influence and public outrage
In July 2026, campaign posters for Gadi Eisenkot, former Israeli army chief-of-staff and candidate in Israel’s elections, popped up along highways around Larnaca airport, generating an unusual debate over Israel’s growing influence in Cyprus.
This event echoed wider concerns. “Israeli buyers are purchasing significant land parcels and strategic economic assets. This cannot but sound the alarm for us,” Stefanos Stefanou, a spokesperson for the Progressive Party of Working People (AKEL), warned in June 2025.
And this trend has become a significant issue across the political spectrum, from the election posters to the redevelopment of abandoned villages.
“It’s a topic most circles on the island discuss - no matter though you are from the left, the far-right, the centre, we can all see the growing Israeli presence on the island,” Pipis tells The New Arab.
Growing economic connections also involve powerful business interests. Cypriot-Israeli real estate businessman Yakir Gabay, whose fortune is estimated at around $4 billion, has become a prominent figure in Cyprus.
He is involved in an €856 million investment project around Limassol and recently purchased a 950,000-square-metre plot from the Bank of Cyprus for €28 million.
In February 2026, he also joined the executive committee of the 'Board of Peace'. He visits Israel frequently, operates behind the scenes, and has close personal and business ties to Jared Kushner and, as early as November 2023, reportedly submitted a reconstruction plan for Palestine.
Cyprus, alongside Greece, has recently become an essential part of Israel’s strategic environment. The relationship spans defence, military cooperation and energy, and has developed into a deeper strategic partnership.
Since June 2017, the Israeli military has regularly conducted exercises on the island, including air force, naval, and ground forces units, and intelligence and evacuation drills. The exercises have included simulations relevant to operations in southern Lebanon, making Cyprus a uniquely accessible training environment for Israel’s military.
“Of course, the deepening strategic relationship between both states has made Cyprus an attractive place to Israeli citizens, as a place to invest and live. Both come together,” Harari says.
Sylvain Henry is a writer based in Samos, Greece, and a master's graduate in sociology and political philosophy. He recently worked with the Cyprus Refugee Council
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: How 9/11 Helped Shape Our Politics Today
articles.body:
From the moment they occurred, the terror attacks of Sept. 11, 2001 were seen as inaugurating a new age of asymmetric violence and warfare. President George W. Bush described the war on terror that followed as a generational conflict.
Yet, for all the transformations it produced, Al-Qaeda and Islamic militancy more broadly have, in my view, receded within a decade. Not so much because it was defeated on the battlefield but because it was unable to gain much support among Muslims. When popular uprisings swept the Arab world in the early 2010s, protesters in Tunisia, Egypt, Syria, Bahrain, and elsewhere in the region took to the streets not in the name of Islam, but democracy. The Arab Spring, more than any military victory, signaled the decline of militancy. Al Qaeda faced its greatest defeat at Tahrir Square.
Islamic militancy flourished principally on the battlefields of war on terror, in countries such as Afghanistan and Iraq, a trajectory epitomized by the emergence of the Islamic State from within the American prison system in Iraq. While Islamic militancy still survives in pockets of weak or fractured states, elsewhere it has petered out into the province of petty criminals or psychologically disturbed individuals. What, then, does its brief and brutal career mean for world history?
The End of the Cold War
The dramatic arrival of Al-Qaeda and Islamic militancy in the global public sphere in the early 2000s did not mark the beginning of a new chapter of global history. Perhaps that confrontation between Al-Qaeda and America signaled a historical ending: the true conclusion of the Cold War. By the fall of 2001, the Soviet Union and the bipolar world had been dead for a decade.
The Cold War survived in the institutions and practices it had created: NATO, the United Nations and its conventions, international courts and the multilateral institutions established to knit together a divided world through systems of deterrence, development and compromise born of the fear of an atomic holocaust. For a while, these institutions appeared capable of operating without their founding cause, but that hope proved illusory. In the 1990s, wars swept across the Balkans, the Caucasus, the Middle East and Africa. Al-Qaeda arose at the confluence of post-Cold War globalization and unipolar violence.
With its emergence at the turn of the millennium, Al-Qaeda, I argue, brought the Cold War to a definitive close by overturning its central presuppositions. The war on terror rendered the familiar categories of the Cold War—the balance of power, deterrence, great-power rivalry, and hegemony—increasingly obsolete. Fought in civilian spaces against nonstate actors dispersed around the globe, the war on terror also ended up destroying most of the Cold War’s remaining ideological states in the Middle East, including the socialist republics of Iraq, Libya, and Syria.
Al-Qaeda's emergence also marked the end of Islamism, which was itself a Cold War movement dedicated to revolution and the creation of ideological states. Islamism’s only durable strongholds, Iran and Afghanistan, came to embody its takeover by clerical establishments of the kind it had once sought to displace.
The war on terror also weakened the liberal state, another creature of the Cold War, whose animating purpose had been to pose capitalist liberty against Communist dictatorship. Osama bin Laden used to claim that Westerners thought their interventions in the Middle East would remake the region’s states in the images of their own, but instead it was the Americans and Europeans who came to resemble their despotic and corrupt clients in the region.
One of the goals of Al-Qaeda’s campaign of terror was to precisely achieve that by showing how even violence falling short of a conventional war and posing no genuine existential threat was sufficient in provoking Western democracies to dismantle the civil liberties of their own citizens, exposing their claims to freedom as hypocritical. As the war on terror dragged on, Al-Qaeda’s leaders portrayed the anti-terror laws and the increasingly militarized conduct of the U.S. and its allies not as signs of resolve and strength but as displays of weakness and proof of the shallowness of Western liberalism. Bin Laden might have been disappointed by Al-Qaeda’s inability to mobilize enough Muslims around the world to overthrow their dictatorships, but the U.S. and its European allies, which sustained those authoritarian regimes, sadly behaved much as he had predicted.
A sacrificial, if not nihilistic, movement whose iconic figure was the suicide bomber, Al-Qaeda had little interest in conquest and government. One of its major objectives was to provoke Western states into attacking their own democracies, in a kind of auto-immune response to terrorism, in which the effort to defend the political body corroded it from within. In that particular sense, bin Laden was perversely successful in dragging America and its allies into expensive wars and weakening their liberal norms as they chose widespread use of emergency powers, surveillance, indefinite detention, torture, and rendition. The war also brought suspicion of Muslims, hostility toward immigration, civilizational rhetoric, and border militarization from the political margins to the center of Western public discourse.
America’s preoccupation with the war on terror did squander its unipolar decade. It wasn’t a coincidence that the rise of China—and the China shock—came a few years after the Great Recession of 2008 and a decade after the 9/11 attacks. The cultural and political landscape of Europe and America today—characterized by polarization, populism, and a pervasive distrust of institutions—can be understood, at least in part, as the legacy of the response to the 9/11 attacks by Al-Qaeda. By this measure, my assertion would be that bin Laden won the war on terror much as he had predicted he would.
What sustained the liberal order
The rise of populism and far-right politics in America and Europe has generated great laments for the corrosion of a golden age of liberalism and progress following the victory of the Allied powers against fascism in World War II. The flowering of postwar liberal democracy owed less to the defeat of fascism than to the Cold War, when the existence of a socialist alternative compelled Europe and North America to emphasize social protections, greater equality, and meaningful political rights.
Thus, the crisis of liberal democracy after 9/11 might be better understood not simply as a blowback from the war on terror, but as an aftershock of socialism’s collapse. After the collapse of the Soviet bloc, that pressure disappeared. Though liberal institutions survived formally, the social and economic settlement that sustained them had begun to erode.
During World War II and in its immediate aftermath, the Allies were hardly exemplars of liberal standards. Several allied powers were colonial empires engaged in the violent suppression of nationalist movements in Asia and Africa even as they fought fascism. Nor can any account of Allied conduct ignore the firebombing of German cities or the atomic destruction of Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
Although the war in Europe and the Pacific dominates debates about Allied misconduct, the colonial character of World War II may tell us more about the origins of our present moment. Colonial armies fought in every theater and constituted some of the forces deployed during the war. At least a million soldiers fighting in the British and French armies against fascism were Muslims. Civilians in territories like India, though far from the principal battlefields, also suffered immensely during the war. The Bengal famine, in which some three million people, Hindus and Muslims, starved to death, was, as many have argued, caused in part by wartime disruptions to grain supplies and by imperial policy.
Europe didn’t only take men and material from the colonies for the Great War, but also a repertoire of its illiberal practices in the colonies. The Nazis drew upon precedents established in colonial wars waged by European powers. The Allies, in turn, brought home methods of coercion that had previously been largely confined to their empires. Among them was the revival of medieval doctrines of just war, which subordinated contractual obligations to unilateral claims of moral authority—doctrines that resurfaced during the war on terror to justify pre-emptive attacks and torture.
World War II should be understood not simply as liberalism’s triumph over tyranny but also as a source—and continuation—of Western illiberalism, much like what came to the surface after 9/11. It was the Cold War that provided the real foundation of mid-century liberalism. One might even argue that the post-9/11order, from which today’s far-right movements partly emerged, has its roots in World War II’s struggle for global hegemony, a contest suspended for the duration of the Cold War.
The war on terror represented a failed effort to impose a unipolar order on the world, one that could no longer rely on the economic instrumentality of globalization alone. And its failure also discredited the globalization associated with free trade and mass migration. In its place arose far-right movements in Western Europe and North America dedicated to dividing the world into racial and cultural blocs, divisions often defended in the language of the struggle against terrorism and Islam.
In America, this political vision harks back to the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine; in Europe, it reaches further, to the myth of a culturally homogeneous Christian continent. In both cases, the animating force is not social conservatism alone but hostility toward immigrants, and toward Muslims in particular. Its deeper history may therefore lie in decolonization, which transformed immigration into a defining political reality distinct from the colonial systems of slavery, indenture and managed labor migration that preceded it.
Asian and African decolonization not only overlapped with the Cold War but was, in many important ways, made possible by it. As the rival superpowers courted newly independent countries, they helped secure what sovereignty many of those states possessed. Yet decolonization, no less than the Cold War, also made possible the European Economic Community and, eventually, the European Union. Europe emerged from World War II with most of its colonial possessions more or less intact. It was only decolonization that allowed the continent to cohere into a new kind of economic and political unit.
The long aftermath of decolonization
Immigration has a double history in America, proceeding from two waves of decolonization: the 19th century independence of Latin American countries and that of Asian and African nations in the 20th century. American anti-immigrant politics consequently differs from the European version, remaining more closely bound to the Monroe Doctrine and its vision of hemispheric control.
Europe may possess the older political history, but its encounter with immigration is more recent, starting with labor migration to help with European reconstruction after World War II and expanding again in the wake of the Cold War. The end of the Cold War weakened the sovereignty of many postcolonial states, producing new waves of migration as those countries faced economic pressure or were drawn into conflict. It also reduced European countries from strategic partners in the Cold War to increasingly dependent allies—a relationship laid bare by the war on terror, which expanded American power while disproportionately rewarding American companies.
The end of the Cold War, made visible through 9/11 and its aftermath, has also transformed Europe’s understanding of its past. While World War II is still invoked, especially by liberals, it no longer occupies its former place as the 20th century’s defining event and the founding moment of the international order now coming apart.
The ascendance of immigration—and, with it, race and culture—as the central political concern on both sides of the Atlantic suggests that decolonization has displaced the war in the historical imagination. Narratives about the struggles against fascism or Communism still shape Western identities, but political debate is increasingly dominated by fears of what might be called “reverse colonization.”
Europe’s unwillingness or inability to reckon with colonialism may explain its strange, even pathological identification with the anxieties of its former subjects. The fear of foreign settlement, demographic change, and cultural swamping all echo the language once used in colonized societies of Asia and Africa, where the Christian West was regarded as precisely such a threat. This switching of places is apparent in portrayals of Islam as both an alien and more virile force than Western liberalism, a force whose supposed cohesion and will to dominate must be countered by weapons of solidarity and domination.
European politics has thus increasingly begun to appropriate the defensive posture of the peoples Europe once ruled. Perverse though this identification may be, it reveals the extent to which decolonization—itself part of the Cold War’s history— has become the century’s central historical drama. This switching of places is especially true of Islam seen as an alien but also more virile force than Western liberalism, one whose power thus needs to be countered by its own weapons of solidarity and domination.
For all the spectacle of its asymmetric attacks, Al Qaeda—and Islamist militancy more broadly—never had more than some tens of thousands of committed supporters worldwide. These movements did not emerge from some hermetically sealed Islamic history. They belonged to global events and narratives, which gave them what influence they possessed. The disproportion between their small numbers and enormous consequences cannot be explained primarily by technology, mass media or even the war on terror. It arose from the institutional and political vulnerabilities exposed by the Cold War’s belated conclusion.
We now live amid the detritus of the end of the Cold War and are able to recognize decolonization as the crucial event of the 20th century. Its legacy animates both movements seeking greater inclusion and campaigns promising to restore a national unity defined in racial or cultural terms. More than three decades after the Soviet Union’s collapse, we still live in the wake of the Cold War, an aftermath that first revealed its force in the attacks of Sept. 11, 2001 on New York and Washington, D.C.

articles.title: Israeli strike kills parents and two children in Gaza
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israeli strike kills parents and two children in Gaza, medics say
An Israeli airstrike killed a man, his wife, and their two daughters, aged 8 and 12, in a house in the northern Gaza Strip on Thursday, health officials said, after the Israeli military escalated bombardments over the past two days.
Health officials and relatives in Gaza confirmed the killing of Muamen Ahmed, alongside his wife an children.
At Gaza's Al Shifa Hospital, friends and relatives flocked to pay their respect as the white-shrouded bodies of the family members were laid on the ground before being taken to burials.
Zuhair Al-Haisami, a neighbour of the victims, said an airstrike had hit their home at 2 a.m., while they were sleeping.
"There isn't any truce," he said. "Not a single day passes without martyrs, or (people being) injured," he added.
An October 2025, U.S.-backed ceasefire halted large-scale fighting, but it has not ended Israeli strikes and there has been little progress on steps towards permanent peace.
Hamas accuses Israel of violating the ceasefire and undermining efforts to implement U.S. President Donald Trump's broader plan to end the Gaza conflict, which includes the Israeli withdrawal from the strip and the disarmament of Hamas.
Israel claims Hamas has been violating the deal.
More than 1,300 Palestinians, mostly civilians, have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire took effect, according to the territory's health officials, while the Israeli military says four Israeli soldiers have been killed.
The Israeli military struck at least six homes across Gaza in the past two days, causing damage to nearby houses and tent shelters and forcing many families to flee, residents and medics said.
Some owners of the houses, or their neighbours, got a call from the military ordering them to leave the area shortly before missiles struck the buildings, residents said.
The Israeli military did not comment directly on the strikes on houses, but claimed on Tuesday and Wednesday it had hit and dismantled several weapons storage facilities belonging to Hamas and the Islamic Jihad group.
Ismail Al-Thawabta, director of the Gaza government media office, denied Israeli allegations, saying that Israel's targets were "the civilians and their homes."
More than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israel's genocidal campaign in the coastal enclave, most of them civilians, according to Gaza health authorities.

articles.title: “Weeks, Not Months”: Ukraine’s FP-7 Ballistic Missile Nears Battlefield Debut
articles.body:

“Weeks, Not Months”: Ukraine’s FP-7 Ballistic Missile Nears Battlefield Debut
Ukraine’s FP-7 ballistic missile is now in military trials and could enter operational use within weeks, while its longer-range FP-9 may ultimately have to prove itself the hard way—against real Russian targets.
Ukrainian defense company Fire Point has moved its FP-7 ballistic missile into military trials after successfully completing two earlier stages of testing, bringing the weapon potentially within weeks of operational use.
Fire Point CEO Iryna Terekh announced the milestone during the 34th International Defense Industry Exhibition MSPO, according to a UNITED24 Media correspondent on September 10.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Terekh, the FP-7 has already passed its first two testing phases and is now undergoing military evaluation, which is also part of the missile’s formal codification process.
The earlier stages included ground and laboratory testing, during which individual systems and subsystems were evaluated separately, including the rocket engine and navigation equipment.
“We are erasing the deep rear doctrine from the Russian military vocabulary,” said Terekh.
Flight testing followed, allowing engineers to collect data on the missile’s behavior in the air and determine how closely its actual performance matched design calculations.
The FP-7 has now advanced beyond those stages.
“We’re talking weeks, not months,” Terekh said when asked how soon the missile could move toward operational use.
Fire Point is simultaneously developing the longer-range FP-9 ballistic missile, which is currently undergoing flight testing and remains one stage behind the FP-7.
Testing the FP-9 presents a very different challenge because of its greater range.
According to the developers, the missile has a minimum distance required for ballistic flight. Once it passes a certain point in its trajectory, the test can no longer simply be terminated through software.
That makes conducting a complete test entirely within Ukrainian territory difficult.
As a result, once the current flight-testing phase is completed, the FP-9 could potentially move from testing into military evaluation through actual employment against Russian targets rather than following the same conventional test sequence as the shorter-range FP-7.
Earlier, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed hope that the US will support implementing the FREYJA anti-ballistic missile program, with the interceptor missile being built based on the Fire Point FP-7 ballistic missile.
“We are preparing our own FREYJA program. We very much hope that the Americans will support this program as well. But nevertheless, with the Europeans we will definitely achieve the desired result,” Zelenskyy said.

articles.title: Canada sanctions eight Russians over deported Ukrainian children as only about 2,500 of more than 20,000 have come home
articles.body:
Canada has sanctioned eight people over Russia's deportation of Ukrainian children and their indoctrination and militarization, Ukrinform reported on 11 September. It is the second Canadian package this year built around the removal of children from occupied areas. The measure surfaced during Ukraine's presidential visit to Canada, at a moment when Kyiv's own register counts far more children taken than brought home.
Eight names, and what Ottawa says they did
Canada's foreign ministry says all eight took part, now or earlier, in unlawfully deporting and transferring Ukrainian children, and in subjecting them to indoctrination and militarization. The department published the eight names without setting out the posts they hold. Its own register dates the listing's entry into force to 4 September.
The listing is an administrative measure, not a criminal charge. In most cases, people in Canada and Canadians abroad may not deal in a listed person's property or provide them financial services. Breaking those rules is a criminal offense, investigated by the border agency and the federal police.
Canada pledges more than $1 billion for Ukraine’s critical air defense as Russia intensifies missile and drone attacks
Canada's Ukraine-related listings cover more than 3,500 individuals and entities across its Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, and Moldova regulations. Its separate ship list reached 731 vessels in June, listed for shadow-fleet work moving sanctioned Russian oil, gas, and arms. The previous expansion, in August, hit a manufacturer of armored vehicles.
Thousands of children taken, about 2,000 home
Russia has deported or displaced 20,651 Ukrainian children since February 2022, and Ukraine has brought just over 2,000 of them home through the Bring Kids Back UA initiative. Officials believe the real figure is far higher.
Russian authorities have moved groups of Ukrainian teenagers through military-patriotic camps, occupation schools, and youth movements in occupied areas and inside Russia, and Ukraine has named the people running that work.

articles.title: BRICS Summit 2026: Putin, Modi reaffirm partnership
articles.body:
BRICS Summit 2026: Putin, Modi reaffirm partnership
Published September 11, 2026last updated September 11, 2026
What you need to know
Here is a roundup of some of the top headlines from the BRICS Summit 2026 in India.
- Putin and Modi discussed a wide range of issues including the Ukraine-Russia conflict, energy cooperation and trade across several sectors
- In the evening, Modi is expected to hold bilateral talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Modi, Putin reaffirm partnership on issues of mutual interest
Indian PM Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin held bilateral talks on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit that will begin on Saturday.
The two leaders "exchanged views on India-Russia engagement in the multilateral sphere, in particular in BRICS under India’s Chairship for 2026," a statement by India's Ministry of External Affairs said.
In the meeting, the leaders also exchanged views on "key regional and global issues of mutual interest, including the conflicts in West Asia and the Black Sea region which have impacted maritime trade and the safety and security of Indian seafarers."
Reaffirming their ties, the two leaders committed to "remain engaged in an effort to strengthen further the Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership between the two countries," the statement added.
Pezeshkian arrives for BRICS Summit
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian landed in Delhi to attend the BRICS Summit.
This is the first visit by an Iranian President to India in over eight years.
Pezeshkian is scheduled to hold bilateral talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi at 6.15 p.mz. local time Friday to advance two-way trade and strengthen overall ties.
His participation at the BRICS Summit and bilateral talks with Modi holds significance as it comes at a time when tensions are rife in the Middle East and energy market disruptions have shaken the economy worldwide.
WATCH — India's difficult BRICS chairship
With BRICS nations now representing nearly 3.7 billion people and close to 40% of global GDP, leaders are meeting amid rising geopolitical tensions, trade disputes and energy challenges.
While the expanded bloc is seeking a stronger voice in the global economy, disagreements over an alternative payment system and China's dominant role could test unity. Renewable energy and green infrastructure financing are emerging as key areas to watch.
Former UN diplomat: BRICS is 'voice of Global South,' but 'contradictions remain'
Speaking to DW about the BRICS Summit, former UN diplomat Shashi Tharoor said that the expansion of the bloc has made it the voice of the Global South.
The BRICS coalition started out with four member countries; Brazil, Russia, India and China but now has 11 members and partner countries after the economic bloc decided to open up membership for more countries in 2023.
Tharoor noted that while Iran joined the coalition, US strategic partners Egypt and Ethiopia also joined
"The expansion that took place in Johannesburg turned out to be one in which both sets of geopolitical points of view were accommodated," Tharoor noted in an interview with DW.
He argued that, "in some ways the expansion has made it much more the voice of the global south."
However, he also said that while the majority of the world is represented in the new 11-member BRICS, the chances of having a consensus has also decreased.
"I would say that BRICS is functioning, but the contradictions remain, and some contradictions have become even more apparent," he said.
He said that when BRICS leaders met this year, they "could not agree on any particular language, and so the chair, India, issued a chair statement instead… it wasn't just Iran, it was also Ukraine that they couldn't agree on."
Tharoor noted that the bloc has a "built-in set of geopolitical divergences which will crop up whenever issues divide the members."
Piyush Goyal proposes 'borderless' digital trade at BRICS
Indian Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal on Friday urged BRICS member countries to link their payment systems, encourage trade in local currencies, and make digital trade more accessible globally.
Addressing the opening ceremony of the BRICS Business Forum on Friday, Goyal highlighted India's digital payments ecosystem, including the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), as a potential foundation for deeper cross-border financial cooperation among BRICS economies.
"Today, it is also accepted in 11 countries and I would urge the Brics member countries and partner countries to link our payment systems, trade in each other's local currencies, make digital trade global and build together for the future emerging technologies," Goyal said as reported by Indian newspaper Deccan Herald.
Modi, Putin to meet on the sidelines of BRICS
Russian President Vladimir Putin landed in Delhi on Friday to attend the BRICS Summit being held at the Bharat Mandapam on September 12 and 13.
He will be meeting Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in the afternoon. Talks are expected to focus on enhancing cooperation in a range of areas, including defence, energy, technology, pharmaceuticals and people-to-people exchanges.
"Warmly welcome President Vladimir Putin of Russia for the 18th BRICS Summit. He was received by MoS K V Singh at the airport. India and Russia share multifaceted and longstanding ties anchored in Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership," Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said in a post on X.
This is Putin's first in-person participation at a BRICS Summit held outside Russia since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Later in the evening, Modi will also be holding a bilateral talk with Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian.
Welcome to our coverage
Hello! This is Midhat from the New Delhi bureau, bringing you the biggest headlines emerging from across India.
With just one day to go before the BRICS Summit kicks off, Delhi is all geared up and welcoming the dignitaries — several of whom have already arrived in the capital, including Russian President Vladimir Putin.
From Friday onwards, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi will be holding bilateral talks with several leaders, including China's Xi Jinping, Iran's Masoud Pezeshkian and Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.
Security in the capital has been intensified with thousands of personnel deployed. All schools in Delhi, including government, and private schools will remain closed on September 11 due to the BRICS Summit.
Commuters in Delhi will see traffic restrictions and diversions over the bext three days. Authorities have advised travelers to plan journeys and use the Metro where possible.
Stay tuned as we bring you more on the BRICS Summit and everything else making a buzz in the country.

articles.body:
Ahmad Adil
11 September 2026•Update: 11 September 2026
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday told Russian President Vladimir Putin that “dialogue and diplomacy” remains the way forward in resolving conflicts, as Ukraine and Iran wars continue.

Putin arrived in India’s capital early Friday, and is scheduled to hold a number of meetings on the sidelines of the summit.

articles.title: Anthropic reveals five biological weapon risk cases
articles.body:
Anthropic reveals five biological weapon risk cases
Anthropic says it has caught scientists using its AI models for research that could help develop biological weapons, including work aimed at making dangerous pathogens more transmissible and harmful.
Five cases of biological researchers using Claude raised serious security concerns, according to a company threat intelligence report published on Thursday.
One case, to be carried out at a military research institute, involved gain-of-function research aimed at making the chikungunya virus more transmissible and better able to evade the immune system.
Another scientist used Claude while researching highly dangerous bird flu and ways the virus could adapt to mammals. Other cases involved work on viruses related to smallpox and the redesign of dangerous toxins.
Anthropic said some of the researchers went to considerable lengths to get around its restrictions, including hiding their identities, routing traffic through other countries and using services designed to bypass safety controls. The accounts involved have been banned while the services used to get around the safeguards have been shut down.
The company stopped short of saying the scientists were definitely trying to build biological weapons. However, it warned that sophisticated actors may deliberately hide malicious aims behind legitimate-looking research.
Anthropic acknowledged that its AI is becoming more capable, saying older models were too weak to meaningfully assist sophisticated users with dangerous biological research, but that it can no longer make the same assurance about today’s systems.
The findings come just weeks after US scientists used AI to design complete viral genomes and successfully created 16 functioning viruses that did not previously exist in nature. Although those viruses infected bacteria rather than humans, researchers have warned that the experiment demonstrates how quickly AI’s biological capabilities are advancing.
Anthropic’s report also detailed other alleged misuse of Claude, including cyberattacks, surveillance, propaganda, fraud and assistance with conventional weapons such as missiles, armed drones and bombs.
Just days before the threat assessment was published, Anthropic researcher Evan Hubinger publicly stated that he believes there is a greater than 10% chance AI could “kill all humans” within the next decade, adding that the company still has no clear plan for safely controlling superintelligence.
His admission came after another Anthropic researcher, Jacob Coxon, resigned, accusing Anthropic and OpenAI of ignoring the “civilizational stakes” and “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” He separately warned that sufficiently advanced AI could hack critical infrastructure or help create “extinction-level bioweapons.”

Zelensky: Canada’s anti-ballistic sanctions could take effect in October
The Ukrainian President said this while speaking to media representatives in Canada, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
“Canada is preparing several important packages of sanctions against Russia. First, it is important to accelerate the anti-ballistic sanctions. These are precisely the sanctions that will make it more difficult for Russia to produce ballistic missiles,” Zelensky said.
He noted that efforts should simultaneously be made to secure Patriot missiles and to increase pressure on every Russian enterprise and every Russian contractor in other countries that helps the aggressor state manufacture ballistic missiles.
“Canada is preparing such an anti-ballistic sanctions package for the fall. I want to thank them for this. We very much hope that the package will be accelerated so that it can take effect as early as October,” the President said.
Zelensky added that Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry and sanctions coordinators are also working with other countries to introduce anti-ballistic sanctions.
“I thank Canada for imposing sanctions on all those individuals and all those enterprises that Russia uses to prevent the return of our Ukrainian children, stolen from our land, from our occupied cities and villages,” he said.
Zelensky noted that thousands of Ukrainian children remain in Russia and must be brought home. He expressed gratitude to Canada for supporting initiatives by Ukraine’s First Lady aimed at returning and helping the children abducted by Russia adapt after their return.
As Ukrinform reported, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in Canada yesterday for a three-day visit. During the visit, the two countries signed a number of bilateral documents, including the 100-Year Partnership Declaration.

Violence erupts in Yemen again: why it matters globally and how it is linked to the US-Iran war
Houthis try to take control of more of Yemen’s Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed government, giving Iran and its allies control over a key shipping lane
Violence has erupted again in Yemen, killing and wounding around 1,000 people and displacing tens of thousands. It is the most significant fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces in years.
Saudi Arabia and the Houthis have targeted each other with air, missile and drone strikes, threatening to open another front in the US-Iran war. At stake is the balance of power in Yemen, as well as another waterway critical to global shipping.
Though the immediate catalyst for the fighting has been the US-Iran war, it stems from years of conflict in Yemen itself.
Who are the warring parties in Yemen’s civil war and who are their backers?
The two main parties fighting in Yemen’s civil war are the Yemeni government forces alongside their allies, and the Houthi movement. Yemen’s government controls the north-east of the country, and its southern port. The government is the internationally-recognised authority in the country, but is chiefly backed by Saudi Arabia and a coalition of Arab countries which intervened on behalf of the government during Yemen’s civil war.
The Saudi-led coalition, in addition to supporting the Yemeni government forces, directly intervenes militarily in the country, mainly through airstrikes.
The government’s control of the country is contested by the Houthis, who hold the western part of the country, including its capital, Sana’a. The Shia group is broadly aligned with Iran and comprises part of the “axis of resistance”, a coalition of Iran-aligned armed groups in the Middle East, such as Hezbollah. But while the group is aligned ideologically with Iran, which supplies some arms shipments, the Houthis are considered an independent group with their own policies.
A variety of smaller armed groups are also active in the country.
How did the war in Yemen begin?
The civil war began in 2014 when fighting broke out between the Houthis and the Yemeni army after Houthi supporters were shot at during mass protests against fuel subsidy cuts in the capital, Sana’a. The Houthis promptly seized the capital, and by 2015 had toppled the government.
A coalition of mostly Arab countries, led by Saudi Arabia, then intervened on behalf of the ousted government, with a mostly aerial campaign that was widely criticised for its deadly impact on the civilians of Yemen.
The Yemeni government declared the southern port city of Aden to be its temporary capital, while the Houthis continued to maintain their control over Sana’a and much of the rest of north-west Yemen.
The government-aligned side was made up of several groups that fractured over the course of the war, primarily along the lines of their two chief backers: Saudi Arabia, which backed the Yemeni government itself, and the United Arab Emirates, which mainly supported the Southern Transitional Council (STC) and the Joint Forces.
The country also fractured, with al-Qaida seizing territory in east Yemen, and separatist groups, such as the STC, pushing for division of the country. The Saudi-led coalition also brought foreign mercenaries into the conflict.
Frontlines hardened and the war entered a deadlock. The Saudi-led coalition’s intervention was becoming increasingly unpopular internationally and had not led to the defeat of the Houthis. Weary of fighting, warring parties agreed to a temporary UN-mediated truce in 2022. The truce was extended twice, and calm largely held across the country until this September.
Why has the UN-brokered peace plan broken down?
The peace plan has been strained since the war in Gaza started on 7 October 2023. Israel launched the war in response to a Hamas-led attack in Israel that killed around 1,200 people. Israel’s war in Gaza, which has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians and earned widespread condemnation for what a UN committee said was genocide, drew the axis of resistance into the fray.
The Houthis, in what it said was a move of solidarity with the people of Gaza, began targeting ships in the Red Sea that it said were heading for Israel. The western coast of Yemen occupies a strategic position for global shipping because it overlooks Bab al-Mandab, a strait that links the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean.
The Houthi campaign brought about a US military intervention and strained the truce in Yemen. At the same time, its intervention brought the Houthis support regionally and within the territory they hold.
With the Houthis’ position strengthened, the group stopped seriously engaging in negotiations, frustrating Saudi Arabia.
In July, an Iranian plane landed in Sana’a airport, despite the protests of the Yemeni government, leading Saudi Arabia to strike the airport. The Houthis then declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea, a key route for Saudi oil since Iran closed the strait of Hormuz in March.
Why did fighting start again last week?
Last week the Houthis launched a wide-ranging offensive to take parts of the western coast of Yemen and gain a more strategic position over Bab al-Mandab. Fighting then broke out across multiple fronts in Yemen as the Saudi-backed government forces tried to reconsolidate their position, with clashes starting in al-Jawf, al-Baydaa, Taiz and Hodeida.
The Yemeni government forces then released a statement saying they were launching their own campaign to try to retake Sana’a from the Houthis.
It was the most significant fighting in the country since the UN-brokered peace plan in 2022.
What has been the humanitarian impact of the war?
The war in Yemen, and the Saudi-led coalition aerial campaign in particular, has devastated the country’s population. At least 150,000 people have been killed since 2014 by fighting alone, while hundreds of thousands more have died from related causes, such as hunger and disease. About 4.5 million people have been displaced by fighting and more than 18.2 million are in dire need of humanitarian assistance, according to the UN.
The renewed fighting has further exacerbated humanitarian conditions. The World Health Organization said the latest clashes have killed or wounded more than 1,000 people and displaced tens of thousands.
Why is Bab al-Mandab emerging as a new flashpoint in the region?
Bab al-Mandab is a critical waterway for shipping, with about 10% of global maritime trade passing through the strait. It has become more important since the US started its war against Iran and the latter closed the strait of Hormuz.
The Red Sea, via Bab al-Mandab, has become a vital lifeline for Saudi Arabia to export its oil. If the Houthis gained control over the strait, the group would be able to virtually close shipping through the waterway, or charge tolls. It would give Iran and its allies control over two key shipping lanes in the region.

articles.title: Canada unveils US$254 million air defence package for Ukraine
articles.body:
Canada unveils US$254 million air defence package for Ukraine
Kyiv is running critically low on US-made Patriot interceptors, as Russia steps up its ballistic missile attacks
Canada has agreed to a C$350 million (US$254 million) aid package for Kyiv to acquire air defence interceptors, Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Thursday, after meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Kyiv is running critically low on US-made Patriot interceptors capable of stopping Russia’s ballistic missiles at a time when Moscow is stepping up its attacks.
“As Russia escalates its barbaric aerial warfare indiscriminately targeting civilian populations, Ukraine’s air defences are critical,” Carney told reporters in Calgary.
“Earlier today Canada and Ukraine finalised an agreement to deliver critical air defence interceptors … this C$350 million equipment package will help protect Ukraine’s people, infrastructure, and skies,” he said.
He did not give details of which interceptors would be delivered or when the aid would start flowing.
The weapons will be provided through a US programme that allows third-party nations to quickly buy and supply weapons such as Patriot missiles to Ukraine.

articles.title: SBU, National Police prevent illegal sale of about half a tonne of explosives in Kharkiv region
articles.body:
Military counterintelligence of Ukraine's Security Service (SBU), together with the National Police and with the support of the commander-in-chief of Ukraine's Armed Forces, has foiled an attempt to sell one of the largest batches of explosives on the black market since the start of the full-scale war, the SBU said.
"As a result of preemptive action in Kharkiv region, a commander of a unit within a mechanized brigade of Ukraine's Armed Forces was detained while attempting to illegally sell nearly 500 kg of TNT," the SBU said on Telegram on Friday.
The investigation found that the service member sought potential buyers through relevant Telegram channels and offered to personally deliver the "product" to clients in a service vehicle.
"SBU officers caught the suspect red-handed near a military unit in Chuhuiv district while he was selling the explosives," the agency said.
Investigators established that the suspect had stored the TNT in hideouts he had prepared in advance in a frontline area of the region, where his unit was temporarily deployed.
According to the SBU, the entire batch of explosives prepared for sale was seized from the suspect at the scene of his detention, along with a smartphone containing evidence of his contacts with clients.
The detainee has been notified of suspicion under Part 1, Article 263 of Ukraine's Criminal Code (illegal handling of weapons, ammunition or explosives).
The suspect is in custody.
Investigative actions are continuing to establish all the circumstances of the crime and identify everyone involved.
The operation was carried out under the procedural guidance of the Kharkiv Specialized Prosecutor's Office for Defense in the Eastern Region.

articles.title: Interior minister: Russia strikes busy shopping mall in central Pavlohrad
articles.body:
Russian troops struck a shopping and entertainment center in downtown Pavlohrad, Dnipropetrovsk region, in the middle of the day when the streets were crowded, killing two people and injuring at least 18, Head of Ukraine's Ministry of Internal Affairs Ivan Vyhovsky said.
"About an hour ago, the Russians struck a shopping and entertainment center in downtown Pavlohrad. It happened in the middle of the day, when the streets were crowded. We already have reports of two fatalities. My condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims. At least 18 people were injured. Rescue workers and police are on the scene," Vyhovsky said on his Telegram channel following a working visit to Dnipropetrovsk region.
According to him, the issues of responding to such attacks and protecting civilians were discussed during an expanded meeting in Dnipro. Participants included the head of Dnipropetrovsk Regional State Administration, Oleksandr Hanzha; representatives of the region's security and defense forces; members of parliament; and heads of units within the Ministry of Internal Affairs.
"Since the beginning of the year alone, the Russians have launched over 18,000 strikes on the region, mostly UAV attacks. Recently, the occupiers have intensified their attacks on food warehouses, residential neighborhoods, trains, and shopping malls," the Minister of Internal Affairs said.
During the meeting, participants also discussed ways to strengthen coordination, protect critical social infrastructure, and prepare for the fall and winter months. According to Vyhovsky, decisions and corresponding directives were adopted following the meeting.
In addition, during a business trip to Dnipropetrovsk region, the Minister of Internal Affairs visited combat units of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and met with National Guard members and border guards serving on one of the most challenging sections of the front line in Donetsk region.
He also held a meeting with Denys Prokopenko, who, according to Vyhovsky, recently took command of the Azov military group by decision of the President of Ukraine. The parties discussed the process of expanding the area of responsibility, the management decisions necessary for this, and the strengthening of logistical support.
Vyhovsky also held a meeting with commanders of State Border Guard Service units and National Guard brigades "Bureviy," "Rubizh," "Azov," "Chervona Kalyna," and "Liubart."
"The occupiers continue to attempt assault operations and seize territory. But our fighters' response is thwarting their plans," he said.
According to Vyhovsky, in August alone, servicemen from the Azov units of the First Corps of the National Guard neutralized more than 5,200 occupiers, hundreds of vehicles and armored vehicles, and thousands of drones. He also noted that counter-sabotage operations are proceeding successfully.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Russians strike Kyivstar building
articles.body:
Russian forces have been deliberately targeting gas stations in Kyiv throughout Friday, and also struck a Kyivstar company building, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
"Throughout the day, Russians have been deliberately striking gas stations in Kyiv. Two people were killed today from these strikes alone. My condolences to the families and loved ones of those killed. Nine more people were injured, including a rescuer who was hurt in a repeat strike. They also hit a Kyivstar company building," Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram.
Russian forces also struck Kyiv, Kirovohrad, Dnipropetrovsk, Odesa, Donetsk, Kherson, Kharkiv and Mykolaiv regions.
"We can't just wait while Russia refines its repertoire of killing. Right now we need maximum focus on covering the skies and finding solutions to protect people, and on scaling up our response to Russian drones," Zelenskyy said.
He thanked everyone helping to strengthen Ukraine's air force and air defense systems with the missiles they need.

articles.title: Tusk warns of future attacks after ‘direct threat’ averted at Poland-Ukraine border
articles.body:
Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk attends a press conference after a meeting of the Visegrád Group leaders in Bratislava, on Sept. 10, 2026. | Tomas Benedikovic/AFP via Getty Images
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said a ‘direct threat’ was averted at a border crossing with Ukraine on Wednesday night and warned of further incidents linked to Russia in the near future.
His comments came just one day after a Russian drone hit a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, killing two people and wounding several others.
“Last night, thanks to cooperation between our services and their Ukrainian counterparts, a direct threat to a border crossing was averted,” Tusk said in a press conference after a meeting of the Visegrád Group leaders in Bratislava Thursday.
Advertisement
Tusk did not provide any further details about the nature of the threat or which of the 18 border crossings between Poland and Ukraine was affected.
The prime minister added that the incident was just a taste of what is to come and noted he had received a “fairly precise report” from the CIA regarding possible events in the coming months.
“We must anticipate various scenarios; both Poland and all of Europe need to be prepared for different possibilities concerning the situation not only on the Russian-Ukrainian front but also along the EU’s eastern flank.”
The incident at the border crossing between Moldova and Ukraine’s Odesa region left two people dead, causing President Maia Sandu to call for further European air defense support for Ukraine.
Russia also struck a Moldova-Ukraine border crossing in August.
“As you know, Russia has already resorted to provocative attacks on border crossings—for instance, in Moldova. We expect similar actions targeting border crossings with Ukraine in other countries, including Poland,” said Tusk.
Advertisement
In August, after a briefing with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, he warned that “escalation from Russia’s side is progressing,” and called for more air support for Ukraine as it is “crucial for our security.”
He said the next six months would be decisive and made it clear that provocations against NATO members should not be ruled out.
The CIA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Israeli-made film about Gaza gets 25-minute ovation in Venice
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israeli-made film about Gaza gets 25-minute ovation at Venice premiere
A chilling new documentary about Israel's AI-powered mass killing of civilians in Gaza from two Oscar-winning Israeli filmmakers received a 25-minute ovation at its premiere at the Venice Film Festival on Thursday.
The audience clapped continuously for Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor after the screening, an AFP reporter witnessed, setting what is thought to be a new record in Venice after a 23-minute ovation for another film about Gaza last year.
In their film "NAZA", Abraham and Szor used conversations with 24 different Israeli military or intelligence whistleblowers who spoke on condition that their identities be protected.
"We are letting the soldiers and the officers speak about what they did," Abraham told AFP.
"The goal was very simple: we wanted to hear in as much detail as possible, how the systems of killing in Gaza looked like, how they operated."
The 80-minute film left many audience members stunned, with interviewees describing how they felt like they worked in a killing "factory" or a lethal video game.
"NAZA" draws its name from a euphemism used by Israeli intelligence to indicate the number of civilians that are expected to be killed in an airstrike.
It was described as an "urgent, gut-punch" by film magazine Screen, while The Hollywood Reporter said it inspired "outrage...indignity as well. Most certainly disgust, on a profound level, for the current Israeli regime".
Israel's bombardment of Gaza has killed more than 73,600 Palestinians and wounded over 174,500 others since October 2023, according to Gaza's health ministry, whose figures the United Nations deems reliable.
First-person testimony
The men and women featured in "NAZA", with their voices and faces digitally altered, detail an AI-powered system known as "Lavender" that was used to identify people for assassination.
"It was done on a mass scale, like a factory," one says, filmed like all of them at night on a roof terrace with an eerily quiet Tel Aviv as the background.
"Lavender" uses data from the mass surveillance of Gaza, where the entire telecommunications network is monitored by Israel, to identify targets based on their phone calls, movements and interactions.
"The systems parameters are so complex, it's hard to understand," one interviewee, who said he worked on the system, told the filmmakers.
Others describe the systematic destruction of civilian homes, the disregard for war and humanitarian laws, and a "general atmosphere" of "hatred" towards Palestinians.
"It's like a video game because everything is done remotely," one interviewee involved in identifying targets says at one point.
Another describes it as "insanely fun".
Gaza films
The result of a nearly three-year investigation, "NAZA" is the only documentary in competition at this year's Venice Film Festival, which wraps up on Saturday.
Along with Palestinian peers Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, Abraham and Szor won an Oscar in 2025 for their film "No Other Land" about Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank.
Their latest movie has been produced by Britain's Jim Wilson with help from Jonathan Glazer -- the team behind Auschwitz-set Oscar winner "The Zone of Interest" -- as well as Britain's Guardian newspaper.
The war in Gaza retains broad Israeli public support, but Abraham and Szor said they hoped it would encourage Western nations to drop their backing for Israel and apply pressure through sanctions.
"Those of us inside Israel and Palestine trying to fight for change, need it," Abraham told AFP. "You are weakening the people inside who are supporting human rights and a political solution by refusing to act."
Israel denies deliberately targeting civilians in Gaza, accusing Hamas of hiding among the population of the densely packed and besieged enclave where around two million people lived before the war. The Palestinian group rejects these claims.
Last year, "The Voice of Hind Rajab", a docu-drama about the killing of a five-year-old Palestinian girl by Israeli forces, picked up second prize at the festival after receiving a 23-minute standing ovation at its premiere.
Increasing numbers of top entertainment figures are openly criticising the far-right Israeli government, as part of a shift in public opinion in Western countries against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's policies.
Foreign journalists have been prevented from reporting from Gaza since the start of the conflict, except under tightly controlled conditions with the Israeli military.

articles.title: Anthropic foils AI surveillance targeting dissidents in China, Iran and West Africa
articles.body:
China, Iran among countries using AI to spy on dissidents and minorities, Anthropic says
Anthropic said Thursday it had disrupted several state-sponsored surveillance operations using its artificial intelligence models, warning of the growing AI use to target dissidents and minorities. The campaigns, detected between January and July, originated in China, Iran and West Africa and targeted diaspora communities, including Hong Kong pro-democracy activists.
Anthropic said Thursday it shut down multiple cases of state-sponsored surveillance operations that used its artificial intelligence (AI) models, and warned that governments and state-aligned actors are increasingly using AI to spy on ethnic minorities and dissidents.
The incidents were found and disrupted between January and July, and they originated in China, Iran and west Africa, Anthropic said in a report about misuse of its models.
These surveillance campaigns "targeted the same diaspora and dissident communities these regimes have historically targeted. These include pro-democracy figures in Hong Kong, Tibetan and Falun Gong communities across Asia, and Iranian minority communities and opponents of the Iranian regime abroad," the report said.
In one case, Iranian actors developed a way to identify people through their social media accounts; in another, a contractor working for Malian national security authorities used Claude "to design the underlying software that enabled the intelligence gathering."
"AI is now being used in place of an engineering workforce," the report said.
Anthropic also disrupted efforts by users to design weapons, conduct questionable biological research, and create dating scams.
The San Francisco-based AI lab also accused Chinese developers of deceptively using Claude to produce responses to user queries while simultaneously "distilling" that data to improve their own models.
Distilling is an industry term that refers to a process where one AI model is used to train another one.
Read moreOpenAI says its models solved one of math's hardest problems as researchers cry foul
Chinese developers have previously been accused of using that technique without permission, essentially stealing resources from American labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI.
Now Anthropic alleges that China's Moonshot and Deepseek have also secretly used Claude to generate answers given to its users.
"In one instance, over a ten-day period, Moonshot relayed almost 300,000 customer requests to Anthropic" through a "network of 5,380 fraudulent accounts, most of which appeared to be located in Singapore and Japan," the report said.
Some of that data contained sensitive user information, potentially in violation of privacy agreements.
"We do not know if Moonshot notified their customers that their requests were being rerouted to Anthropic and exposed to a third party," the report said.
Deepseek used similar techniques.
When it comes to the research Anthropic detected and blocked that was related to biological weapons, the intent of the actors was less clear-cut and the AI lab did not identify them.
"The individuals implicated in these case studies are working scientists. We do not assert that they intended harm, and identifying them or their labs could expose them to harm," the report said.
The scientific research in those cases involved work around the mosquito-born chikungunya virus, a "highly-pathogenic" strain of the bird flu, a family of viruses that include smallpox and mpox, venoms and other toxins.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)
